Choose the fixed $M$ so large that $\psi(s)\ge C_2s$ dominates this variation, the offset variation, and the height bound at the outer collar end. The logarithmic-slope term is now negative. On $s\le1/n$ it dominates $Cd$; on the rest of the collar the negative margin proportional to $s$ does so. The upper barrier is strict at every possible positive contact. Its slopes lie in $[Me^{-2A},M]$, an interval independent of $n$.

To check the comparison signs, at a negative interior minimum of $h-h_0$ the Hessian of $h$ dominates that of $h_0$, the gradients and $Z$ agree, and hence so do $t,l,A_\chi$. The right side is strictly increasing in the height. Thus a strict positive residual for a lower barrier contradicts the equation. At a positive maximum the inequalities reverse, proving the upper-barrier assertion. Taking the one-sided derivative at $s=0$ proves the black part of <a href="#n3:apriori:signed-slopes" data-reference-type="eqref" data-reference="n3:apriori:signed-slopes">[n3:apriori:signed-slopes]</a>. Replacing $(h,K,C)$ by $(-h,-K,-C)$ proves the white part.

In the third stage the boundary height is the assigned interpolated constant, say $b_\zeta$. Construct tests $b_\zeta+\psi(s)$ and $b_\zeta-\psi(s)$ with large positive $\psi'$ and $(\log\psi')'=-\beta_n$. At $s=0$, the two directional inequalities of Proposition <a href="#n3:deformation:homotopy" data-reference-type="ref" data-reference="n3:deformation:homotopy">23</a> say precisely that the positive-slope test has nonpositive limiting residual and the negative-slope test nonnegative limiting residual. At every comparison contact, the fixed positive barrier slope and Equation <a href="#n3:apriori:contact-degeneracy" data-reference-type="eqref" data-reference="n3:apriori:contact-degeneracy">[n3:apriori:contact-degeneracy]</a> give $d\le C\ell$, so $a\ge1/2$ for large $n$. On $1/2\le|w|\le1$, the first $w$-derivatives of $A_\chi$ in Equation <a href="#n3:deformation:axial-matrices" data-reference-type="eqref" data-reference="n3:deformation:axial-matrices">[n3:deformation:axial-matrices]</a> are bounded independently of $0\le p\le n$. The other collar terms have fixed smooth coefficients on the bounded height range. Thus, at fixed boundary height the coefficient and geometric errors are $O(s+d+\chi)$, since $|w-(\pm N)|=1-a\le d$ and the radial comparison segment stays in this range. Changing the test height supplies, by height monotonicity, a residual of magnitude at least $\psi(s)$ with the required sign. Large fixed slopes dominate the $O(s)$ error and the outer-end height bound. The logarithmic-slope term has the required sign for both tests, as follows from <a href="#n3:apriori:collar-trace" data-reference-type="eqref" data-reference="n3:apriori:collar-trace">[n3:apriori:collar-trace]</a>; it dominates the $O(d)$ error on the initial $1/n$ interval. The remaining margin dominates it beyond that interval. This proves the two-sided upper derivative bound, without using sublevel exclusion in the third stage.

Finally, on each own-color collar the lower barrier just constructed gives the required one-sided height bound. On the rest of a fixed compact region use Lemma <a href="#n3:apriori:sublevels" data-reference-type="ref" data-reference="n3:apriori:sublevels">29</a>; the opposite height bound on an own-color collar follows from that lemma as well, since the closed collar is disjoint from the other region. A finite cover proves $b_-\le h\le b_+$ on the compact regions in the statement. ◻

</details>

<a id="pm-h-33"></a>
###### A trace estimate with polynomial constants

The collar trace estimate must have polynomial constants: it will control the boundary flux both here and in the mass estimate. We therefore prove it before comparing with the ordinary product graph.

<a id="stmt-n3-apriori-trace"></a>
<div id="n3:apriori:trace" class="lemma">

<a id="n3:apriori:weighted-trace"></a>
<a id="n3:apriori:unweighted-trace"></a>
**Lemma 31** (Weighted and unweighted collar traces). *In the first two stages let $\mathcal C$ be a fixed union of disjoint collars of the inner faces, shortened if necessary. For every nonnegative smooth function $\varphi$ supported in those collars, $$\begin{aligned}
 \int_B L\varphi\,\mathrm dA_g
 &\le\Pi_n\int_{\mathcal C}u
       \bigl[(1+\sqrt{\mathcal T})\varphi
                          +|d\varphi|_{A_\chi}\bigr]\,\mathrm dV_g,
 \label{n3:apriori:weighted-trace}\\
 \int_B\varphi\,\mathrm dA_g
 &\le\Pi_n\int_{\mathcal C}\sqrt D
       \bigl[(1+\sqrt{\mathcal T})\varphi
                          +|d\varphi|_{A_\chi}\bigr]\,\mathrm dV_g.
 \label{n3:apriori:unweighted-trace}
\end{aligned}$$ The estimates also hold without a support condition on $\varphi$ if the right sides include a fixed collar cutoff equal to one on $B$, with its derivative included in the coefficient of $\varphi$.*

</div>

<details id="proof-stmt-n3-apriori-trace"><summary>Proof of stmt-n3-apriori-trace</summary>

<a id="n3:apriori:W-gradient"></a>
<a id="n3:apriori:W-divergence"></a>
<a id="n3:apriori:W-divergence-unweighted"></a>
*Proof.* For $\sigma>0$, write $e_f=\nabla f/\sigma$, the axis denoted by $e$ in Section <a href="#n3:deformation:section" data-reference-type="ref" data-reference="n3:deformation:section">4</a>. Set $$W=l\bar\nabla f=\frac{l\nabla f}{D}=\sqrt d\,a e_f.$$ Its norm in $\bar g$ is $a\le1$. For any covector $\xi$, $$|\xi(W)|\le |\xi|_{A_d}
                  \le\sqrt{1+n/4}\,|\xi|_{A_\chi}.
 \label{n3:apriori:W-gradient}$$ Direct differentiation, using $uW=Lw$, gives $$\begin{aligned}
 \frac{\mathop{\mathrm{div}}(uW)}u
 &=\sqrt d\left[
       \mathop{\mathrm{tr}}_{A_d}H^f+(dp+p_L)a\partial_{e_f}t\right],
 \label{n3:apriori:W-divergence}\\
 \frac{\mathop{\mathrm{div}}(\sqrt D\,W)}{\sqrt D}
 &=\sqrt d\left[
       \mathop{\mathrm{tr}}_{A_d}H^f+dp\,a\partial_{e_f}t\right].
 \label{n3:apriori:W-divergence-unweighted}
\end{aligned}$$ For example, $\mathop{\mathrm{div}}w=\mathop{\mathrm{tr}}_{A_d}H^f+dp\,a\partial_{e_f}t$, while differentiating $L$ adds $p_La\partial_{e_f}t$ to the first formula. Coercivity in Lemma <a href="#n3:deformation:coercivity" data-reference-type="ref" data-reference="n3:deformation:coercivity">21</a> bounds both right sides by $\Pi_n(1+\sqrt{\mathcal T})$. More explicitly, writing $q=(K+H^f)_{e_fe_f}$, the normal Hessian term has coefficient $d^{3/2}$, so it is bounded by $\sqrt d|q|+C$. The other Hessian terms are transverse traces, and the gradient term is at most $(2n+2)\sqrt d|\partial_{e_f}t|$. All are controlled by the stated coercivity estimate. This also establishes the formulas and bounds at zero gradient by their smooth direction-free extensions.

Let $\varepsilon_B=1$ on a black collar and $-1$ on a white collar. The signed slopes give $w_\nu=\varepsilon_B a$ on $B$ and $a\ge1/2$ for large $n$. Thus $$uW_\nu=\varepsilon_B La,
 \qquad \sqrt D\,W_\nu=\varepsilon_B a.$$ The outward integration normal is $-\nu$. Apply the divergence theorem to $-\varepsilon_B uW\varphi$, with a fixed collar cutoff. Its boundary flux is $La\varphi$. Equations <a href="#n3:apriori:W-gradient" data-reference-type="eqref" data-reference="n3:apriori:W-gradient">[n3:apriori:W-gradient]</a> and <a href="#n3:apriori:W-divergence" data-reference-type="eqref" data-reference="n3:apriori:W-divergence">[n3:apriori:W-divergence]</a>, and the fixed cutoff derivative, give <a href="#n3:apriori:weighted-trace" data-reference-type="eqref" data-reference="n3:apriori:weighted-trace">[n3:apriori:weighted-trace]</a>. Replace $u$ by $\sqrt D$ and use <a href="#n3:apriori:W-divergence-unweighted" data-reference-type="eqref" data-reference="n3:apriori:W-divergence-unweighted">[n3:apriori:W-divergence-unweighted]</a> for <a href="#n3:apriori:unweighted-trace" data-reference-type="eqref" data-reference="n3:apriori:unweighted-trace">[n3:apriori:unweighted-trace]</a>. No factor $\ell^{-1}$ was used. ◻

</details>

<a id="pm-h-34"></a>
###### High-level energy and the first upper bound

<a id="n3:apriori:high-source"></a>
The first stage contains the drift in the divergence equation. We first bound this stage uniformly for $\lambda\in[0,1]$. There is a number $M_0=M_0(n)>0$ such that $$\Xi\ge\delta_0\mathcal T+\rho+
                      \tfrac12\delta_0\tau a\sigma
          \quad\hbox{on }\{Z>M_0\}.
 \label{n3:apriori:high-source}$$ Indeed, outside the support of $m_0$ this is immediate. On its support, $-\epsilon\le t\le-\epsilon+1/n$, so $l$ is comparable to $\ell$. The identity $D=e^{8(Z-t)}$ shows that $a\sigma$ tends uniformly to infinity as $Z\to\infty$ in that band. The penalty $\mathcal P$ is bounded on the whole exterior by $\Pi_n$. It is therefore absorbed by $\delta_0\tau a\sigma/2$ above a fixed $M_0(n)$. This choice is independent of $R$ and $\lambda$.

Choose a smooth nondecreasing $k_0$ equal to zero on $Z\le M_0$, equal to one on $Z\ge M_0+1$, and with bounded derivative. Test $\mathop{\mathrm{div}}V_\lambda=u\Xi$ by $k_0(Z)$. Its outer boundary term vanishes since $Z=0$. The drift cross term is bounded by $$u k_0'\left|\langle dZ,K(w,\cdot)\rangle_{A_\chi}\right|
 \le 2u k_0'|dZ|_{A_\chi}^2+C u k_0'|K|^2.$$ The last term has bounded integral: it is supported on a fixed compact set and on $M_0\le Z\le M_0+1$, where the floor and $D=e^{8(Z-t)}$ bound $u$ and $\sigma$ by $C(n)$.

<a id="n3:apriori:small-boundary-flux"></a>
<a id="n3:apriori:high-energy-before-trace"></a>
At a black face $F-P_B=H$, $w_\nu=a$; at a white face $F-P_B=-H$, $w_\nu=-a$. In both cases $$-H+w_\nu(F-P_B)=(a-1)H.$$ The additional omitted-drift term in the homotopy boundary condition has absolute value at most $C\chi\le Cd$, since $A_\chi K(w,\cdot)$ has normal component $\chi w_\nu K(\nu,\nu)$. The remaining term is $-N_Bd$, and the boundary multiplier lies between zero and one. Hence $$|(V_\lambda)_\nu|\le Cud=CL\sqrt d
                       \le C\frac\tau\ell L\quad\hbox{on }B,
 \label{n3:apriori:small-boundary-flux}$$ where the last inequality uses the lower slope in <a href="#n3:apriori:signed-slopes" data-reference-type="eqref" data-reference="n3:apriori:signed-slopes">[n3:apriori:signed-slopes]</a>. Integration now gives $$\begin{aligned}
 &\int_{\Omega_R}u k_0
       \left(\delta_0\mathcal T+\rho+
                      \tfrac12\delta_0\tau a\sigma\right)\,\mathrm dV_g
       +2\int_{\Omega_R}u k_0'|dZ|_{A_\chi}^2\,\mathrm dV_g\notag\\
 &\hspace{18mm}\le C(n)+C\frac\tau\ell
                                  \int_B Lk_0\,\mathrm dA_g.
 \label{n3:apriori:high-energy-before-trace}
\end{aligned}$$

<a id="n3:apriori:high-energy"></a>
Apply <a href="#n3:apriori:weighted-trace" data-reference-type="eqref" data-reference="n3:apriori:weighted-trace">[n3:apriori:weighted-trace]</a> with the fixed collar cutoff. The boundary cost is at most $$\Pi_n\frac\tau\ell\int_{\mathcal C}u
       \left[k_0(1+\sqrt{\mathcal T})
                              +k_0'|dZ|_{A_\chi}\right]\,\mathrm dV_g.$$ Let $\rho_{\mathcal C}>0$ be the minimum of $\rho$ on the closed collars. Pointwise, $1+\sqrt{\mathcal T}\le C(\rho+\delta_0\mathcal T)$ there, with $C$ fixed. Since $\Pi_n\tau/\ell\to0$, the first summand is absorbed in the first integral of <a href="#n3:apriori:high-energy-before-trace" data-reference-type="eqref" data-reference="n3:apriori:high-energy-before-trace">[n3:apriori:high-energy-before-trace]</a>. Young’s inequality bounds the derivative summand by $$u k_0'|dZ|_{A_\chi}^2+
          C(\Pi_n\tau/\ell)^2u k_0'.$$ The second term again has bounded compact integral because it lies in the transition strip of $k_0$. We obtain $$\int u k_0(\mathcal T+\rho+\tau a\sigma)\,\mathrm dV_g
       +\int u k_0'|dZ|_{A_\chi}^2\,\mathrm dV_g\le C(n).
 \label{n3:apriori:high-energy}$$ The smallness requirement on $n$ in this absorption is independent of $M_0$; only its resulting right-hand constant depends on $M_0$.

<a id="n3:apriori:L2"></a>
The polynomial boundary absorption is complete. We may now use arbitrary fixed-$n$ comparison constants. Write $\Gamma$ for the ordinary product graph of $f$ in $g+(\,\mathrm db_0)^2$, and $\,\mathrm d\Gamma=\sqrt{1+\sigma^2}\,\mathrm dV_g$. The measures $\,\mathrm d\Gamma$ and $\sqrt D\,\mathrm dV_g$ are comparable by constants depending only on $\ell$. On every fixed compact set $Q$, $$\int_{\Gamma\cap\pi^{-1}(Q)}e^{2Z}\,\mathrm d\Gamma\le C_Q(n),
 \label{n3:apriori:L2}$$ where $\pi$ is projection to the base. To check this without an upper bound for $t$, observe that $$e^{2Z}=e^{2t}D^{1/4},\qquad u=le^{2t}\sqrt D,
 \qquad D^{1/4}\le C(n)(1+\tau a\sigma).$$ The last inequality follows by splitting $l\sigma\le1$ and $l\sigma>1$, using $\ell\le l\le e$; on the second set $a\ge1/\sqrt2$ and the right side grows linearly in $\sigma$, whereas $D^{1/4}$ grows at most as $C\sqrt\sigma$. Thus the high-level part of <a href="#n3:apriori:L2" data-reference-type="eqref" data-reference="n3:apriori:L2">[n3:apriori:L2]</a> follows from <a href="#n3:apriori:high-energy" data-reference-type="eqref" data-reference="n3:apriori:high-energy">[n3:apriori:high-energy]</a> and the positive minimum of $\rho$ on $Q$. On $Z\le M_0+1$, both $\sigma$ and $e^{2Z}$ are bounded by the floor identity, which controls the remaining compact integral.

<a id="pm-h-35"></a>
###### Sobolev inequality and iteration on the ordinary graph

The comparisons in this subsection are uniform in the solution, $R$, and the homotopy parameter, but may depend arbitrarily on $n$. If $d_0=(1+\sigma^2)^{-1}$, then $$|d\varphi|_{A_{d_0}}=|\nabla_\Gamma\varphi|,
 \qquad
 \frac{d}{d_0}=\frac{1+\sigma^2}{1+l^2\sigma^2}.$$ The last ratio is bounded above and below by constants depending only on $\ell$; Equation <a href="#n3:apriori:parameter-comparisons" data-reference-type="eqref" data-reference="n3:apriori:parameter-comparisons">[n3:apriori:parameter-comparisons]</a> therefore compares $A_{d_0},A_d,A_\chi$ without any bound for $Z$.

<a id="stmt-n3-apriori-sobolev"></a>
<div id="n3:apriori:sobolev" class="lemma">

**Lemma 32** (Local graph Sobolev inequality). *For a smooth function $\omega$ supported over a fixed compact base patch, which may meet an inner face, <a id="n3:apriori:sobolev-equation"></a>$$\|\omega\|_{L^6(\,\mathrm d\Gamma)}^2
 \le C(n)\int_\Gamma
       \left[|\nabla_\Gamma\omega|^2+
                            (1+\mathcal T)\omega^2\right]\,\mathrm d\Gamma.
 \label{n3:apriori:sobolev-equation}$$*

</div>

<details id="proof-stmt-n3-apriori-sobolev"><summary>Proof of stmt-n3-apriori-sobolev</summary>

*Proof.* Extend the fixed base patch smoothly and embed a compact enlargement isometrically in Euclidean space by Nash’s embedding theorem (Nash 1956, Theorem 2) <a id="pm-cite-18"></a>[[Nash1956](#ref-Nash1956)]. Its product with the vertical line gives an isometric Euclidean immersion of the graph. The second fundamental form of the base embedding is bounded, so its contribution to the graph mean curvature vector is bounded. The scalar mean curvature in the product is $$H_\Gamma=
 \frac{\sqrt D}{l\sqrt{1+\sigma^2}}
       \left(\mathop{\mathrm{tr}}_{e_f^\perp}H^f+d_0H^f(e_f,e_f)\right).$$ The prefactor is bounded by $C(n)$, and $d_0/\sqrt d=\sqrt{1+l^2\sigma^2}/(1+\sigma^2)\le e$. Coercivity therefore gives $|\boldsymbol H_\Gamma|\le C(n)(1+\sqrt{\mathcal T})$. This estimate involves controlled quadratic energy, not a pointwise bound for the Hessian.

The ordinary Michael–Simon inequality (Michael and Simon 1973) <a id="pm-cite-19"></a>[[MichaelSimon1973](#ref-MichaelSimon1973)], in the compact-support form stated in (Simon 2014, chap. 4, Section 5, Theorem 5.7) <a id="pm-cite-20"></a>[[Simon2014](#ref-Simon2014)], gives after the boundary extension described below, for nonnegative $\varphi$, $$\left(\int_\Gamma\varphi^{3/2}\,\mathrm d\Gamma\right)^{2/3}
 \le C\left[
       \int_\Gamma(|\nabla_\Gamma\varphi|
                          +|\boldsymbol H_\Gamma|\varphi)\,\mathrm d\Gamma
       +\int_{\partial\Gamma}\varphi\,\mathrm dA\right].$$ One can obtain the boundary form directly from the compact-support version by smoothly extending each smooth graph across its boundary and cutting off on a collar tending to zero: the cutoff derivative integral converges to the boundary integral, and the added curvature integral tends to zero. This argument is applied to each smooth graph before the uniform estimate is taken. The only boundary in the support is an inner face, where $f$ is constant and $\,\mathrm dA=\,\mathrm dA_g$. Equation <a href="#n3:apriori:unweighted-trace" data-reference-type="eqref" data-reference="n3:apriori:unweighted-trace">[n3:apriori:unweighted-trace]</a> and the fixed-$n$ graph comparisons bound its contribution by $$C(n)\int_\Gamma
       [(1+\sqrt{\mathcal T})\varphi
                               +|\nabla_\Gamma\varphi|]\,\mathrm d\Gamma.$$ Apply the resulting inequality to $\varphi=|\omega|^4$. Cauchy–Schwarz bounds its right side by $$C(n)\|\omega\|_6^3
 \left(\int_\Gamma
       [|\nabla_\Gamma\omega|^2+(1+\mathcal T)\omega^2]
                                      \,\mathrm d\Gamma\right)^{1/2}.$$ The left side is $\|\omega\|_6^4$; division, with the zero case separate, and squaring prove the assertion. ◻

</details>

To turn the integral bound into an upper bound, let $\eta$ be a nonnegative cutoff over a fixed compact patch. For $k$ sufficiently large, independently of $R$ and the solution, test the first-stage divergence equation by $$q=\eta^2e^{2kZ}/L.$$ The positive measure after cancellation of $L$ is $\sqrt D\,\mathrm dV_g$. The differentiated test is $$dq=\frac{e^{2kZ}}L
       [2\eta\,d\eta+\eta^2(2k\,dZ-p_L\,dt)].$$ Its principal exponential contribution is $8k\eta^2e^{2kZ}|dZ|_{A_\chi}^2$. The source is bounded below by $\delta_0\mathcal T-\Pi_n$ everywhere. Coercivity and $A_\chi\le A_d$ give $$4p_L|\langle dt,dZ\rangle_{A_\chi}|
 \le\tfrac14\delta_0\mathcal T+C(n)|dZ|_{A_\chi}^2.$$ Choose $k\ge k_*(n)$ so that the second term is absorbed by the principal contribution. The drift terms, with $|K(w,\cdot)|_{A_\chi}
\le |K|$, obey $$\begin{aligned}
 2k|\langle K(w,\cdot),dZ\rangle_{A_\chi}|
   &\le k|dZ|_{A_\chi}^2+Ck|K|^2,\\
 p_L|\langle K(w,\cdot),dt\rangle_{A_\chi}|
   &\le\tfrac14\delta_0\mathcal T+C(n)|K|^2.
\end{aligned}$$ The cutoff cross terms are handled by the same Cauchy inequalities, leaving $C(n)k e^{2kZ}(|d\eta|_g^2+\eta^2)$. The penalty is bounded and contributes to this latter expression. Finally, Equation <a href="#n3:apriori:small-boundary-flux" data-reference-type="eqref" data-reference="n3:apriori:small-boundary-flux">[n3:apriori:small-boundary-flux]</a> before its last inequality gives $|q(V_\lambda)_\nu|\le C\eta^2e^{2kZ}\sqrt d
\le C\eta^2e^{2kZ}$. Converting to the ordinary graph yields <a id="n3:apriori:iteration-energy-boundary"></a>$$\begin{aligned}
 &\int_\Gamma e^{2kZ}\eta^2
       (\mathcal T+k|\nabla_\Gamma Z|^2)\,\mathrm d\Gamma\notag\\
 &\quad\le C(n)k\int_\Gamma e^{2kZ}
                (\eta^2+|d\eta|_g^2)\,\mathrm d\Gamma
               +C(n)\int_B e^{2kZ}\eta^2\,\mathrm dA_g.
 \label{n3:apriori:iteration-energy-boundary}
\end{aligned}$$

<a id="n3:apriori:iteration-energy"></a>
Use the unweighted trace with $\varphi=e^{2kZ}\eta^2$. The boundary term is at most $$C(n)\int_\Gamma e^{2kZ}
   \left[\eta^2(1+\sqrt{\mathcal T}
                   +k|\nabla_\Gamma Z|)+\eta|d\eta|_g\right]
                                                   \,\mathrm d\Gamma.$$ Young’s inequality absorbs its $\sqrt{\mathcal T}$ term into the $\mathcal T$ integral and its $k|\nabla_\Gamma Z|$ term into the $k|\nabla_\Gamma Z|^2$ integral. The latter absorption costs $C(n)k\eta^2e^{2kZ}$, which has the allowed size. Hence $$\int_\Gamma e^{2kZ}\eta^2
       (\mathcal T+k|\nabla_\Gamma Z|^2)\,\mathrm d\Gamma
 \le C(n)k\int_\Gamma e^{2kZ}
                   (\eta^2+|d\eta|_g^2)\,\mathrm d\Gamma,
 \label{n3:apriori:iteration-energy}$$ with constants independent of $k\ge k_*$.

<a id="n3:apriori:moser-step"></a>
<a id="n3:apriori:moser-interpolation"></a>
Apply Lemma <a href="#n3:apriori:sobolev" data-reference-type="ref" data-reference="n3:apriori:sobolev">32</a> to $\omega=\eta e^{kZ}$ and use <a href="#n3:apriori:iteration-energy" data-reference-type="eqref" data-reference="n3:apriori:iteration-energy">[n3:apriori:iteration-energy]</a>. For nested base patches $U_r\subset U_{r'}$ and a cutoff satisfying $|d\eta|_g\le C/(r'-r)$, this gives $$\|e^Z\|_{L^{6k}(\Gamma|_{U_r})}
 \le\left[C(n)k^2(1+(r'-r)^{-2})\right]^{1/(2k)}
                  \|e^Z\|_{L^{2k}(\Gamma|_{U_{r'}})}.
 \label{n3:apriori:moser-step}$$ Here $\Gamma|_U$ denotes the part of the graph projecting to $U$. Iterate with $k_j=3^jk_*$ and radii decreasing geometrically from $r'$ to $r$. The sums $\sum k_j^{-1}$ and $\sum j/k_j$ are finite. Taking the product in <a href="#n3:apriori:moser-step" data-reference-type="eqref" data-reference="n3:apriori:moser-step">[n3:apriori:moser-step]</a> therefore gives <a id="n3:apriori:moser-high-norm"></a>$$S(r):=\sup_{U_r}e^Z
 \le C(n)(r'-r)^{-A(n)}
             \|e^Z\|_{L^{2k_*}(\Gamma|_{U_{r'}})}.
 \label{n3:apriori:moser-high-norm}$$ Take all these patches inside a slightly larger fixed patch on which <a href="#n3:apriori:L2" data-reference-type="eqref" data-reference="n3:apriori:L2">[n3:apriori:L2]</a> holds. Increasing $k_*$ to at least two, interpolation gives $$\|e^Z\|_{2k_*}
 \le S(r')^{1-1/k_*}
                  \left(\int e^{2Z}\,\mathrm d\Gamma\right)^{1/(2k_*)}.$$ Thus $S(r)\le C(n)(r'-r)^{-A(n)}S(r')^{1-1/k_*}$. For every $\alpha>0$, Young’s inequality makes this $$S(r)\le\alpha S(r')+
                   C(n,\alpha)(r'-r)^{-A(n)k_*}.
 \label{n3:apriori:moser-interpolation}$$ Choose radii increasing geometrically to a fixed outer radius $r_1$, and then choose $\alpha<2^{-A(n)k_*-1}$. Iterating <a href="#n3:apriori:moser-interpolation" data-reference-type="eqref" data-reference="n3:apriori:moser-interpolation">[n3:apriori:moser-interpolation]</a> has a convergent geometric sum. Its final remainder $\alpha^jS(r_j)$ tends to zero, because each individual smooth solution is bounded on the closed outer patch. The resulting smaller-patch bound is independent of that individual supremum. A finite cover proves a uniform compact upper bound for $Z$, including at every inner face.

Beyond a fixed sphere containing the drift support, the equation is $\mathop{\mathrm{div}}(4uA_\chi\nabla Z)=u\Xi$, and $\Xi>0$ above $M_0$. At an interior maximum above $M_0$ its left side is nonpositive, because $dZ=0$ and $\mathop{\mathrm{Hess}}Z\le0$. The outer boundary value is zero. The compact bound on that fixed sphere consequently extends the first-stage upper bound to the whole truncation.

<a id="pm-h-36"></a>
###### The remaining stages and the bounded-variable conclusion

In the second and third stages the drift is zero. Their source has the same high-$Z$ positivity as <a href="#n3:apriori:high-source" data-reference-type="eqref" data-reference="n3:apriori:high-source">[n3:apriori:high-source]</a>, with a uniform threshold for the bounded homotopy range. By Lemma <a href="#n3:apriori:collars" data-reference-type="ref" data-reference="n3:apriori:collars">30</a>, on an inner face <a id="n3:apriori:high-boundary-t"></a>$$Z=t+\tfrac18\log(1+l^2\sigma^2)
       \le t+\tfrac18\log(1+e^2C_*^2/\tau^2).
 \label{n3:apriori:high-boundary-t}$$ Thus sufficiently high boundary $Z$ forces $j(t)=1$. The prescribed boundary flux is then zero, since $\lambda=0$. At the face $A_\chi\nu=\chi\nu$, so this is exactly $\partial_\nu Z=0$. The maximum principle excludes a high interior maximum, and the boundary point principle excludes a high maximum on a smooth inner face with this zero conormal derivative. Both principles are applied to the smooth individual solution on its finite domain; its coefficients are positive definite there. Locating the maximum requires no uniform ellipticity constant. The outer value is zero, so these two stages also have a uniform upper bound.

In the fourth stage $f=0$ and $t=Z$. When the common source/flux scale is positive, the same maximum and boundary argument works with its positive high-level source. At scale zero the homogeneous mixed problem and the outer zero Dirichlet value give $Z=0$. The upper bound is consequently uniform also as the scale tends to zero.

<a id="stmt-n3-apriori-bounds"></a>
<div id="n3:apriori:bounds" class="proposition">

**Proposition 33** (Bounds before regularity). *Fix the prepared data and $\epsilon>0$. There are $n_0$ and $R_{\min}(n)\to\infty$ such that, for each fixed $n\ge n_0$ and every $R\ge R_{\min}(n)$, all smooth solutions of the four-stage homotopy with $t\ge-\epsilon$ satisfy <a id="n3:apriori:bounded-variables"></a>$$|h|\le C_0,\qquad |f|\le C_0/\tau,\qquad
 -\epsilon\le t\le Z\le C(n),\qquad
 |\nabla f|\le C(n).
 \label{n3:apriori:bounded-variables}$$ The constants are uniform in $R$ and in the homotopy parameter. They include putative floor-contact solutions, which are then excluded by Proposition <a href="#n3:deformation:floor" data-reference-type="ref" data-reference="n3:deformation:floor">28</a>. The fixed signed slopes, the third-stage upper slopes, and the polynomial trace estimates are those of Lemmas <a href="#n3:apriori:collars" data-reference-type="ref" data-reference="n3:apriori:collars">30</a> and <a href="#n3:apriori:trace" data-reference-type="ref" data-reference="n3:apriori:trace">31</a>.*

</div>

<details id="proof-stmt-n3-apriori-bounds"><summary>Proof of stmt-n3-apriori-bounds</summary>

*Proof.* It remains to extract the bounds for the conformal variable and the gradient. Since $Z=t+\log D/8$ and $D\ge1$, the floor gives $-\epsilon\le t\le Z$. The upper bound for $Z$ gives $$\sigma^2=\frac{e^{8(Z-t)}-1}{l^2}
       \le\ell^{-2}\bigl(e^{8(C(n)+\epsilon)}-1\bigr).$$ This proves the asserted fixed-$n$ gradient bound. The height bounds are Lemma <a href="#n3:deformation:height" data-reference-type="ref" data-reference="n3:deformation:height">24</a>. The finite collection of sublevel and collar estimates and the polynomial absorption choose $n_0$ once. Enlarge $R_{\min}(n)$ to include the outer estimates and all fixed compact patches used above. The next section derives Hessian and continuity estimates from these bounds and uses them to prove existence. ◻

</details>

<a id="n3:existence:section"></a>
##### Regularity and existence of the elliptic deformation

We now pass from the bounded variables in Proposition <a href="#n3:apriori:bounds" data-reference-type="ref" data-reference="n3:apriori:bounds">33</a> to smooth solutions. The second equation contains Hessian squares, so classical estimates cannot yet be applied directly. We first control the gradient of the first unknown with a measurable axial coefficient. Its Hessian Morrey bound then gives continuity of the second unknown and permits classical regularity. Finally we define the scalar Dirichlet solution operator on all bounded input sets and apply degree to Proposition <a href="#n3:deformation:homotopy" data-reference-type="ref" data-reference="n3:deformation:homotopy">23</a>.

Throughout this section, ordinary regularity constants may depend on all fixed deformation parameters, including $n$ and $\tau$. No such constant will be used as a polynomial-in-$n$ estimate. Bounds uniform in the outer truncation radius will be stated explicitly.

<a id="pm-h-38"></a>
###### An estimate for a measurable axial coefficient

We use $D$ for coordinate derivatives in the analytic lemmas. Balls are Euclidean coordinate balls, and a boundary ball is their intersection with one side of a smooth boundary. A family of boundary patches has bounded geometry here if normal-coordinate charts, their inverses, the metric and its inverse, and the derivatives through the orders used below have fixed bounds. We only apply the lemmas to smooth metrics and smooth boundaries. Their doubled metrics will be Lipschitz and smooth on each side of a single plane.

<a id="stmt-n3-existence-gradient"></a>
<div id="n3:existence:gradient" class="lemma">

<a id="n3:existence:axial-equation"></a>
<a id="n3:existence:gradient-estimate"></a>
<a id="n3:existence:hessian-morrey"></a>
**Lemma 34** (Axial gradient estimate). *Let $U'$ be compactly contained in an interior or boundary coordinate patch $U$ in dimension three. In a boundary patch assume that $z$ is constant on the boundary face. Suppose $z$ is smooth up to that face, $|\nabla z|\le L$, and, almost everywhere, $$\label{n3:existence:axial-equation}
 A_\chi:\mathop{\mathrm{Hess}}z=G,\qquad
 A_\chi=I-(1-\chi)e\otimes e,\qquad
 e=\frac{\nabla z}{|\nabla z|},\qquad
 0<\chi_0\le\chi\le1,$$ where $\|G\|_\infty\le Q$. At zero gradients any measurable unit axis for which the equation holds is allowed. Then there are $\alpha\in(0,1)$ and $C<\infty$, depending only on $\chi_0$, the patch geometry and the separation of $U'$ from the other patch boundaries, such that $$\label{n3:existence:gradient-estimate}
 \|\nabla z\|_{C^{0,\alpha}(U')}
 \le C(L+Q).$$ For all sufficiently small coordinate balls centered in $U'$, with intersection with the domain understood at a boundary, one also has $$\label{n3:existence:hessian-morrey}
 \int_{B_r\cap U}|\mathop{\mathrm{Hess}}z|^2\,\mathrm dV_g
 \le C(L+Q)^2r^{1+2\alpha}.$$ In particular, the constants are independent of continuity moduli of $\chi$ and $G$.*

</div>

<details id="proof-stmt-n3-existence-gradient"><summary>Proof of stmt-n3-existence-gradient</summary>

*Proof.* The proof combines a Cordes estimate, a divergence identity for the gradient, and improvement of affine approximations. We first establish these estimates, then handle boundary reflection and the iteration.

<a id="pm-h-39"></a>
###### A Cordes estimate above exponent two.

<a id="n3:existence:cordes-defect"></a>
<a id="n3:existence:local-cordes"></a>
For a Euclidean unit vector $e$, $$\label{n3:existence:cordes-defect}
 \|I-A_\chi\|_F=1-\chi\le1-\chi_0.$$ For a compactly supported smooth function $v$, Plancherel’s theorem gives $\|D^2v\|_2=\|\Delta v\|_2$. The Calderón–Zygmund operator taking $\Delta v$ to the full array $D^2v$ is bounded on $L^p$, and interpolation makes its norm arbitrarily close to one as $p\to2$. Choose once and for all <a id="n3:existence:p-zero"></a>$$\label{n3:existence:p-zero}
 2<p_0<3,\qquad
 C_{p_0}(1-\chi_0/2)<1.$$ Rescale a metric-normalized patch until the coordinate principal matrix differs from its Euclidean axial matrix by less than $\chi_0/2$ in Frobenius norm. Absorbing this difference in the Laplacian estimate, applying a cutoff, and using $\|Dv\|_p\le\eta\|D^2v\|_p+C_\eta\|v\|_p$ gives $$\label{n3:existence:local-cordes}
 \|D^2v\|_{L^{p_0}(B_{1/2})}
 +\|Dv\|_{L^{p_0}(B_{1/2})}
 \le C\bigl(\|v\|_{L^{p_0}(B_1)}
       +\|A_\chi:\mathop{\mathrm{Hess}}v\|_{L^{p_0}(B_1)}\bigr).$$ The Christoffel terms are bounded first-order terms in this estimate. The same argument applies when $v=z-L_0$ and $L_0$ is coordinate affine: its extra right side is bounded by $C\|Dg\|_\infty|DL_0|$. The estimate uses bounded measurable principal coefficients only; the smoothness of the solutions allows all of its applications without an approximation issue. The linear estimates just used are the ordinary Laplacian estimates; see (Gilbarg and Trudinger 2001, chap. 7 and 9) <a id="pm-cite-21"></a>[[GilbargTrudinger2001](#ref-GilbargTrudinger2001)].

<a id="pm-h-40"></a>
###### The identity controlling a near-maximal gradient.

<a id="n3:existence:gradient-flux"></a>
<a id="n3:existence:bochner-flux"></a>
<a id="n3:existence:positive-hessian"></a>
Write $H=\mathop{\mathrm{Hess}}z$ and $P=\nabla z$. Equation <a href="#n3:existence:axial-equation" data-reference-type="eqref" data-reference="n3:existence:axial-equation">[n3:existence:axial-equation]</a> gives the pointwise vector identity $$\label{n3:existence:gradient-flux}
 A_\chi\nabla\frac{|P|^2}{2}-GP
       =(H-\Delta z\,g)P.$$ Indeed $HP=|P|H(e,\cdot)$ and $G=\Delta z-(1-\chi)H(e,e)$, so the two axial terms cancel. The identity is also valid at $P=0$. Taking the divergence of its right side, rather than differentiating $\chi$, yields $$\label{n3:existence:bochner-flux}
 \mathop{\mathrm{div}}\left(A_\chi\nabla\frac{|P|^2}{2}-GP\right)
 =|H|^2-(\Delta z)^2+\mathop{\mathrm{Ric}}(P,P).$$ Choose $a_0>0$ so small that $(1+a_0)(1-\chi_0)^2<1$. Young’s inequality and the equation show $$\label{n3:existence:positive-hessian}
 |H|^2-(\Delta z)^2
 \ge c_0|H|^2-C_0G^2,$$ where $c_0>0$ depends only on $\chi_0$.

<a id="n3:existence:s-supersolution"></a>
Consider solutions normalized by $|\nabla z|\le1$ on $B_1$. After making the scale small, let the forcing and the rescaled geometric errors have size at most $\delta$. The nonnegative function $s=1-|\nabla z|^2$ then satisfies $$\label{n3:existence:s-supersolution}
 \mathop{\mathrm{div}}(A_\chi\nabla s+2G\nabla z)
 \le -2c_0|\mathop{\mathrm{Hess}}z|^2+C\delta$$ in a weak sense. In the Euclidean case the last term can be replaced by $C\delta^2$. We allow $C\delta$ to include the geometric errors.

<a id="n3:existence:low-truncation"></a>
<a id="n3:existence:hessian-flat-limit"></a>
For the compactness step, suppose the normalized errors tend to zero in a sequence and $\inf_{B_{1/2}}s\to0$. The inhomogeneous weak Harnack inequality, applied to Equation <a href="#n3:existence:s-supersolution" data-reference-type="eqref" data-reference="n3:existence:s-supersolution">[n3:existence:s-supersolution]</a> after dropping its favorable Hessian term, gives $s\to0$ in measure on $B_{1/2}$. The boundedness $0\le s\le1$ also gives convergence in every finite $L^p$ norm there. To recover the Hessian information, take a cutoff $\eta$ supported inside $B_{1/2}$ and use $\eta^2(b-s)_+$ in the weak supersolution inequality. Ellipticity and Young’s inequality give $$\label{n3:existence:low-truncation}
 \int_{\{s<b\}}\eta^2|Ds|^2
 \le Cb^2\int|D\eta|^2+o(1)$$ for each fixed $b>0$ as the errors vanish. The error fields in Equation <a href="#n3:existence:s-supersolution" data-reference-type="eqref" data-reference="n3:existence:s-supersolution">[n3:existence:s-supersolution]</a> are bounded and tend to zero, so their products with $Ds$ are absorbed in deriving this inequality. Equation <a href="#n3:existence:local-cordes" data-reference-type="eqref" data-reference="n3:existence:local-cordes">[n3:existence:local-cordes]</a> supplies a uniform $L^2$ bound for $Ds$. Its integral over $\{s\ge b\}$ tends to zero in $L^1$ by Cauchy’s inequality and convergence in measure. On $\{s<b\}$ use Equation <a href="#n3:existence:low-truncation" data-reference-type="eqref" data-reference="n3:existence:low-truncation">[n3:existence:low-truncation]</a>, then let $b\downarrow0$. Thus $Ds\to0$ locally in $L^1$. Testing Equation <a href="#n3:existence:bochner-flux" data-reference-type="eqref" data-reference="n3:existence:bochner-flux">[n3:existence:bochner-flux]</a> with a nonnegative compact cutoff and using Equations <a href="#n3:existence:positive-hessian" data-reference-type="eqref" data-reference="n3:existence:positive-hessian">[n3:existence:positive-hessian]</a> and <a href="#n3:existence:gradient-flux" data-reference-type="eqref" data-reference="n3:existence:gradient-flux">[n3:existence:gradient-flux]</a> now gives $$\label{n3:existence:hessian-flat-limit}
 \int_{B_{1/4}}|\mathop{\mathrm{Hess}}z|^2\longrightarrow0.$$ Uniform Lipschitz compactness implies that, after subtracting a constant and taking a subsequence, $z$ tends uniformly on a smaller ball to an affine function. Its slope has length one because $|\nabla z|\to1$ in measure and the Hessians tend to zero.

<a id="n3:existence:drop-or-flat"></a>
Consequently, for any prescribed sufficiently small $b_*>0$ there are fixed $r_*\in(0,1/4)$, $k_*\in(r_*,1)$ and $\delta_*>0$ such that every normalized solution with errors at most $\delta_*$ has one of the following properties: $$\label{n3:existence:drop-or-flat}
 \begin{split}
 &\sup_{B_{r_*}}|\nabla z|\le k_*;\qquad\text{or}\\
 &\sup_{B_{r_*}}|z-L_0|\le b_*r_*,
       \qquad \tfrac12\le|DL_0|\le2.
 \end{split}$$ If this conclusion failed, solutions whose gradient suprema approach one and whose errors approach zero would contradict Equation <a href="#n3:existence:hessian-flat-limit" data-reference-type="eqref" data-reference="n3:existence:hessian-flat-limit">[n3:existence:hessian-flat-limit]</a>. A gradient-drop constant can always be weakened toward one to ensure $k_*>r_*$.

<a id="pm-h-41"></a>
###### A fixed-axis equation.

<a id="n3:existence:fixed-axis"></a>
<a id="n3:existence:axial-derivative-morrey"></a>
Once a nonzero affine slope appears, we compare with an equation whose axis is fixed. Fix a Euclidean unit vector $e_0$. Suppose $$\label{n3:existence:fixed-axis}
 \Delta_{e_0^\perp}Y_0+\chi(x)\partial_{e_0e_0}Y_0=0
 \quad\text{in }B_{3/4},\qquad
 \|Y_0\|_{W^{2,2}(B_{3/4})}\le C_1.$$ The derivative $v=\partial_{e_0}Y_0$ belongs to $W^{1,2}$ and, in distributions, satisfies <a id="n3:existence:axial-derivative-divergence"></a>$$\label{n3:existence:axial-derivative-divergence}
 \Delta_{e_0^\perp}v+
 \partial_{e_0}(\chi\,\partial_{e_0}v)=0.$$ This follows by differentiating the distribution $\chi\partial_{e_0}v$ as a whole. It does not assume a derivative of $\chi$ exists as a function. De Giorgi’s estimate for this uniformly elliptic divergence equation, followed by Caccioppoli applied to $v-v(x_0)$, gives an exponent $\alpha_1\in(0,1)$ and $$\label{n3:existence:axial-derivative-morrey}
 [v]_{C^{0,\alpha_1}(B_{1/2})}\le C,
 \qquad
 \int_{B_r(x_0)}|Dv|^2\le Cr^{1+2\alpha_1}$$ for balls in a smaller fixed interior region. These are the scalar divergence estimates with ellipticity $\chi_0$; see (Gilbarg and Trudinger 2001, chap. 8) <a id="pm-cite-22"></a>[[GilbargTrudinger2001](#ref-GilbargTrudinger2001)].

<a id="n3:existence:model-gradient"></a>
All components of $DY_0$, not only $v$, are controlled by this estimate. In fact, <a id="n3:existence:poisson-source"></a>$$\label{n3:existence:poisson-source}
 \Delta Y_0=f_0,\qquad
 f_0=(1-\chi)\partial_{e_0}v,
 \qquad
 \int_{B_r(x_0)}|f_0|\le Cr^{2+\alpha_1}.$$ The last inequality follows from Cauchy’s inequality and Equation <a href="#n3:existence:axial-derivative-morrey" data-reference-type="eqref" data-reference="n3:existence:axial-derivative-morrey">[n3:existence:axial-derivative-morrey]</a>. Take the Newton potential of $f_0$ restricted to a slightly larger interior ball; its difference from $Y_0$ is harmonic in that ball. For two points at distance $h$, the contribution to the difference of gradient potentials from annuli of radius $r\le2h$ is bounded by $C\sum r^{\alpha_1}\le Ch^{\alpha_1}$. On the remaining annuli the difference of gradient kernels is at most $Ch r^{-3}$, so their contribution is <a id="n3:existence:potential-annuli"></a>$$\label{n3:existence:potential-annuli}
 C h\sum_{r\ge2h}r^{\alpha_1-1}
 \le Ch^{\alpha_1}.$$ The harmonic remainder has its usual interior derivative estimates. Therefore, decreasing the interior ball if needed, $$\label{n3:existence:model-gradient}
 \|Y_0\|_{C^{1,\alpha_1}(B_{1/4})}\le C.$$

<a id="pm-h-42"></a>
###### Improvement of a nonzero affine approximation.

<a id="n3:existence:flat-input"></a>
<a id="n3:existence:normalized-residual"></a>
<a id="n3:existence:axis-error"></a>
<a id="n3:existence:small-fixed-axis-source"></a>
Suppose now $$\label{n3:existence:flat-input}
 \|z-L_0\|_{L^\infty(B_1)}\le b,
 \qquad \tfrac14\le|DL_0|\le4,
 \qquad |\nabla z|\le8.$$ Let the forcing and the first-derivative metric errors be at most $b\delta$. For $Y=(z-L_0)/b$, Equation <a href="#n3:existence:local-cordes" data-reference-type="eqref" data-reference="n3:existence:local-cordes">[n3:existence:local-cordes]</a> on fixed nested balls gives $$\label{n3:existence:normalized-residual}
 \|Y\|_{W^{2,p_0}(B_{7/8})}\le C.$$ In particular, this estimate does not require a bound for $DY$ in the supremum norm. Since $Dz=DL_0+bDY$, the variable axis converges in measure to $e_0=DL_0/|DL_0|$ as $b\to0$. More quantitatively, the coefficient error $E$ caused by replacing this axis by $e_0$ is bounded and satisfies $$\label{n3:existence:axis-error}
 \|E\|_{L^q(B_{7/8})}\le Cb^{\vartheta}+Cb\delta,
 \qquad q=\frac{2p_0}{p_0-2},
 \qquad \vartheta=\frac{p_0-2}{2}>0.$$ Indeed the unit-direction map is Lipschitz where $|bDY|<|DL_0|/2$, and elsewhere its difference is bounded; the $L^{p_0}$ bound in Equation <a href="#n3:existence:normalized-residual" data-reference-type="eqref" data-reference="n3:existence:normalized-residual">[n3:existence:normalized-residual]</a> and interpolation give Equation <a href="#n3:existence:axis-error" data-reference-type="eqref" data-reference="n3:existence:axis-error">[n3:existence:axis-error]</a>. The same estimate includes the metric principal-part error. Hölder’s inequality, with $1/2=1/q+1/p_0$, shows that $$\label{n3:existence:small-fixed-axis-source}
 \bigl\|[I-(1-\chi)e_0\otimes e_0]:D^2Y\bigr\|_{L^2(B_{3/4})}
 \le C(b^{\vartheta}+\delta).$$

<a id="n3:existence:fixed-axis-correction"></a>
Solve for a zero-Dirichlet correction $w$ on $B_{3/4}$ with the left side of Equation <a href="#n3:existence:small-fixed-axis-source" data-reference-type="eqref" data-reference="n3:existence:small-fixed-axis-source">[n3:existence:small-fixed-axis-source]</a> as its source. This does not require a nondivergence Green function. The convex Dirichlet Hessian inequality $\|D^2w\|_2\le\|\Delta w\|_2$ and Equation <a href="#n3:existence:cordes-defect" data-reference-type="eqref" data-reference="n3:existence:cordes-defect">[n3:existence:cordes-defect]</a> make the Laplace solution operator a contraction on $W^{2,2}\cap W^{1,2}_0$. Hence $$\label{n3:existence:fixed-axis-correction}
 \|w\|_{W^{2,2}(B_{3/4})}
 \le C\chi_0^{-1}(b^{\vartheta}+\delta),\qquad
 \|w\|_\infty\le C(b^{\vartheta}+\delta).$$ The last implication uses $W^{2,2}\hookrightarrow C^{0,1/2}$ in dimension three. The convex Hessian inequality is the Miranda–Talenti estimate; see (Talenti 1965, sec. 2, Theorem 3) <a id="pm-cite-23"></a>[[Talenti1965](#ref-Talenti1965)]. Now $Y_0=Y-w$ satisfies Equation <a href="#n3:existence:fixed-axis" data-reference-type="eqref" data-reference="n3:existence:fixed-axis">[n3:existence:fixed-axis]</a> with a uniform $W^{2,2}$ bound.

<a id="n3:existence:improved-flatness"></a>
Choose $0<\alpha_2<\alpha_1$ and then a fixed $\lambda_0\in(0,1/4)$ such that $C\lambda_0^{1+\alpha_1}\le\lambda_0^{1+\alpha_2}/4$ in Equation <a href="#n3:existence:model-gradient" data-reference-type="eqref" data-reference="n3:existence:model-gradient">[n3:existence:model-gradient]</a>. By first taking $\delta$ small and then $b\le b_*$ small, Equation <a href="#n3:existence:fixed-axis-correction" data-reference-type="eqref" data-reference="n3:existence:fixed-axis-correction">[n3:existence:fixed-axis-correction]</a> has supremum norm at most $\lambda_0^{1+\alpha_2}/4$. Taylor expansion of $Y_0$ at the center therefore gives an affine function $L_1$ with $$\label{n3:existence:improved-flatness}
 \sup_{B_{\lambda_0}}|z-L_1|
 \le b\lambda_0^{1+\alpha_2},\qquad
 |DL_1-DL_0|\le Cb.$$ All constants are uniform in the slope range in Equation <a href="#n3:existence:flat-input" data-reference-type="eqref" data-reference="n3:existence:flat-input">[n3:existence:flat-input]</a>.

<a id="pm-h-43"></a>
###### Reflection at a constant Dirichlet face.

Subtract the boundary value and use normal coordinates with the face given by $x_3=0$. Reflect the metric across this plane and reflect $z$ oddly. Tangential derivatives of $z$ vanish on the face, so the extension is $C^1$. There is no distributional Hessian atom. The doubled metric is Lipschitz; the coefficient and lower-order estimates in Equation <a href="#n3:existence:local-cordes" data-reference-type="eqref" data-reference="n3:existence:local-cordes">[n3:existence:local-cordes]</a> hold with its essential first-derivative bound.

The flux in Equation <a href="#n3:existence:gradient-flux" data-reference-type="eqref" data-reference="n3:existence:gradient-flux">[n3:existence:gradient-flux]</a> may have a normal jump. On either side of the face its normal trace is <a id="n3:existence:reflected-flux"></a>$$\label{n3:existence:reflected-flux}
 \bigl((\mathop{\mathrm{Hess}}z-\Delta z\,g)\nabla z\bigr)_\nu
   =-(\mathop{\mathrm{tr}}_T\mathop{\mathrm{Hess}}z)\,\partial_\nu z.$$ Because the boundary value is constant, $\mathop{\mathrm{tr}}_T\mathop{\mathrm{Hess}}z$ is its mean-curvature coefficient times $\partial_\nu z$. The jump is therefore bounded by $C|\mathrm{II}|\,|\nabla z|^2$. At scale $r$ it is a bounded plane density of size $O(r)$. Write the plane density and flux after multiplication by the reflected coordinate volume density, so that the following divergence is Euclidean. Such a signed density $a(x')\,\delta_{\{x_3=0\}}$ is the divergence of the bounded field $a(x')\mathbf 1_{\{x_3>0\}}\partial_3$. Thus its negative part is another small divergence error in Equation <a href="#n3:existence:s-supersolution" data-reference-type="eqref" data-reference="n3:existence:s-supersolution">[n3:existence:s-supersolution]</a>. Smooth-side curvature errors are $O(r^2)$. Weak Harnack and the low-truncation argument remain valid, and the flatness comparison uses the same Lipschitz metric estimates. This proves all the preceding alternatives for balls meeting the reflection plane as well.

<a id="pm-h-44"></a>
###### Iteration and the Morrey consequence.

Keep $\alpha_2,\lambda_0$ from the affine improvement fixed. Choose $b_*$ sufficiently small that $Cb_*/(1-\lambda_0^{\alpha_2})<1/4$, with $C$ the slope-increment constant in Equation <a href="#n3:existence:improved-flatness" data-reference-type="eqref" data-reference="n3:existence:improved-flatness">[n3:existence:improved-flatness]</a>. Then choose $r_*,k_*,\delta_*$ in Equation <a href="#n3:existence:drop-or-flat" data-reference-type="eqref" data-reference="n3:existence:drop-or-flat">[n3:existence:drop-or-flat]</a> for this fixed $b_*$. Normalize initially by a fixed multiple of $L+Q$ and choose a uniformly small initial radius so that the metric and forcing errors satisfy all the preceding smallness conditions. If the first case of Equation <a href="#n3:existence:drop-or-flat" data-reference-type="eqref" data-reference="n3:existence:drop-or-flat">[n3:existence:drop-or-flat]</a> holds, rescale the ball by $r_*$ and the gradient bound by $k_*$. The normalized forcing decreases by $r_*/k_*<1$. Repeating this step either continues forever or reaches the second case. In the former case the gradient decays with exponent $\log k_*/\log r_*$. In the latter case apply Equation <a href="#n3:existence:improved-flatness" data-reference-type="eqref" data-reference="n3:existence:improved-flatness">[n3:existence:improved-flatness]</a> successively, retaining exponent $\alpha_2$. At each affine step, rescale $z$ by dividing by the spatial scale, subtracting only an additive constant; this preserves its gradient bound. Its slope changes have total size at most $Cb_*/(1-\lambda_0^{\alpha_2})$, so the slopes remain in $[1/4,4]$. At the $j$th step the error size is $b_*\lambda_0^{j\alpha_2}$, while the normalized forcing and metric first-derivative errors have size $O(\lambda_0^j)$. Since $\alpha_2<1$, their ratio to the error size only decreases. This justifies every subsequent application of the improvement lemma. To combine the two branches, now choose <a id="n3:existence:iteration-exponent"></a>$$\label{n3:existence:iteration-exponent}
 0<\alpha\le\min\left\{\alpha_2,
              \frac{\log k_*}{\log r_*}\right\},\qquad \alpha<1.$$

At every center we have consequently obtained affine functions $L_{x,r}$ satisfying <a id="n3:existence:campanato-affine"></a>$$\label{n3:existence:campanato-affine}
 \sup_{B_r(x)}|z-L_{x,r}|
 \le C(L+Q)r^{1+\alpha}.$$ The slope differences at consecutive radii are bounded by $C(L+Q)r^\alpha$; comparing the affine approximations on overlapping balls gives Equation <a href="#n3:existence:gradient-estimate" data-reference-type="eqref" data-reference="n3:existence:gradient-estimate">[n3:existence:gradient-estimate]</a>. This also identifies their limiting slope with $Dz$, since $z$ is smooth. The reflected version gives the estimate up to a boundary.

Finally apply the $L^2$ version of Equation <a href="#n3:existence:local-cordes" data-reference-type="eqref" data-reference="n3:existence:local-cordes">[n3:existence:local-cordes]</a> to $z-L_{x,2r}$ after rescaling. The affine error contributes $C(L+Q)r^{1/2+\alpha}$ to the Hessian $L^2$ norm; the bounded forcing and affine Christoffel term contribute $C(L+Q)r^{3/2}$. Squaring and using $\alpha<1$ proves Equation <a href="#n3:existence:hessian-morrey" data-reference-type="eqref" data-reference="n3:existence:hessian-morrey">[n3:existence:hessian-morrey]</a>. ◻

</details>

<a id="pm-h-45"></a>
###### Bounded solutions with quadratic gradient growth

The Hessian Morrey bound controls the forcing in the second equation through the following oscillation estimate. A positive measure in the source bound also accommodates reflected boundary terms.

<a id="stmt-n3-existence-natural-growth"></a>
<div id="n3:existence:natural-growth" class="lemma">

<a id="n3:existence:natural-source"></a>
**Lemma 35** (Natural-growth oscillation estimate). *On a three-dimensional ball suppose $Z$ is bounded, $|Z|\le M$, and is a smooth solution, or a reflected weak solution, of <a id="n3:existence:natural-equation"></a>$$\label{n3:existence:natural-equation}
 \mathop{\mathrm{div}}(aDZ+b)=e.$$ Assume $a$ is measurable and symmetric, $\lambda I\le a\le\Lambda I$, $|b|\le B$, and $$\label{n3:existence:natural-source}
 |e|\le C_0(1+|DZ|^2)\,\mathrm dx+\mu,\qquad
 \mu(B_r(x))\le C_\mu r^{1+\beta}$$ for some $\beta>0$ and every sufficiently small ball in the patch. Then $Z$ has a local Hölder estimate whose constants depend only on the displayed bounds and the patch separation. The conclusion also holds up to a smooth boundary with bounded conormal flux or constant Dirichlet data, provided the corresponding reflected measure satisfies Equation <a href="#n3:existence:natural-source" data-reference-type="eqref" data-reference="n3:existence:natural-source">[n3:existence:natural-source]</a>.*

</div>

<details id="proof-stmt-n3-existence-natural-growth"><summary>Proof of stmt-n3-existence-natural-growth</summary>

*Proof.* Write $\mathcal L=-\mathop{\mathrm{div}}(aD)$ and, for $s\in\{-1,1\}$, set $V_s=e^{skZ}$. The weak chain rule gives <a id="n3:existence:exponential-identity"></a>$$\label{n3:existence:exponential-identity}
 \mathcal L V_s
 =\mathop{\mathrm{div}}(skV_sb)-skV_se
       -k^2V_s\bigl(aDZ\cdot DZ+b\cdot DZ\bigr).$$ Choose $k\ge\max\{1,2C_0/\lambda\}$ and use $B|DZ|\le(\lambda/2)|DZ|^2+B^2/(2\lambda)$. Since $e^{-kM}\le V_s\le e^{kM}$, we obtain <a id="n3:existence:exponential-subsolution"></a>$$\label{n3:existence:exponential-subsolution}
 \mathcal L V_s\le\mathop{\mathrm{div}}F_s+\nu,
 \qquad |F_s|\le ke^{kM}B,
 \qquad \nu\le C\,\mathrm dx+C\mu.$$

On a ball $B_R$ compactly contained in the patch, solve $\mathcal L w_s=\mathop{\mathrm{div}}F_s+\nu$ with zero Dirichlet data. The bounded vector source has a solution of supremum norm at most $CR$: apply the $L^p$ source estimate, $p>3$, whose scaled factor is $R^{1-3/p}$, to $\|F_s\|_p\le CR^{3/p}$. For the positive measure source use the Green bound $0\le\mathcal G(x,y)\le C|x-y|^{-1}$ for uniformly elliptic measurable divergence coefficients (Littman, Stampacchia, and Weinberger 1963, sec. 7, Theorem (7.1) and Remark 2) <a id="pm-cite-24"></a>[[LittmanStampacchiaWeinberger1963](#ref-LittmanStampacchiaWeinberger1963)]. To use that interior comparison uniformly for all $x,y\in B_R$, extend the coefficients elliptically to $B_{2R}$. Domain monotonicity bounds the zero-Dirichlet Green function on $B_R$ by the one on $B_{2R}$, where $B_R$ is a fixed compact interior region after rescaling. This gives the stated uniform bound. Integration over concentric annuli gives <a id="n3:existence:green-morrey-correction"></a>$$\label{n3:existence:green-morrey-correction}
 \sup_{x\in B_R}\int_{B_R}\mathcal G(x,y)\,\mathrm d\nu(y)
 \le C\int_0^{2R}\frac{\nu(B_t(x))}{t^2}\,\mathrm dt
       +CR^{-1}\nu(B_{2R}(x))
 \le C(R^2+R^\beta).$$ One may first approximate the measure by smooth positive densities. The uniform potential bound and the energy identity $\int aDw\cdot Dw=\int w\,\mathrm d\nu$ give a bounded sequence in $W^{1,2}_0$ and hence the required weak solution. Thus, with $\gamma=\min\{1,\beta\}>0$, <a id="n3:existence:correction-size"></a>$$\label{n3:existence:correction-size}
 \|w_s\|_\infty\le\varepsilon_R,
 \qquad \varepsilon_R=CR^\gamma.$$

Let $M_R=\sup_{B_R}Z$ and $m_R=\inf_{B_R}Z$. The functions <a id="n3:existence:exponential-deficits"></a>$$\label{n3:existence:exponential-deficits}
 H_+=e^{kM_R}-e^{kZ}+w_++\varepsilon_R,
 \qquad
 H_-=e^{-km_R}-e^{-kZ}+w_-+\varepsilon_R$$ are nonnegative and satisfy $\mathcal L H_\pm\ge0$. Weak Harnack controls their $L^q$ means on $B_{R/2}$ by their infima on $B_{R/4}$. Each exponential deficit is comparable, with constants depending on $kM$, to $M_R-Z$ or $Z-m_R$, respectively. At least one of the sets $$\{Z\le(M_R+m_R)/2\}\cap B_{R/2},\qquad
 \{Z\ge(M_R+m_R)/2\}\cap B_{R/2}$$ has at least half the measure of $B_{R/2}$. Apply weak Harnack to the corresponding deficit. It follows that either the upper supremum decreases, or the lower infimum increases, by at least $c(M_R-m_R)-C\varepsilon_R$ on $B_{R/4}$. Consequently <a id="n3:existence:oscillation-contraction"></a>$$\label{n3:existence:oscillation-contraction}
 \operatorname{osc}_{B_{R/4}}Z
 \le(1-c)\operatorname{osc}_{B_R}Z+CR^\gamma.$$ Iteration proves a Hölder estimate with any sufficiently small positive exponent below both $\gamma$ and $-\log(1-c)/\log4$.

For the boundary estimate, flatten a face and put $S=\operatorname{diag}(1,1,-1)$. An even extension of $Z$ uses $a_-=Sa_+S$ and $b_-=Sb_+$. Its flux has a plane jump whose density is twice the prescribed normal flux, hence bounded. An odd extension after subtracting a constant Dirichlet value uses $a_-=Sa_+S$, $b_-=-Sb_+$, and the sign-reflected bulk source. Its normal flux is continuous. The transformed metrics and volume densities are absorbed into the displayed coefficients. A bounded plane density has ball mass $O(r^2)$, so it is admissible with exponent one. This proves the asserted boundary version. ◻

</details>

<a id="stmt-n3-existence-classical-bounds"></a>
<div id="n3:existence:classical-bounds" class="proposition">

**Proposition 36** (Classical bounds for bounded-variable solutions). *Fix the deformation parameters and assume the bounds in Proposition <a href="#n3:apriori:bounds" data-reference-type="ref" data-reference="n3:apriori:bounds">33</a>. Every smooth solution in the homotopy of Proposition <a href="#n3:deformation:homotopy" data-reference-type="ref" data-reference="n3:deformation:homotopy">23</a>, with $t\ge-\epsilon$, has uniform local classical estimates of every finite order, up to the inner and outer faces. At fixed $n$ the constants are independent of the homotopy parameter and of all sufficiently large outer radii $R$. The local patches can be chosen with a uniform positive radius throughout the end.*

</div>

<details id="proof-stmt-n3-existence-classical-bounds"><summary>Proof of stmt-n3-existence-classical-bounds</summary>

<a id="n3:existence:f-morrey-application"></a>
*Proof.* Start with the bounds for $f,Z,t,\sigma$ from Proposition <a href="#n3:apriori:bounds" data-reference-type="ref" data-reference="n3:apriori:bounds">33</a>. At fixed parameters they bound $u,l,D$ above and away from zero, and give a uniform $\chi_0>0$. After dividing the scalar trace equation by $l/\sqrt D$, its right side is <a id="n3:existence:normalized-f-source"></a>$$\label{n3:existence:normalized-f-source}
 G_f=\frac{\sqrt D}{l}
         \bigl(F_s-\mathop{\mathrm{tr}}_{A_\chi}K\bigr).$$ It is bounded throughout the homotopy, including its added collar terms. Lemma <a href="#n3:existence:gradient" data-reference-type="ref" data-reference="n3:existence:gradient">34</a> therefore gives a uniform $C^{1,\alpha}$ estimate for $f$ and $$\label{n3:existence:f-morrey-application}
 \int_{B_r}|\mathop{\mathrm{Hess}}f|^2\le Cr^{1+2\alpha}$$ on the uniform patches, including boundary patches where $f$ is constant.

After multiplying by the Riemannian volume density, the second equation has coordinate principal coefficients $a^{ij}=4\sqrt{\det g}\,uA_\chi^{ij}$, a bounded flux vector $b$, and a source bounded in absolute value by <a id="n3:existence:Z-quadratic-source"></a>$$\label{n3:existence:Z-quadratic-source}
 C\bigl(1+|DZ|^2+|D^2f|^2\bigr).$$ Indeed $t$ is a smooth function of $x,Z,Df$ on the bounded variable range. Thus $Dt$ is a bounded linear combination of $DZ,D^2f$ and fixed smooth terms; the expression $\mathcal T$ is quadratic in these quantities. All other source terms have lower order. The same volume density is included in $b,e$; it is smooth and bounded above and away from zero on the chosen patches, so it preserves these bounds and uniform ellipticity. The prescribed conormal flux at the inner boundary is bounded. At the outer face $Z=0$. Apply Lemma <a href="#n3:existence:natural-growth" data-reference-type="ref" data-reference="n3:existence:natural-growth">35</a>, with $\mu=C|D^2f|^2\,\mathrm dx$ and the bounded reflected plane density. Equation <a href="#n3:existence:f-morrey-application" data-reference-type="eqref" data-reference="n3:existence:f-morrey-application">[n3:existence:f-morrey-application]</a> supplies its measure growth hypothesis. We obtain a uniform positive Hölder exponent for $Z$.

<a id="n3:existence:ordinary-normal-condition"></a>
Now $Z$ and $Df$ are Hölder, so all coefficients and the right side of the scalar $f$-equation are Hölder on their bounded variable range. Interior and constant-Dirichlet boundary Schauder estimates give $f\in C^{2,\theta}$ for a uniform $\theta>0$. Expand the $Z$-equation in nondivergence form. Its principal coefficients are uniformly elliptic and $C^{0,\theta}$, while its right side is bounded by $C(1+|DZ|^2)$. On an inner face $Df$ is normal. Therefore $A_\chi$ has zero normal–tangential components there and normal eigenvalue $\chi$. Its boundary equation solves for $$\label{n3:existence:ordinary-normal-condition}
 \partial_\nu Z=\mathcal H_s(x,Z,f,Df),$$ where $\mathcal H_s$ is smooth on a fixed bounded variable range. Its derivatives with respect to $x$ and its displayed scalar arguments are bounded at fixed parameters. The outer condition remains constant Dirichlet. These are different, disjoint smooth boundary components; there is no change of boundary condition along an edge or a corner.

<a id="n3:existence:Wp-pre-absorption"></a>
It remains to absorb the quadratic gradient growth. Fix $p>3$. The linear local $W^{2,p}$ estimate for the leading nondivergence operator with Equation <a href="#n3:existence:ordinary-normal-condition" data-reference-type="eqref" data-reference="n3:existence:ordinary-normal-condition">[n3:existence:ordinary-normal-condition]</a> or outer Dirichlet data has the form, on fixed nested patches $U_x\Subset V_x$, $$\label{n3:existence:Wp-pre-absorption}
 \|Z\|_{W^{2,p}(U_x)}
 \le C\left(1+\|DZ\|_{L^{2p}(V_x)}^2
                 +\|Z\|_{W^{1,p}(V_x)}\right).$$ Here the boundary norm is controlled by <a id="n3:existence:boundary-trace-composition"></a>$$\label{n3:existence:boundary-trace-composition}
 \|\mathcal H_s(x,Z,f,Df)\|_{W^{1-1/p,p}(\partial V_x)}
 \le C\bigl(1+\|Z\|_{W^{1,p}(V_x^+)}\bigr),$$ using trace and composition after extending its smooth expression through the collar. The derivatives of $f,Df$ entering this extension are already bounded. The leading matrix has a fixed Hölder modulus, so its small oscillation on sufficiently small patches permits the usual freezing and absorption in the linear estimate. The normal boundary operator is uniformly oblique and satisfies the complementing condition. These are the classical local elliptic boundary estimates (Agmon, Douglis, and Nirenberg 1959, 1964) <a id="pm-cite-25"></a>[[AgmonDouglisNirenberg1959](#ref-AgmonDouglisNirenberg1959), [AgmonDouglisNirenberg1964](#ref-AgmonDouglisNirenberg1964)].

<a id="n3:existence:small-oscillation-GN"></a>
<a id="n3:existence:global-local-GN"></a>
Let $[Z]_{C^{0,\theta}}\le H_0$. On balls or half-balls of radius $h$, the scaled Gagliardo–Nirenberg inequality, applied after subtracting a constant, gives $$\label{n3:existence:small-oscillation-GN}
 \begin{split}
 \|DZ\|_{L^{2p}(B_h)}^2
 &\le C\operatorname{osc}_{B_h}Z\,
                    \|D^2Z\|_{L^p(B_h)}\\
 &\quad+Ch^{3/p-2}(\operatorname{osc}_{B_h}Z)^2.
 \end{split}$$ One can use a bounded extension operator on a half-ball; its constants are uniform in the boundary charts. This is the interpolation inequality of (Nirenberg 1959, Lecture II, Equation (2.2)) <a id="pm-cite-26"></a>[[Nirenberg1959](#ref-Nirenberg1959)] with its lower-order term on a bounded patch. Cover $V_x$ by radius-$h$ patches of bounded overlap and take the $\ell^p$ sum of Equation <a href="#n3:existence:small-oscillation-GN" data-reference-type="eqref" data-reference="n3:existence:small-oscillation-GN">[n3:existence:small-oscillation-GN]</a>. It follows that $$\label{n3:existence:global-local-GN}
 \|DZ\|_{L^{2p}(V_x)}^2
 \le CH_0h^\theta\|D^2Z\|_{L^p(V_x^+)}
           +CH_0^2h^{2\theta-2}.$$ Also, for any $\eta>0$, $\|Z\|_{W^{1,p}(V_x)}
 \le\eta\|D^2Z\|_{L^p(V_x^+)}+C_\eta$. Each enlarged patch $V_x^+$ is covered by a bounded number of the patches $U_y$, independently of $R$. Set $S=\sup_y\|Z\|_{W^{2,p}(U_y)}$, finite for each smooth finite-domain solution. Equations <a href="#n3:existence:Wp-pre-absorption" data-reference-type="eqref" data-reference="n3:existence:Wp-pre-absorption">[n3:existence:Wp-pre-absorption]</a> and <a href="#n3:existence:global-local-GN" data-reference-type="eqref" data-reference="n3:existence:global-local-GN">[n3:existence:global-local-GN]</a> give <a id="n3:existence:uniform-local-absorption"></a>$$\label{n3:existence:uniform-local-absorption}
 S\le C(H_0h^\theta+\eta)S+C(h,\eta).$$ Choose $h$ and then $\eta$ so the first coefficient is less than $1/2$. We obtain a uniform $W^{2,p}$ bound and hence a $C^{1,1-3/p}$ bound for $Z$.

The coefficients in both equations and in the normal boundary condition now have the regularity required for Schauder bootstrap. First the nondivergence $Z$-equation has Hölder source, giving $Z\in C^{2,\theta'}$; the scalar $f$-equation then gains another derivative. Repetition gives every finite classical derivative supported by the smooth data. The same procedure holds on the uniform unit patches of the asymptotic end and on the large outer spheres, whose normal-coordinate constants are uniform. This proves the asserted independence of $R$. The reduced background has end symbol bounds of every order by Proposition <a href="#n3:reduction:rest-reduction" data-reference-type="ref" data-reference="n3:reduction:rest-reduction">12</a>; the bootstrap here does not assume additional derivatives of the original asymptotic data. ◻

</details>

<a id="pm-h-46"></a>
###### The scalar Dirichlet solution operator

The compact map requires a scalar solve for every bounded input $Z$. Its definition must therefore work without a floor bound on the input.

<a id="stmt-n3-existence-scalar-solve"></a>
<div id="n3:existence:scalar-solve" class="lemma">

**Lemma 37** (Scalar solve for unrestricted bounded inputs). *Fix $n\ge4$, $\tau>0$, a finite smooth truncation $\Omega_R$, and a homotopy parameter $s\in[0,4]$. For every $Z\in C^{1,b}(\overline{\Omega_R})$, $0<b<1$, the scalar trace equation of Proposition <a href="#n3:deformation:homotopy" data-reference-type="ref" data-reference="n3:deformation:homotopy">23</a>, with its prescribed componentwise constant Dirichlet values for $f$, has a unique solution. It lies in $C^{3,b}$ and is smooth to the extent allowed by the input. The solution operator <a id="n3:existence:scalar-operator"></a>$$\label{n3:existence:scalar-operator}
 f=\mathcal S_s(Z)$$ is continuous in $(s,Z)$, including across the concatenation points of the homotopy. On bounded subsets of $C^{1,b}$ its $C^{3,b}$ norm is uniformly bounded at these fixed parameters. No lower bound for $t$ is required.*

</div>

<details id="proof-stmt-n3-existence-scalar-solve"><summary>Proof of stmt-n3-existence-scalar-solve</summary>

<a id="n3:existence:scalar-height"></a>
*Proof.* The implicit definition of $t$ has derivative $\partial Z/\partial t=1+pv/4>0$. Thus $t$ and all the coefficients are smooth functions of $x,Z,Df$, also at $Df=0$. There is no dependence of the principal coefficient on the height $f$ itself. For bounded height the added collar terms in $F_s$ are bounded, and its derivative with respect to $h=\tau f$ is at least one. At $Df=0$ the equation and this height sign give upper and lower constant barriers. Hence every scalar solution satisfies $$\label{n3:existence:scalar-height}
 |h|\le C_0,$$ where the constant can be chosen independently of $Z$ and the homotopy parameter. We include the fixed boundary values in its choice.

<a id="n3:existence:scalar-growth"></a>
We first derive the coefficient bounds at an unbounded slope. If $|Z|\le M$ and $\sigma\to\infty$, the implicit equation forces $t\to-\infty$ uniformly in $Z$. There $p=n$ and $l=e^{nt}$, so its exact form is <a id="n3:existence:implicit-large-slope"></a>$$\label{n3:existence:implicit-large-slope}
 e^{8Z}=e^{8t}+e^{(2n+8)t}\sigma^2.$$ Consequently <a id="n3:existence:large-slope-asymptotics"></a>$$\label{n3:existence:large-slope-asymptotics}
 \begin{split}
 t&=-\frac{\log\sigma}{n+4}+O(1),\qquad
 l\asymp\sigma^{-n/(n+4)},\\
 d&\asymp\sigma^{-8/(n+4)},\qquad
 \chi\asymp\sigma^{-8/(n+4)},\qquad
 \frac{\sqrt D}{l}\asymp\sigma.
 \end{split}$$ The constants are uniform for $|Z|\le M$ at fixed $n$. Since $n\ge4$, the exponent $8/(n+4)$ is at most one. Combining the large-slope estimates with compactness of the remaining variable range yields $$\label{n3:existence:scalar-growth}
 \chi\ge\frac{c}{1+\sigma},\qquad
 |G_f|\le C(1+\sigma)$$ whenever Equation <a href="#n3:existence:scalar-height" data-reference-type="eqref" data-reference="n3:existence:scalar-height">[n3:existence:scalar-height]</a> holds.

<a id="n3:existence:logarithmic-modulus"></a>
We prove a global gradient estimate using this radial ellipticity. Let $\delta$ be smaller than a fixed collar radius, half the distance between distinct boundary components, and a normal injectivity radius of a smooth extension of the finite domain. On a boundary distance collar use $$\label{n3:existence:logarithmic-modulus}
 \psi(r)=k^{-1}\log(1+Br),\qquad
 \psi''=-k(\psi')^2.$$ The upper and lower barriers are the assigned face value plus or minus $\psi$. On these tests the axis is normal to the distance leaves, so their principal trace is $\chi\psi''+\psi'\Delta r$. At slopes at least one, Equation <a href="#n3:existence:scalar-growth" data-reference-type="eqref" data-reference="n3:existence:scalar-growth">[n3:existence:scalar-growth]</a> gives <a id="n3:existence:logarithmic-dominance"></a>$$\label{n3:existence:logarithmic-dominance}
 -k\chi(\psi')^2\le-\tfrac12ck\psi'.$$ Choose $k$ large enough to dominate all the bounded geometry terms and the linear growth in Equation <a href="#n3:existence:scalar-growth" data-reference-type="eqref" data-reference="n3:existence:scalar-growth">[n3:existence:scalar-growth]</a>. Next shrink $\delta$ so that $1/(2k\delta)$ exceeds any fixed large-slope threshold used here. Finally choose $B$ large enough that $B\delta\ge1$ and $\psi(\delta)$ exceeds twice the height oscillation. Then $\psi'\ge1/(2k\delta)$ on this collar and the two barriers compare by the height monotonicity. This gives a uniform boundary gradient bound.

<a id="n3:existence:doubling-function"></a>
For the interior estimate, increase $B$ if necessary and compare two points using $$\label{n3:existence:doubling-function}
 f(x)-f(y)-\psi(\operatorname{dist}(x,y)),
 \qquad 0<\operatorname{dist}(x,y)<\delta.$$ The distance is taken in the fixed smooth extension. The boundary barriers exclude a positive maximum with one endpoint on the boundary. The inequality $\psi(\delta)>2\operatorname{osc}f$ excludes the other boundary of the two-point domain. At a positive interior maximum let $r=\operatorname{dist}(x,y)$ and $q=\psi'(r)$. The two gradients have length $q$ and are parallel transports along the connecting geodesic. Vary both endpoints simultaneously in parallel transverse directions. The second variation formula for the short geodesic yields <a id="n3:existence:two-point-transverse"></a>$$\label{n3:existence:two-point-transverse}
 \mathop{\mathrm{tr}}_{e_x^\perp}\mathop{\mathrm{Hess}}f(x)
 -\mathop{\mathrm{tr}}_{e_y^\perp}\mathop{\mathrm{Hess}}f(y)\le Cqr.$$ Varying each endpoint separately along that geodesic gives $f_{;e_xe_x}(x)\le\psi''(r)$ and $f_{;e_ye_y}(y)\ge-\psi''(r)$. Subtracting the two scalar equations therefore gives <a id="n3:existence:two-point-contradiction"></a>$$\label{n3:existence:two-point-contradiction}
 -2C(1+q)
 \le G_f(x)-G_f(y)
 \le Cqr+(\chi_x+\chi_y)\psi''(r).$$ By Equations <a href="#n3:existence:scalar-growth" data-reference-type="eqref" data-reference="n3:existence:scalar-growth">[n3:existence:scalar-growth]</a> and <a href="#n3:existence:logarithmic-modulus" data-reference-type="eqref" data-reference="n3:existence:logarithmic-modulus">[n3:existence:logarithmic-modulus]</a>, the last term is at most $-ckq$ at the large comparison slopes. Our choice of $k$ gives a contradiction. Thus Equation <a href="#n3:existence:doubling-function" data-reference-type="eqref" data-reference="n3:existence:doubling-function">[n3:existence:doubling-function]</a> is nonpositive. Reversing $x,y$ proves the same bound for the absolute difference and, on letting $y\to x$, a global Lipschitz bound for $f$. This argument used no continuity modulus for $\chi_x-\chi_y$; only the common transverse eigenvalues and the radial lower bound were needed.

For existence interpolate the normalized equation with $\Delta f=\tau f$, retaining the given boundary values. Explicitly, for $a\in[0,1]$ take principal matrix $(1-a)I+aA_\chi$ and right side $(1-a)\tau f+aG_f$. The height sign, the linear gradient growth, and Equation <a href="#n3:existence:scalar-growth" data-reference-type="eqref" data-reference="n3:existence:scalar-growth">[n3:existence:scalar-growth]</a> persist uniformly in $a$. The height and logarithmic gradient bounds just proved are therefore uniform. After these bounds the interpolating equations are uniformly elliptic. Their matrices still have the axial form, with axial eigenvalue $(1-a)+a\chi$, so Lemma <a href="#n3:existence:gradient" data-reference-type="ref" data-reference="n3:existence:gradient">34</a> applies. Schauder estimates then give a uniform $C^{2,\theta}$ bound at fixed input $Z$. The coefficients and right side are now Lipschitz in position on bounded input sets, which permits their $C^{0,b}$ estimates and an upgrade to $C^{2,b}$. Differentiating once, or using the next Schauder estimate, yields $f\in C^{3,b}$ because $Z\in C^{1,b}$.

The scalar linearization has the form $a^{ij}D_{ij}\varphi+b^iD_i\varphi-c\varphi$ with $c\ge c_1\tau>0$ on the bounded variable range. Indeed the principal matrix is independent of the height, while $\partial_fG_f\ge\tau\sqrt D/l>0$. The Dirichlet maximum principle gives uniqueness and a zero kernel; the linear elliptic Dirichlet theory gives an inverse. The implicit-function theorem gives openness of the interpolation parameter set. The uniform classical bounds and compactness give closedness, starting from the invertible Laplace endpoint. This proves existence. The same maximum principle applied to the difference of two solutions proves uniqueness of the nonlinear solution. The implicit-function theorem, or compactness and uniqueness, gives continuous dependence on $Z$ and on the homotopy parameter. At the finitely many concatenation points the scalar equations agree, so the same continuity holds there. ◻

</details>

<a id="pm-h-47"></a>
###### A compact equation and the order of parameter choices

Recall the parameter $s\in[0,4]$ of Proposition <a href="#n3:deformation:homotopy" data-reference-type="ref" data-reference="n3:deformation:homotopy">23</a>: $s=0$ is the desired system, $s=1$ has zero drift, $s=2$ has the full collar modification, and $s=3$ has $f=0$. On $[3,4]$ the scalar source and inner flux are scaled to zero; at $s=4$ the scalar equation still has the unique solution $f=0$. We will define a compact map along this path and show that its fixed points remain in the admissible set.

<a id="stmt-n3-existence-deformation"></a>
<div id="n3:existence:deformation" class="theorem">

**Theorem 38** (Existence on finite truncations). *For the prepared domain of Proposition <a href="#n3:domains:prepared-domain" data-reference-type="ref" data-reference="n3:domains:prepared-domain">19</a> and every sufficiently small fixed $\epsilon>0$, there is an integer $n_0\ge4$ and, for each $n\ge n_0$, a radius $R_{\min}(n)$, with $R_{\min}(n)\to\infty$, such that the original deformation system has a smooth solution on every $\Omega_R$ with $R\ge R_{\min}(n)$. It satisfies $t>-\epsilon$ on the closure. At fixed $n$, these solutions have the local bounds of Proposition <a href="#n3:existence:classical-bounds" data-reference-type="ref" data-reference="n3:existence:classical-bounds">36</a>, uniformly as $R\to\infty$. In particular, any sequence $R_j\to\infty$ of such radii has a subsequence converging smoothly on compact subsets of $\overline\Omega$ to a solution of the original equations with $t\ge-\epsilon$.*

</div>

<details id="proof-stmt-n3-existence-deformation"><summary>Proof of stmt-n3-existence-deformation</summary>

<a id="n3:existence:outer-gradient"></a>
<a id="n3:existence:R-choice"></a>
*Proof.* We first make the radius convention precise. Fix the prepared data, all thresholds and collars, and $\epsilon$. Increase $n_0$ so that <a id="n3:existence:n-choice"></a>$$\label{n3:existence:n-choice}
 n_0\ge\max\{4,\lceil2/\epsilon\rceil\}$$ and so that the floor test and all estimates of Proposition <a href="#n3:apriori:bounds" data-reference-type="ref" data-reference="n3:apriori:bounds">33</a> apply for $n\ge n_0$. Let $R_{\mathrm{ap}}(n)$ be a sufficient lower radius for those estimates, and let $R_{\mathrm{geo}}$ contain all compact boundary faces and supports used in the construction. The end barrier of that proposition gives a constant $C_{\mathrm{out}}$, independent of $n,R,s$, such that every admissible or floor-contact homotopy solution has $$\label{n3:existence:outer-gradient}
 |\nabla f|\le
       C_{\mathrm{out}}\tau^{-1}R^{-1-\gamma}
       \quad\text{on the outer sphere}.$$ The scalar last stage has $f=0$ and satisfies the same bound. Choose, enlarging to a radius of a smooth truncation if necessary, $$\label{n3:existence:R-choice}
 \begin{split}
 R_{\min}(n)=\max\biggl\{&n,R_{\mathrm{geo}},R_{\mathrm{ap}}(n),\\
 &\left(\frac{2C_{\mathrm{out}}\ell}
               {\tau\sqrt{e^{8\epsilon}-1}}
        \right)^{1/(1+\gamma)}\biggr\}.
 \end{split}$$ At $Z=0$, the value of its implicit expression at $t=-\epsilon$ is $-\epsilon+\frac18\log(1+\ell^2\sigma^2)$. Equations <a href="#n3:existence:outer-gradient" data-reference-type="eqref" data-reference="n3:existence:outer-gradient">[n3:existence:outer-gradient]</a> and <a href="#n3:existence:R-choice" data-reference-type="eqref" data-reference="n3:existence:R-choice">[n3:existence:R-choice]</a> make this strictly negative. Strict monotonicity of that expression in $t$ therefore excludes an outer floor contact. The term $n$ in Equation <a href="#n3:existence:R-choice" data-reference-type="eqref" data-reference="n3:existence:R-choice">[n3:existence:R-choice]</a> ensures $R_{\min}(n)\to\infty$.

The sublevel and collar estimates apply to arbitrary smooth admissible or floor-contact solution sequences with $n\to\infty$ and expanding outer cutoffs, uniformly over the compact ranges of the homotopy parameters. If the needed conclusion failed for arbitrarily large $n$ with $R\ge R_{\min}(n)$, one could select such a violating sequence. The chosen radius convention would make it precisely an expanding sequence excluded by those proofs. Thus a single $n_0$, followed by the radius choices above, suffices for every homotopy parameter. No upper bound for $Z$ is inserted in the earlier contact estimates: there $\sigma\asymp\tau^{-1}$ and $l\ge\ell$ alone give $d\lesssim(\tau/\ell)^2$.

<a id="n3:existence:compact-map-equation"></a>
Fix now $n\ge n_0$ and $R\ge R_{\min}(n)$ for the rest of the degree argument. Let <a id="n3:existence:banach-space"></a>$$\label{n3:existence:banach-space}
 X_b=\{Z\in C^{1,b}(\overline{\Omega_R}):
                       Z=0\text{ on the outer face}\},
 \qquad 0<b<1.$$ For an input $Z\in X_b$, first solve $f=\mathcal S_s(Z)$ by Lemma <a href="#n3:existence:scalar-solve" data-reference-type="ref" data-reference="n3:existence:scalar-solve">37</a>. Compute $t,u,A_\chi,\mathcal T$ and the full homotopy source from this input pair. Write $B_s$ for the frozen drift summand in the flux, $E_s$ for the full right side of its divergence equation, and $q_s$ for the prescribed inner flux. Thus before the final scaling $B_s=\lambda_suA_\chi K(w,\cdot)$ and $E_s=u\Xi$; on the final interval $E_s$ and $q_s$ have the simultaneous scalar factor prescribed in Proposition <a href="#n3:deformation:homotopy" data-reference-type="ref" data-reference="n3:deformation:homotopy">23</a>. Define $\mathcal K_s(Z)=\widetilde Z$ by the linear mixed problem $$\label{n3:existence:compact-map-equation}
 \begin{cases}
  \mathop{\mathrm{div}}(4uA_\chi\nabla\widetilde Z+B_s)=E_s
                           &\text{in }\Omega_R,\\
  (4uA_\chi\nabla\widetilde Z+B_s)_\nu=q_s
                           &\text{on }B,\\
  \widetilde Z=0           &\text{on the outer face}.
 \end{cases}$$ The normal $\nu$ in the second line points into $\Omega_R$; the variational formulation uses its negative as the integration normal. This changes the sign of the boundary functional, not coercivity. On a bounded input set, the scalar gradient estimate bounds the coefficients above and away from zero. The nonempty outer Dirichlet face gives a Poincaré inequality, so the linear problem is uniquely solvable by its coercive bilinear form.

On bounded input sets in $C^{1,b}$, Lemma <a href="#n3:existence:scalar-solve" data-reference-type="ref" data-reference="n3:existence:scalar-solve">37</a> bounds $f$ in $C^{3,b}$. Hence the leading coefficient and drift in Equation <a href="#n3:existence:compact-map-equation" data-reference-type="eqref" data-reference="n3:existence:compact-map-equation">[n3:existence:compact-map-equation]</a> are $C^{1,b}$, the bulk source is $C^{0,b}$, and the prescribed boundary data are $C^{1,b}$. The derivatives of $t(x,Z,Df)$ involve only $DZ$ and $D^2f$, so this assertion includes the quadratic expression $\mathcal T$. Linear regularity gives a bounded output set in $C^{2,b}$. The inclusion $C^{2,b}\hookrightarrow C^{1,b}$ is compact on the finite domain. Continuous dependence of the scalar solve and the linear problem makes $(s,Z)\mapsto\mathcal K_s(Z)$ a continuous compact homotopy on bounded sets. These assertions hold also at the concatenation parameters because the defining equations coincide there. A fixed point solves the coupled system; repeated Schauder estimates make it smooth.

Admissibility is evaluated after the scalar solve. Define the open subset of the parameter–input product <a id="n3:existence:admissible-open-set"></a>$$\label{n3:existence:admissible-open-set}
 \mathcal O=\{(s,Z)\in[0,4]\times X_b:
       \min_{\overline{\Omega_R}}t_s[Z]>-\epsilon,
