Subtract a Sobolev extension of the normal datum, or of the Dirichlet datum, to obtain homogeneous boundary data. Even reflection for homogeneous normal data and odd reflection for homogeneous Dirichlet data give the constant-coefficient half-space estimate. The extension costs precisely the $W^{1-1/p,p}$ norm for the normal datum. Coefficient oscillation contributes $\sup|a_2-a_2(x_0)|\,\|D^2Z\|_p$ and is absorbed on small patches, uniformly by the established Hölder bound. Cutoffs and interpolation handle the first order terms. Scaling shows that the coefficient of the interior $L^p$ source norm is the constant $C_*$, independent of $h$; the lower order and trace terms account for $C_h$. This proves <a href="#four:reg:Z-linear" data-reference-type="eqref" data-reference="four:reg:Z-linear">[four:reg:Z-linear]</a> by the scalar local estimates (Gilbarg and Trudinger 2001) <a id="pm-cite-69"></a>[[GilbargTrudinger2001](#ref-GilbargTrudinger2001)]. The construction requires no meeting of different boundary types, and the inner and outer faces here are disjoint.

<a id="four:reg:quadratic-interpolation"></a>
For use in its nonlinear right hand side, the scaled scalar interpolation inequality on $Q_h$ is $$\label{four:reg:quadratic-interpolation}
 \|DZ\|_{L^{2p}(Q_h)}^2
 \le C\,\operatorname{osc}_{Q_h}Z\,
                  \|D^2Z\|_{L^p(Q_h)}
       +Ch^{4/p-2}\bigl(\operatorname{osc}_{Q_h}Z\bigr)^2.$$ One can obtain it on the unit patch by subtracting a constant, using a bounded Sobolev extension on a smooth ball or half-patch, and applying the Gagliardo–Nirenberg inequality with derivative orders $1,2$, exponents $2p,p,\infty$ and parameter $1/2$ (Li and Zhang 2022, Theorem 1.3) <a id="pm-cite-70"></a>[[LiZhang2022](#ref-LiZhang2022)]. To see the interpolation mechanism directly for a compactly supported function $v$, integration by parts gives $$\int|Dv|^{2p}
 \le C_p\|v\|_\infty
             \int|Dv|^{2p-2}|D^2v|
 \le C_p\|v\|_\infty
      \left(\int|Dv|^{2p}\right)^{1-1/p}\|D^2v\|_p.$$ Division gives the required product estimate. Extension and cutoff produce the additional $\|v\|_\infty^2$ term on a bounded unit patch. Finally rescaling $x=hy$ multiplies a squared $L^{2p}$ gradient norm and the Hessian product by $h^{4/p-2}$, which proves precisely the last power in <a href="#four:reg:quadratic-interpolation" data-reference-type="eqref" data-reference="four:reg:quadratic-interpolation">[four:reg:quadratic-interpolation]</a>.

Here is a cover argument that absorbs larger-patch norms without assuming their uniform boundedness in advance. Use uniformly comparable patches of radius $h$ covering the finite truncation, and their fixed-factor enlargements. Each enlargement is covered by at most $N$ smaller patches, where $N$ is independent of $h$, $R$ and the total number of patches. Let $$S=\sup_j\|D^2Z\|_{L^p(Q_h^j)}.$$ For each individual smooth solution on the finite truncation, $S$ is finite. The Hölder estimate for $Z$ gives $\operatorname{osc}_{Q_{2h}^j}Z\le C(n)h^\gamma$. Apply <a href="#four:reg:quadratic-interpolation" data-reference-type="eqref" data-reference="four:reg:quadratic-interpolation">[four:reg:quadratic-interpolation]</a> in the enlarged patches and then cover them by smaller ones. Its contribution to <a href="#four:reg:Z-linear" data-reference-type="eqref" data-reference="four:reg:Z-linear">[four:reg:Z-linear]</a> is at most $C_*C(n)h^\gamma N^{1/p}S+C(n,h)$. Choose $h$ small enough, also satisfying the linear freezing condition, that this coefficient is at most $1/4$. For the remaining first order term, local interpolation gives, for any $\varepsilon>0$, $$\|DZ\|_{L^p(Q_{2h}^j)}
 \le\varepsilon\|D^2Z\|_{L^p(Q_{2h}^j)}
                   +C(h,\varepsilon)\|Z\|_{L^p(Q_{2h}^j)}.$$ Choose $\varepsilon$ so that $C_h\varepsilon N^{1/p}\le1/4$. The bounded range controls the last term. Taking the supremum in <a href="#four:reg:Z-linear" data-reference-type="eqref" data-reference="four:reg:Z-linear">[four:reg:Z-linear]</a> now gives $S\le C(n,h)+S/2$, and hence a uniform bound for $S$. First order interpolation supplies the corresponding local $W^{2,p}$ bounds for $Z$. All constants may depend on the now fixed $h$ and on $n$, but not on the total number of patches or $R$.

<a id="pm-h-153"></a>
###### Alternating Schauder estimates and uniform geometry.

Since $p>4$, Sobolev embedding gives $Z\in C^{1,\theta'}$ for some $\theta'>0$. In conjunction with <a href="#four:reg:f-schauder" data-reference-type="eqref" data-reference="four:reg:f-schauder">[four:reg:f-schauder]</a>, the trace equation now has $C^{1,\theta''}$ coefficients and source for $0<\theta''\le\min\{\theta,\theta'\}$. One differentiation and the scalar Dirichlet Schauder estimate give $f\in C^{3,\theta''}$. The equation for $Z$ then has $C^{0,\theta''}$ source, and its normal datum <a href="#four:reg:normal-data" data-reference-type="eqref" data-reference="four:reg:normal-data">[four:reg:normal-data]</a> is $C^{1,\theta''}$. The scalar normal-derivative or Dirichlet Schauder estimate gives $Z\in C^{2,\theta''}$. The boundary estimate is justified by the same frozen half-space problem used above: its normal derivative does not annihilate a nonzero decaying solution of the homogeneous principal equation. Smooth normal coordinates and smooth normal field therefore satisfy its obliqueness condition.

Repeating in the order $f$ then $Z$ increases the number of derivatives by one each time. The trace equation uses $Z$ without derivatives; the expanded second equation uses only $D^2f$ and $DZ$ in its lower terms; and its boundary expression uses only $Df$. These are exactly the derivative counts needed for the iteration. The smooth fixed coefficients give all finite orders.

The compact inner faces have uniform smooth collars. On the prepared end, the metric and all fixed coefficient fields have uniform bounds on unit patches. Large coordinate spheres have boundary normal charts with uniform bounds of each finite order, and are separated from the inner faces. Thus every radius, ellipticity bound, chart constant and local covering number used above is independent of the sufficiently large truncation radius. Finally a uniform local $C^2$ bound controls any prescribed $C^{1,\alpha_0}$ norm, $\alpha_0<1$, on a fixed finite truncation. This proves the proposition. ◻

</details>

<a id="stmt-four-reg-scalar-trial-interface"></a>
<div id="four:reg:scalar-trial-interface" class="remark">

*Remark 135*. Theorem <a href="#four:thm:axial-regularity" data-reference-type="ref" data-reference="four:thm:axial-regularity">132</a> also applies in the scalar trial problem below. Its separate height and gradient bounds give bounded source and a positive axial eigenvalue without the floor. Interpolation of the principal matrix with $\mathop{\mathrm{Id}}$ preserves its three unit transverse eigenvalues. A trial $Z\in C^{1,\alpha_0}$ then supplies the coefficient regularity for scalar Schauder estimates through $f\in C^{3,\alpha_0}$; this requires $DZ$, but no second derivative of the trial input.

</div>

<a id="four:sec:existence"></a>
##### Existence and the energy comparison

We now construct solutions of the system, exhaust the asymptotically flat end, and compare the resulting Riemannian energy with the energy of the prepared data. The distinction between two kinds of constants is essential. Constants in the scalar solution map and in local regularity may depend arbitrarily on a fixed $n$; constants used in the final flux estimate are the polynomial bounds $\Pi_n$ established earlier.

<a id="pm-h-155"></a>
###### A scalar solution map on the whole trial space

Fix $0<\alpha<1$, a sufficiently large integer $n$, and an allowed truncation $\Omega_R$. In this subsection constants may depend on $R$, $n$, and a bound for the trial input in $$X_R=\{Z\in C^{1,\alpha}(\overline\Omega_R):Z|_{S_R}=0\}.$$ The four stages of the homotopy are parametrized consecutively by $s\in[0,4]$, with $s=0$ the desired system and $s=4$ its zero terminal scale. Denote their trace prescriptions by $F_s^{\mathrm{presc}}(x,w,h,t)$. All dependence suppressed in this notation is the smooth dependence specified in the homotopy.

<a id="stmt-four-ex-scalar-trial"></a>
<div id="four:ex:scalar-trial" class="lemma">

**Lemma 136** (Scalar trial problem). *For every $Z\in X_R$ and $s\in[0,4]$, the prescribed trace equation with the assigned constant Dirichlet value on every boundary component has a unique solution $f_s[Z]\in C^{3,\alpha}(\overline\Omega_R)$. The map $(s,Z)\mapsto f_s[Z]$ is continuous into $C^{3,\alpha}$ and maps bounded trial sets to bounded sets, uniformly in $s$. No lower bound for the implicitly defined $t$ is imposed on the trial inputs.*

</div>

<details id="proof-stmt-four-ex-scalar-trial"><summary>Proof of stmt-four-ex-scalar-trial</summary>

<a id="four:ex:scalar-interpolation"></a>
*Proof.* The normalized equation is <a id="four:ex:scalar-normalized"></a>$$\label{four:ex:scalar-normalized}
 A_\chi:\mathop{\mathrm{Hess}}_g f=G_s(x,Z,f,\,\mathrm df),\qquad
 G_s=\frac{\sqrt D}{l}
       \bigl(F_s^{\mathrm{presc}}-\mathop{\mathrm{tr}}_{A_\chi}K\bigr).$$ The implicit relation defining $t$ is smoothly solvable for every $(Z,\,\mathrm df)$. Neither $t$, the matrix, nor the positive prefactor $\sqrt D/l$ depends on the value of $f$. The prescriptions satisfy $$|F_s^{\mathrm{presc}}-h|\le C,
 \qquad \partial_h F_s^{\mathrm{presc}}\ge1,
 \qquad h=\eta_n f,$$ with the other arguments held fixed. For a second parameter $\beta\in[0,1]$, use the scalar interpolation $$\label{four:ex:scalar-interpolation}
 A_\beta:\mathop{\mathrm{Hess}}_g f=G_\beta,
 \quad A_\beta=(1-\beta)\mathop{\mathrm{Id}}+\beta A_\chi,
 \quad G_\beta=(1-\beta)\eta_n f+\beta G_s,$$ with the same Dirichlet values. At a positive interior maximum above a fixed height threshold, both source summands are positive, whereas the left side is nonpositive. The negative minimum argument is identical with signs reversed. Including the assigned boundary values gives $|h|\le C$, uniformly in both parameters and the bounded trial set.

<a id="four:ex:linear-growth"></a>
We next check the degeneracy at large gradient, before invoking any regularity theorem. Put $\sigma=|\,\mathrm df|_g$. Uniformly for bounded $Z$, $\sigma\to\infty$ forces $t\to-\infty$: a lower bound on $t$ would bound $e^{6t}l(t)^2$ away from zero, contradicting $e^{6Z}=e^{6t}(1+l(t)^2\sigma^2)$. Thus eventually $t<0$ and $l(t)=e^{nt}$, giving the exact equation <a id="four:ex:large-gradient-equation"></a>$$\label{four:ex:large-gradient-equation}
 e^{6Z}=e^{6t}+e^{(2n+6)t}\sigma^2.$$ Writing $\gamma_n=6/(n+3)$, its consequences, uniformly for $Z$ in a fixed bounded interval, are <a id="four:ex:large-gradient"></a>$$\begin{aligned}
 t&=-\frac{\log\sigma}{n+3}+\frac{3Z}{n+3}+o(1),\nonumber\\
 d&=e^{-6nZ/(n+3)}\sigma^{-\gamma_n}(1+o(1)),
 &\chi&=\frac{3}{n+3}d(1+o(1)),\label{four:ex:large-gradient}\\
 \frac{\sqrt D}{l}&=\sigma(1+o(1)).\nonumber
\end{aligned}$$ For example, the first line follows by taking logarithms of $e^{(2n+6)t}\sigma^2=e^{6Z}(1-d)$; the last follows directly from $\sqrt D/l=(\sigma^2+l^{-2})^{1/2}$. Since $n\ge4$, one has $\gamma_n<1$. Compactness of the remaining bounded-gradient range therefore gives constants $c,C>0$ such that $$\label{four:ex:linear-growth}
 \chi_\beta:=1-\beta+\beta\chi\ge\frac{c}{1+\sigma},
 \qquad |G_\beta|\le C(1+\sigma).$$ The estimate for the source uses the height bound just proved. Notice also the exact structural identity $$A_\beta=\mathop{\mathrm{Id}}-(1-\chi_\beta)e\otimes e,
 \qquad e=\mathop{\mathrm{grad}}f/|\mathop{\mathrm{grad}}f|,
 \qquad 0<\chi_\beta\le1.$$ In particular, all three transverse eigenvalues remain exactly one throughout the scalar interpolation.

<a id="four:ex:log-choices"></a>
Here is a gradient estimate using only <a href="#four:ex:linear-growth" data-reference-type="eqref" data-reference="four:ex:linear-growth">[four:ex:linear-growth]</a>. Extend $g$ smoothly across the boundary to a compact enlargement. All distances below are distances of this extension, at scales below its injectivity radius. If $H_0$ is the uniform bound for $|f|$, set $$\psi(r)=\frac1k\log(1+B'r),\qquad
 q_1(r)=\psi'(r),\qquad \psi''(r)=-kq_1(r)^2.$$ First choose $k$ large relative to the constants in <a href="#four:ex:linear-growth" data-reference-type="eqref" data-reference="four:ex:linear-growth">[four:ex:linear-growth]</a> and the bounded geometry. Next choose $h_0<1/(4k)$ below all collar, injectivity, and distinct-boundary-component separation scales. Finally choose $B'$ so large that $$\label{four:ex:log-choices}
 q_1\ge1\quad(0\le r\le h_0),\qquad
 \psi(h_0)>2H_0.$$ These requirements are compatible: $q_1(h_0)$ tends to $1/(kh_0)>4$ and $\psi(h_0)$ tends to infinity as $B'\to\infty$.

<a id="four:ex:boundary-modulus"></a>
On the inward collar of a boundary face with constant value $f_0$, let $r$ be its distance function. The functions $f_0\pm\psi(r)$ are upper and lower barriers. To check the upper barrier at a hypothetical positive maximum of $f-f_0-\psi(r)$, the common gradient is $q_1\mathop{\mathrm{grad}}r$. The tangential Hessian of the barrier contributes at most $Cq_1$, and its axial contribution is at most $-ckq_1^2/(1+q_1)$. By enlarging $k$ this is strictly less than $-C(1+q_1)$, the lower bound for the equation’s source at the solution height. Ellipticity and the second derivative test contradict the equation. For the lower barrier both inequalities reverse. At the outer edge of the collar the comparisons follow from <a href="#four:ex:log-choices" data-reference-type="eqref" data-reference="four:ex:log-choices">[four:ex:log-choices]</a>. Consequently $$\label{four:ex:boundary-modulus}
 |f(x)-f_0|\le\psi\bigl(\operatorname{dist}(x,\mathrm{face})\bigr)
 \quad\hbox{in its $h_0$ collar}.$$

For completeness, the same modulus controls interior pairs. Suppose that $$f(x)-f(y)-\psi\bigl(\operatorname{dist}(x,y)\bigr)$$ has a positive maximum on pairs of distance at most $h_0$. Neither the diagonal nor the distance-$h_0$ set contains such a maximum. If an endpoint lies on a face, the other endpoint lies in that face’s collar; <a href="#four:ex:boundary-modulus" data-reference-type="eqref" data-reference="four:ex:boundary-modulus">[four:ex:boundary-modulus]</a> and monotonicity of $\psi$ exclude this as well. Thus both endpoints are interior. Let $r>0$ be their distance and orient their unique short geodesic from $y$ to $x$. The first derivative test says that their gradients are $q_1(r)$ times the corresponding parallel unit tangent vectors.

Vary both endpoints in each of three parallel transverse directions. The index-form estimate for the second variation of distance, using the parallel field along the geodesic, is bounded above by $Cr$. The second derivative test for the two-point maximum therefore gives $$\mathop{\mathrm{tr}}_{e^\perp}\mathop{\mathrm{Hess}}f(x)-\mathop{\mathrm{tr}}_{e^\perp}\mathop{\mathrm{Hess}}f(y)
 \le Cq_1r.$$ Separate axial variations at the two endpoints give $$\mathop{\mathrm{Hess}}f(x)(e,e)\le\psi'',\qquad
 \mathop{\mathrm{Hess}}f(y)(e,e)\ge-\psi''.$$ Because the transverse coefficients are exactly one at both endpoints, while the axial coefficients satisfy <a href="#four:ex:linear-growth" data-reference-type="eqref" data-reference="four:ex:linear-growth">[four:ex:linear-growth]</a>, the difference of the two left sides of <a href="#four:ex:scalar-interpolation" data-reference-type="eqref" data-reference="four:ex:scalar-interpolation">[four:ex:scalar-interpolation]</a> is at most $$Cq_1r-\frac{2ckq_1^2}{1+q_1}.$$ Their source difference is at least $-2C(1+q_1)$. Since $q_1\ge1$, these inequalities contradict each other for the already sufficiently large $k$. No comparison of the two axial coefficients was used. Only variations of the interior endpoints were required, so the short geodesic need not remain inside $\Omega_R$. We have proved the two-point modulus; letting $y\to x$ gives $|\,\mathrm df|\le\psi'(0)=B'/k$ everywhere, including the boundary by <a href="#four:ex:boundary-modulus" data-reference-type="eqref" data-reference="four:ex:boundary-modulus">[four:ex:boundary-modulus]</a>.

The scalar interpolation is now uniformly elliptic. On the given smooth interior and constant-Dirichlet boundary patches, its equation has the exact form required by Theorem <a href="#four:thm:axial-regularity" data-reference-type="ref" data-reference="four:thm:axial-regularity">132</a>: the gradient and source are bounded, and $0<\chi_0\le\chi_\beta\le1$. That theorem first gives a uniform Hölder bound for $\,\mathrm df$, at some positive exponent. The coefficients and source in <a href="#four:ex:scalar-interpolation" data-reference-type="eqref" data-reference="four:ex:scalar-interpolation">[four:ex:scalar-interpolation]</a> are smooth compositions of $x,Z,f,\,\mathrm df$, so the scalar Dirichlet Schauder estimate gives $C^{2,\alpha'}$ bounds for some $\alpha'>0$. These bounds make $f,\,\mathrm df$ Lipschitz. Together with $Z\in C^{1,\alpha}$, this yields $C^{0,\alpha}$ coefficients and source, hence $C^{2,\alpha}$ bounds. The compositions are now $C^{1,\alpha}$ and the next Dirichlet estimate gives a $C^{3,\alpha}$ bound.

Subtract a smooth extension of the assigned boundary values and work in the affine space with model $Y_R=C^{3,\alpha}_0(\overline\Omega_R)$, where the zero trace is on the entire boundary. The equation defines a continuously differentiable map into $C^{1,\alpha}(\overline\Omega_R)$. Its derivative in $f$ is $$L\varphi=A_\beta^{ij}\nabla_i\nabla_j\varphi
          +b^i\nabla_i\varphi-c(x)\varphi,
 \qquad
 c(x)=\eta_n\left[(1-\beta)+
 \beta\frac{\sqrt D}{l}\partial_hF_s^{\mathrm{presc}}\right]>0.$$ Derivatives of $A_\beta$ and $t$ with respect to $\,\mathrm df$ contribute only first derivative terms in $\varphi$. Its coefficients are $C^{1,\alpha}$ and the ellipticity and positivity are uniform on the bounded range. The maximum principle removes the homogeneous Dirichlet kernel. Linear Dirichlet solvability and Schauder estimates therefore make $L:Y_R\to C^{1,\alpha}$ an isomorphism (Gilbarg and Trudinger 2001) <a id="pm-cite-71"></a>[[GilbargTrudinger2001](#ref-GilbargTrudinger2001)]. The implicit function theorem proves openness in $\beta$. The bounds above prove closedness: subsequences converge in lower Hölder norms, their limits solve the equation, and the uniform $C^{3,\alpha}$ estimates retain that regularity. At $\beta=0$ the equation is $\Delta_gf=\eta_nf$, with ordinary Dirichlet solvability. Thus the scalar equation is solvable at $\beta=1$.

For uniqueness, at a positive maximum of the difference of two solutions their gradients agree. Their matrices and positive prefactors therefore agree, whereas strict height monotonicity makes the source difference positive, contradicting the Hessian comparison. The reverse comparison completes uniqueness. Applying the same implicit function theorem with parameters $(s,Z)$ proves continuous dependence into $C^{3,\alpha}$. At stage junctions use one-sided parameter neighborhoods and the agreement of the prescriptions. The estimates were uniform on bounded trial sets, which proves the last assertion. ◻

</details>

<a id="pm-h-156"></a>
###### The frozen return map and degree

For a trial pair $(f_s[Z],Z)$, evaluate all expressions in the homotopy at that pair. Write $A=uA_\chi$, let $B_s=\lambda uA_\chi K(w,\cdot)$ be its drift, and write $Q_s$ and $q_s$ for the prescribed interior source and inner flux, including the common terminal scale. Define $T_sZ=Y$ by the linear problem <a id="four:ex:frozen-problem"></a>$$\label{four:ex:frozen-problem}
 \begin{aligned}
 \mathop{\mathrm{div}}_g(3A\mathop{\mathrm{grad}}Y+B_s)&=Q_s &&\hbox{in }\Omega_R,\\
 (3A\mathop{\mathrm{grad}}Y+B_s)\cdot\nu&=q_s &&\hbox{on }B,\\
 Y&=0 &&\hbox{on }S_R.
 \end{aligned}$$ Thus only the occurrence of $3\mathop{\mathrm{grad}}Z$ in the flux is replaced by $3\mathop{\mathrm{grad}}Y$; the coefficients, source, and boundary expression are frozen. In $q_s$ the value of $F$ is always its trace prescription.

<a id="four:ex:compact-map"></a>
The matrix $A$ is symmetric positive definite and $C^{1,\alpha}$. On bounded trial sets its ellipticity constants, $C^{1,\alpha}$ norm, and those of $B_s,q_s$ are bounded; $Q_s$ is bounded in $C^{0,\alpha}$. In particular the source uses $\,\mathrm dZ$ and $\mathop{\mathrm{Hess}}f$, whose regularity is already available. With $$\mathcal H_R=\{Y\in H^1(\Omega_R):Y|_{S_R}=0\},$$ the weak problem has coercive bilinear form $3\int_{\Omega_R} A\mathop{\mathrm{grad}}Y\cdot\mathop{\mathrm{grad}}\varphi$. Indeed $\Omega_R$ is connected and $S_R$ is nonempty, so Poincaré’s inequality holds on $\mathcal H_R$. The prescribed flux is a bounded linear functional by the trace inequality. Lax–Milgram gives a unique weak solution. At an inner face $f$ is constant, so $A_\chi\nu=\chi\nu$, and its flux condition is equivalently $$\partial_\nu Y=\frac{q_s-B_s\cdot\nu}{3u\chi}.$$ This is a $C^{1,\alpha}$ ordinary normal datum. The disjoint Dirichlet and normal faces have no corners. Linear boundary and interior estimates give $Y\in C^{2,\alpha}$ with bounds uniform on bounded trial sets; the weak energy estimate supplies the lower norm in these estimates. Coefficient dependence and uniqueness, or the same linear estimates applied to differences, give continuous dependence. Consequently $$\label{four:ex:compact-map}
 T:[0,4]\times X_R\longrightarrow X_R
 \quad\hbox{is continuous and compact on bounded sets}.$$ Here compactness uses the compact embedding $C^{2,\alpha}\hookrightarrow C^{1,\alpha}$ on the fixed truncation.

Every fixed point is smooth. Initially it has $Z\in C^{2,\alpha}$ and $f\in C^{3,\alpha}$. The trace equation raises the regularity of $f$, and then expansion of the divergence equation, with its normal boundary datum, raises the regularity of $Z$. Repetition gives all orders. The smooth a priori estimates from the preceding sections therefore apply to every fixed point.

<a id="stmt-four-prop-existence"></a>
<div id="four:prop:existence" class="proposition">

**Proposition 137** (Existence and exhaustion). *Fix the prepared geometry and $0<\epsilon<1$. For every sufficiently large $n$ and every allowed $R$, system <a href="#four:eq:system" data-reference-type="eqref" data-reference="four:eq:system">[four:eq:system]</a> has a smooth solution on $\overline\Omega_R$ with $t>-\epsilon$. For each such fixed $n$ there is a sequence $R\to\infty$ whose solutions converge smoothly on compact subsets up to $B$ to a solution on $\overline\Omega$ with $t\ge-\epsilon$. This solution satisfies the prescribed inner boundary conditions, the height interval <a href="#four:eq:height-interval" data-reference-type="eqref" data-reference="four:eq:height-interval">[four:eq:height-interval]</a>, and the weighted trace and flux estimates of Lemma <a href="#four:lem:weighted-trace" data-reference-type="ref" data-reference="four:lem:weighted-trace">128</a>.*

</div>

<details id="proof-stmt-four-prop-existence"><summary>Proof of stmt-four-prop-existence</summary>

*Proof.* Choose $n$ large enough for Proposition <a href="#four:prop:height-exclusion" data-reference-type="ref" data-reference="four:prop:height-exclusion">126</a>, the collar estimates, and the polynomial absorption conditions used in Proposition <a href="#four:prop:bounded-range" data-reference-type="ref" data-reference="four:prop:bounded-range">131</a>. Fix an allowed $R$. By <a href="#four:eq:bounded-range" data-reference-type="eqref" data-reference="four:eq:bounded-range">[four:eq:bounded-range]</a> and Proposition <a href="#four:prop:coupled-regularity" data-reference-type="ref" data-reference="four:prop:coupled-regularity">134</a>, choose $M_0$ strictly larger than every $C^{1,\alpha}$ norm of an above-floor fixed point on this truncation. Define <a id="four:ex:moving-sections"></a>$$\label{four:ex:moving-sections}
 \mathcal O_s=\left\{Z\in X_R:
 \|Z\|_{C^{1,\alpha}}<M_0,\quad
 \min_{\overline\Omega_R}t\bigl(Z,\,\mathrm df_s[Z]\bigr)>-\epsilon\right\}.$$ Lemma <a href="#four:ex:scalar-trial" data-reference-type="ref" data-reference="four:ex:scalar-trial">136</a> and smooth implicit dependence of $t$ make their union relatively open in $[0,4]\times X_R$.

For clarity, the varying domain causes no extra degree assumption. Let $\mathcal K$ consist of fixed points in the closure of this union with norm at most $M_0$. A sequence in $\mathcal K$ has a convergent subsequence because of <a href="#four:ex:compact-map" data-reference-type="eqref" data-reference="four:ex:compact-map">[four:ex:compact-map]</a>; continuity makes its limit a fixed point. The limit has $\min t\ge-\epsilon$. Proposition <a href="#four:prop:floor-exclusion" data-reference-type="ref" data-reference="four:prop:floor-exclusion">125</a> excludes equality, and the choice of $M_0$ excludes contact with the norm boundary. Thus $\mathcal K$ is compact and lies in the open union of the sections.

Fix a parameter $s_0$. Cover its compact fixed point slice by finitely many small open balls in $X_R$ whose closed balls remain in all $\mathcal O_s$ for $s$ close to $s_0$. Let $U$ be their union. All fixed points in the closed sections for sufficiently close parameters lie in $U$: otherwise a sequence of omitted fixed points converging to the slice would contradict compactness and its containment in the open set $U$. Excision identifies the degree on $\mathcal O_s$ with that on $U$, and fixed-domain homotopy invariance makes the latter constant. If the slice is empty, compactness gives no fixed points nearby and the same conclusion with degree zero. Hence $\deg(\mathop{\mathrm{Id}}-T_s,\mathcal O_s,0)$ is locally constant, and therefore constant, on $[0,4]$ (Deimling 1985) <a id="pm-cite-72"></a>[[Deimling1985](#ref-Deimling1985)].

At $s=4$, the scalar prescription is $\mathop{\mathrm{tr}}_{A_\chi}H^f=h+D_1(x,w)$ with zero boundary heights. At an interior extremum $w=0$ and $D_1=0$, so the maximum principle gives $f=0$ for every trial $Z$, and then $t=Z$. The terminal scale sets both frozen right sides to zero and the drift is absent. Testing the frozen equation with $Y$ gives $Y=0$; thus $T_4$ is the zero map, even though its positive coefficients may depend on the input. Its sole fixed point, $Z=0$, belongs to $\mathcal O_4$ and has degree one. The degree at $s=0$ is consequently one, proving existence there.

Now keep $n$ fixed. The preceding choices of sufficiently large $n$ used only the already proved uniform height and collar results and polynomial losses such as $\Pi_n\eta_n/\ell\to0$. The arbitrary fixed-$n$ constants in the scalar construction impose no subsequent condition on $n$. The bounds in Proposition <a href="#four:prop:coupled-regularity" data-reference-type="ref" data-reference="four:prop:coupled-regularity">134</a> are uniform in allowed $R$ on each compact set, including its portions on $B$. A diagonal Arzelà–Ascoli argument along $R\to\infty$ gives smooth convergence on all these sets. The equation and inner data pass to the limit, as do $t\ge-\epsilon$, the height interval, and the collar estimates. Smooth convergence on the fixed collars passes the weighted trace and flux inequalities as well. Strictness of the floor in this exhaustion limit is unnecessary below. ◻

</details>

<a id="pm-h-157"></a>
###### Decay on the end

<a id="stmt-four-lem-end-decay"></a>
<div id="four:lem:end-decay" class="lemma">

<a id="four:ex:end-f"></a>
<a id="four:ex:end-tz"></a>
**Lemma 138** (End estimates). *For every solution obtained in Proposition <a href="#four:prop:existence" data-reference-type="ref" data-reference="four:prop:existence">137</a>, with $n$ fixed, there is $a_n>0$ such that, for every integer $j\ge0$, $$\label{four:ex:end-f}
 |\nabla^jf|+|\nabla^j(t-Z)|\le C_j(n)e^{-a_nr}
 \quad\hbox{on the distant end}.$$ Moreover $$\label{four:ex:end-tz}
 t,Z=O_2(r^{-2}),\qquad \Delta_gt=O(r^{-4-\delta_1}).$$ The constants in these assertions may depend arbitrarily on $n$. The zeroth-order estimates and <a href="#four:ex:end-f" data-reference-type="eqref" data-reference="four:ex:end-f">[four:ex:end-f]</a> hold uniformly for the finite-truncation solutions up to their outer faces.*

</div>

<details id="proof-stmt-four-lem-end-decay"><summary>Proof of stmt-four-lem-end-decay</summary>

<a id="four:ex:f-end-linear"></a>
*Proof.* Choose a fixed sphere beyond the supports of $K,C$, and all collar terms. Along each finite-truncation solution the trace equation is the homogeneous linear equation $$\label{four:ex:f-end-linear}
 A_\chi:\mathop{\mathrm{Hess}}_g f-c(x)f=0,\qquad
 c(x)=\eta_n\frac{\sqrt D}{l}\ge c_n>0.$$ By <a href="#four:eq:bounded-range" data-reference-type="eqref" data-reference="four:eq:bounded-range">[four:eq:bounded-range]</a> the coefficients are uniformly elliptic; by Proposition <a href="#four:prop:coupled-regularity" data-reference-type="ref" data-reference="four:prop:coupled-regularity">134</a> all their derivatives are bounded on uniform unit patches, independently of $R$. On the end, $$(A_\chi:\mathop{\mathrm{Hess}}_g-c)e^{-ar}
 =e^{-ar}\bigl(a^2A_\chi(\,\mathrm dr,\,\mathrm dr)
          -aA_\chi:\mathop{\mathrm{Hess}}_g r-c\bigr).$$ Choose $a=a_n>0$ so small that the first term is less than $c_n/4$, and then enlarge the fixed sphere so the second term has magnitude less than $c_n/4$. Thus $e^{-a_nr}$ is a strict supersolution. A fixed multiple dominates both signs of $f$ on the initial sphere and dominates the zero Dirichlet data on $S_R$. Linear comparison gives $|f|\le C(n)e^{-a_nr}$ uniformly in $R$. Local estimates for <a href="#four:ex:f-end-linear" data-reference-type="eqref" data-reference="four:ex:f-end-linear">[four:ex:f-end-linear]</a>, including the zero-Dirichlet estimates on the uniform outer-sphere charts, give the same exponential decay for every derivative, after harmless reduction of $a_n$ if necessary. The identity $$Z-t=\tfrac16\log(1+l(t)^2|\,\mathrm df|^2)$$ and the uniform smooth local bounds then give <a href="#four:ex:end-f" data-reference-type="eqref" data-reference="four:ex:end-f">[four:ex:end-f]</a>. Every graph contribution to the metric and to the equations is exponentially small with unit-patch derivatives.

<a id="four:ex:Z-end-equation"></a>
<a id="four:ex:Phi-Poisson"></a>
At zero graph and $K=0$, the exact formulas give $$u=e^{2Z}l(Z),\qquad V=3u\mathop{\mathrm{grad}}Z,
 \qquad \mathcal T=3(p(Z)+1)|\,\mathrm dZ|^2.$$ Hence the actual divergence equation, divided by $u$, becomes $$\label{four:ex:Z-end-equation}
 3\Delta_gZ+3\mathfrak b_n(Z)|\,\mathrm dZ|_g^2
 =\rho-m_0(Z)C_n\rho_0+\mathcal E_n,
 \quad \mathfrak b_n(z)=p(z)+2-\delta_0(p(z)+1),$$ where $\mathcal E_n$ and its derivatives on unit patches are $O_j(e^{-a_nr})$. Define the strictly increasing function <a id="four:ex:Phi"></a>$$\label{four:ex:Phi}
 \Phi(0)=0,\qquad
 \Phi'(z)=\exp\left(\int_0^z \mathfrak b_n(s)\,\,\mathrm ds\right).$$ Its derivative is bounded above and away from zero on the fixed bounded range of $Z$. The chain rule cancels the quadratic term: $$\label{four:ex:Phi-Poisson}
 \Delta_g\Phi(Z)
 =\frac{\Phi'(Z)}3
    \bigl(\rho-m_0(Z)C_n\rho_0+\mathcal E_n\bigr),
 \qquad |\Delta_g\Phi(Z)|\le C(n)r^{-4-\delta_1}.$$ Put $\beta_1=\delta_1/2$ and $W(r)=r^{-2}(1-r^{-\beta_1})$. In dimension four, $$\Delta_\delta W=-\beta_1(2+\beta_1)r^{-4-\beta_1},
 \qquad
 \Delta_gW=-\beta_1(2+\beta_1)r^{-4-\beta_1}+O(r^{-6}).$$ Since $0<\beta_1<\delta_1<1$, a sufficiently large multiple of $W$ is positive and has negative Laplacian dominating the absolute source in <a href="#four:ex:Phi-Poisson" data-reference-type="eqref" data-reference="four:ex:Phi-Poisson">[four:ex:Phi-Poisson]</a> on a sufficiently distant end. Enlarge the multiple to dominate $|\Phi(Z)|$ on its initial sphere. Its value is positive on $S_R$, whereas $\Phi(Z)=0$ there. Applying the maximum principle to both $\Phi(Z)-CW$ and $-\Phi(Z)-CW$ gives $$|\Phi(Z)|\le C(n)r^{-2},\qquad |Z|\le C(n)r^{-2},$$ uniformly on truncations and then in the exhaustion limit.

Here are the differentiated estimates, which do not follow from the pointwise barrier alone. On an annulus of radius $r_1$, rescale by $x=r_1y$ and set $U(y)=r_1^2\Phi(Z(r_1y))$. Its supremum and its Poisson source in the rescaled equation are bounded: the source is $r_1^4$ times the right side of <a href="#four:ex:Phi-Poisson" data-reference-type="eqref" data-reference="four:ex:Phi-Poisson">[four:ex:Phi-Poisson]</a>, of size $O_n(r_1^{-\delta_1})$. The rescaled background coefficients have uniform smooth bounds. Interior $W^{2,p}$ estimates, for a fixed $p>4$, give bounded $C^{1,\theta}$ norms of $U$ on a smaller annulus. The weights have their differentiated power decay, the compositions with $Z$ now have bounded scaled Hölder norms, and the exponential errors remain bounded with all scaled derivatives. The right side therefore has a bounded $C^{0,\theta}$ norm. Schauder estimates give a bounded $C^{2,\theta}$ norm of $U$. The inverse of $\Phi$ has bounded smooth derivatives on the relevant range. Rescaling back gives $Z=O_2(r^{-2})$, and <a href="#four:ex:end-f" data-reference-type="eqref" data-reference="four:ex:end-f">[four:ex:end-f]</a> gives the same statement for $t$. Finally $|\,\mathrm dZ|^2=O(r^{-6})$ in <a href="#four:ex:Z-end-equation" data-reference-type="eqref" data-reference="four:ex:Z-end-equation">[four:ex:Z-end-equation]</a>; since $\delta_1<1$, this is lower order than $r^{-4-\delta_1}$. Equation <a href="#four:ex:end-f" data-reference-type="eqref" data-reference="four:ex:end-f">[four:ex:end-f]</a> now gives the asserted bound for $\Delta_gt$. ◻

</details>

<a id="pm-h-158"></a>
###### Scalar curvature, boundary sign, and finite flux

<a id="four:ex:positive-scalar"></a>
For the desired system $F=h+C$ and $w(h)=\eta_n a\sigma$. Substitute these into <a href="#four:eq:scalar-identity" data-reference-type="eqref" data-reference="four:eq:scalar-identity">[four:eq:scalar-identity]</a> and use $\mathop{\mathrm{div}}V=u\Xi$ to obtain $$\label{four:ex:positive-scalar}
 \begin{split}
 \tfrac12e^{2t}\mathop{\mathrm{Scal}}_{\widehat g}
 ={}&\mu+J(w)+w(C)-\rho-(h+C)\tau\\
 &+(1-\delta_0)(\mathcal T+\eta_n a\sigma)+m_0\mathcal P\ \ge0.
 \end{split}$$ Indeed $|w|\le1$, and on $\mathop{\mathrm{supp}}K$ the height interval <a href="#four:eq:height-interval" data-reference-type="eqref" data-reference="four:eq:height-interval">[four:eq:height-interval]</a> permits use of <a href="#four:eq:trace-slack" data-reference-type="eqref" data-reference="four:eq:trace-slack">[four:eq:trace-slack]</a>: $$\mu+J(w)+w(C)-\rho-(h+C)\tau
 \ge\mu-|J|-|\,\mathrm dC|-\rho-|(h+C)\tau|\ge0.$$ Outside $\mathop{\mathrm{supp}}K$ the same slack inequality needs no height restriction. The other terms are nonnegative by <a href="#four:eq:coercivity" data-reference-type="eqref" data-reference="four:eq:coercivity">[four:eq:coercivity]</a> and the definitions of the penalty and $\delta_0$. Thus the nonmaximal trace term has been retained and controlled at this final step.

<a id="four:ex:negative-boundary"></a>
<a id="four:ex:final-AF"></a>
<a id="four:ex:metric-comparison"></a>
The inner flux condition and <a href="#four:eq:boundary-identity" data-reference-type="eqref" data-reference="four:eq:boundary-identity">[four:eq:boundary-identity]</a> give exactly $$\label{four:ex:negative-boundary}
 H+3\partial_\nu t=-N_B,
 \qquad \widehat H=-e^{-t}\sqrt d\,N_B<0
 \quad\hbox{on every component of }B.$$ All quantities here are finite and $d>0$ for each fixed $n$. Furthermore <a href="#four:ex:end-f" data-reference-type="eqref" data-reference="four:ex:end-f">[four:ex:end-f]</a> and <a href="#four:ex:end-tz" data-reference-type="eqref" data-reference="four:ex:end-tz">[four:ex:end-tz]</a> imply $$\label{four:ex:final-AF}
 \widehat g-\delta=O_2(r^{-2}),\qquad
 \mathop{\mathrm{Scal}}_{\widehat g}=O(r^{-4-\delta_1}).$$ For the scalar estimate one may use the conformal scalar formula with $\bar g=g+O_j(e^{-a_nr})$: $e^{2t}\mathop{\mathrm{Scal}}_{\widehat g}=\mathop{\mathrm{Scal}}_{\bar g}-6\Delta_{\bar g}t
-6|\,\mathrm dt|_{\bar g}^2$. The prepared scalar decay and <a href="#four:ex:end-tz" data-reference-type="eqref" data-reference="four:ex:end-tz">[four:ex:end-tz]</a> give precisely <a href="#four:ex:final-AF" data-reference-type="eqref" data-reference="four:ex:final-AF">[four:ex:final-AF]</a>. The nonnegative scalar curvature is therefore integrable. The inequality $$\label{four:ex:metric-comparison}
 \widehat g=e^{2t}(g+l^2\,\mathrm df\otimes\,\mathrm df)\ge e^{-2\epsilon}g$$ also proves completeness with $B$ included: a $\widehat g$-Cauchy sequence is $g$-Cauchy, its limit belongs to the closed complete exterior, and smooth local metric equivalence gives convergence in $\widehat g$.

<a id="stmt-four-prop-mass-comparison"></a>
<div id="four:prop:mass-comparison" class="proposition">

<a id="four:ex:energy-error"></a>
**Proposition 139** (Energy comparison). *For each fixed $\epsilon>0$ and all sufficiently large $n$, the limiting metric has finite ADM energy and $$\label{four:ex:energy-error}
 E_{\widehat g}\le E_g+\frac{\Pi_n}{3\omega_3}
                  \left(\ell+\frac{\ell^2}{\eta_n}\right).$$ The polynomial $\Pi_n$ depends only on the prepared data, $\epsilon$, and the fixed geometric choices. In particular the error tends to zero as $n\to\infty$ with $\epsilon$ fixed.*

</div>

<details id="proof-stmt-four-prop-mass-comparison"><summary>Proof of stmt-four-prop-mass-comparison</summary>

<a id="four:ex:V-asymptotics"></a>
<a id="four:ex:flux"></a>
*Proof.* We first establish the exact sign and normalization at fixed $n$. Lemma <a href="#four:lem:end-decay" data-reference-type="ref" data-reference="four:lem:end-decay">138</a> gives $u=1+O_n(r^{-2})$ and $$\label{four:ex:V-asymptotics}
 V=3\mathop{\mathrm{grad}}_gt+O_n(r^{-5})+O_n(e^{-a_nr}).$$ Also $u\Xi\in L^1(\Omega,\,\mathrm dV_g)$: on the end the quadratic term is $O_n(r^{-6})$, the graph and height-gradient terms are exponentially small, and the remaining weights are $O_n(r^{-4-\delta_1})$. The divergence theorem on a large truncation consequently gives a finite limit $$\label{four:ex:flux}
 \mathfrak F:=\lim_{r\to\infty}\int_{S_r}V\cdot\nu_g\,\,\mathrm dA_g
   =\int_\Omega u\Xi\,\,\mathrm dV_g+\int_B V_\nu\,\,\mathrm dA_g.$$ The plus sign before the inner flux arises because the domain-outward normal on $B$ is $-\nu$.

<a id="four:ex:mass-flux"></a>
To compute the metric flux, write $\widehat g=e^{2t}g$ up to exponential errors. The leading perturbation relative to $g$ is $2t\delta_{ij}$, so in four dimensions the change of its energy numerator is $$\partial_j(2t\delta_{ij})-\partial_i(2t\delta_{jj})
 =-6\partial_i t.$$ All omitted derivatives are $O_n(r^{-5})$ or exponentially small. Their sphere integrals tend to zero. Since $\,\mathrm dt=O_n(r^{-3})$ and $g-\delta=O_2(r^{-2})$, changing the normal and measure in its flux from Euclidean to background ones also has vanishing error. Equation <a href="#four:ex:V-asymptotics" data-reference-type="eqref" data-reference="four:ex:V-asymptotics">[four:ex:V-asymptotics]</a> thus proves both existence of the new energy and the exact relation $$\label{four:ex:mass-flux}
 E_{\widehat g}-E_g
 =-\frac1{\omega_3}\lim_{r\to\infty}
       \int_{S_r}\partial_{n_\delta}t\,\,\mathrm dA_\delta
 =-\frac{\mathfrak F}{3\omega_3}.$$

We now use polynomial constants only. Apply Lemma <a href="#four:lem:weighted-trace" data-reference-type="ref" data-reference="four:lem:weighted-trace">128</a> with $\varphi=1$ and use <a href="#four:eq:boundary-flux-bound" data-reference-type="eqref" data-reference="four:eq:boundary-flux-bound">[four:eq:boundary-flux-bound]</a>. On the fixed compact collars $\mathcal C$ one has $\min_{\mathcal C}\rho>0$, and therefore $$\begin{split}
 \int_B|V_\nu|\,\,\mathrm dA_g
 &\le\Pi_n\frac{\eta_n}{\ell}
       \int_{\mathcal C}u(1+\sqrt{\mathcal T})\,\,\mathrm dV_g\\
 &\le\Pi_n\frac{\eta_n}{\ell}
       \int_{\mathcal C}u(\rho+\delta_0\mathcal T)\,\,\mathrm dV_g.
 \end{split}$$ The polynomial absorbs the fixed comparison constant in the second line. Because $\eta_n/\ell=e^{-\epsilon n/2}$, for sufficiently large $n$ this is at most one half of $\int_\Omega u(\rho+\delta_0\mathcal T)$.

<a id="four:ex:penalty-band"></a>
<a id="four:ex:penalty-absorption"></a>
It remains to estimate the penalty. Its support in an above-floor solution lies in $-\epsilon\le t\le-\epsilon+1/n$. For $n>1/\epsilon$ this interval is negative, and uniformly there $$\label{four:ex:penalty-band}
 l\asymp\ell,\qquad L_0\asymp\ell,\qquad
 u\le C(\ell+\ell^2\sigma),\qquad
 uv\le C\ell^2\sigma,\qquad
 ua\sigma=L_0l\sigma^2\ge c\ell^2\sigma^2.$$ For example $uv=L_0l^2\sigma^2/\sqrt{1+l^2\sigma^2}
\le L_0l\sigma$. Thus on that band $$um_0\mathcal P\le\Pi_n\bigl[\ell\rho_0+
                         \ell^2\sigma(\rho_0+\rho_1)\bigr].$$ Young’s inequality applied to $\sqrt{\eta_n}\ell\sigma$ and $\Pi_n\ell(\rho_0+\rho_1)/\sqrt{\eta_n}$, together with <a href="#four:ex:penalty-band" data-reference-type="eqref" data-reference="four:ex:penalty-band">[four:ex:penalty-band]</a>, yields everywhere $$\label{four:ex:penalty-absorption}
 um_0\mathcal P\le\tfrac12\delta_0u\eta_n a\sigma
   +\Pi_n\left[\ell\rho_0+
       \frac{\ell^2}{\eta_n}(\rho_0^2+\rho_1^2)\right].$$ The enlarged $\Pi_n$ is still polynomial. The three residual weights are integrable against $\,\mathrm dV_g$ in dimension four: $\rho_0=r^{-4-\delta_1}$, $\rho_0^2=r^{-8-2\delta_1}$, and $\rho_1^2=r^{-6}$ on the end, and they are bounded on the compact part. Combining <a href="#four:ex:flux" data-reference-type="eqref" data-reference="four:ex:flux">[four:ex:flux]</a>, the boundary absorption, and <a href="#four:ex:penalty-absorption" data-reference-type="eqref" data-reference="four:ex:penalty-absorption">[four:ex:penalty-absorption]</a> gives $$\mathfrak F\ge-\Pi_n\left(\ell+\frac{\ell^2}{\eta_n}\right).$$ This and <a href="#four:ex:mass-flux" data-reference-type="eqref" data-reference="four:ex:mass-flux">[four:ex:mass-flux]</a> prove <a href="#four:ex:energy-error" data-reference-type="eqref" data-reference="four:ex:energy-error">[four:ex:energy-error]</a>. Finally $\ell=e^{-\epsilon n}$ and $\ell^2/\eta_n=e^{-\epsilon n/2}$; both dominate every polynomial loss. No constant from the fixed-$n$ decay or Schauder estimates appears in this bound. ◻

</details>

<a id="pm-h-159"></a>
###### A minimal enclosing hypersurface

The boundary $B$ has strictly negative mean curvature in $\widehat g$. The full-perimeter enclosure of Proposition <a href="#rig4:enc:minimizing-hull" data-reference-type="ref" data-reference="rig4:enc:minimizing-hull">102</a> therefore gives the smooth minimal boundary needed for the Riemannian comparison. We relate its total three-volume to the original enclosing quantity $A_*$.

<a id="stmt-four-lem-minimal-enclosure"></a>
<div id="four:lem:minimal-enclosure" class="lemma">

<a id="four:end:area-comparison"></a>
**Lemma 140** (Minimal enclosure). *Let $\Omega$ and $B$ be the exterior and its boundary from Proposition <a href="#four:prop:geometric-preparation" data-reference-type="ref" data-reference="four:prop:geometric-preparation">118</a>, and let $\epsilon>0$. Suppose $\widehat g$ is a smooth metric on $\Omega$, complete with $B$ included, such that $\widehat g-\delta=O_2(r^{-2})$ on its end, $\widehat H_B<0$ for the normal into $\Omega$, and $\widehat g\ge e^{-2\epsilon}g$. Then there is a nonempty compact smooth embedded minimal hypersurface $\Sigma$ enclosing $B$. Its exterior is connected, complete with boundary, and has the same single asymptotically flat end. The hypersurface is outer area-minimizing, with disconnected competitors permitted, and its area $\widehat A=|\Sigma|_{\widehat g}$ satisfies $$\label{four:end:area-comparison}
 \widehat A\ge e^{-3\epsilon}A_*.$$*

</div>

<details id="proof-stmt-four-lem-minimal-enclosure"><summary>Proof of stmt-four-lem-minimal-enclosure</summary>

*Proof.* Proposition <a href="#four:prop:geometric-preparation" data-reference-type="ref" data-reference="four:prop:geometric-preparation">118</a> gives a smooth connected orientable four-dimensional exterior $\Omega$ with nonempty compact smooth boundary $B$ and exactly one asymptotically flat end. By hypothesis, $\widehat g$ is smooth, complete with $B$ included, and satisfies $\widehat g-\delta=O_2(r^{-2})$. Thus $(X,g)=(\Omega,\widehat g)$ satisfies the geometric hypotheses of Proposition <a href="#rig4:enc:minimizing-hull" data-reference-type="ref" data-reference="rig4:enc:minimizing-hull">102</a>, with asymptotic exponent $q=2>1$.

Apply that Proposition to obtain a full-perimeter minimizing enclosure of $B$, and denote its frontier by $\Sigma$. Since $\widehat H_B<0$ for the normal into $\Omega$, the strict inner-barrier conclusion places $\Sigma$ in $\operatorname{int}\Omega$ and makes it a nonempty compact smooth embedded minimal hypersurface. Its closed exterior is smooth, connected, complete with $\Sigma$ included, and has the same single end. The Proposition also gives outer area-minimization there, with all boundary components counted and disconnected enclosing competitors permitted.

For every smooth enclosing cut $\Gamma$ of $B$, its closed connected outer domain is also an admissible outer domain in the original prepared manifold, by Proposition <a href="#four:prop:geometric-preparation" data-reference-type="ref" data-reference="four:prop:geometric-preparation">118</a>. This includes frontier coincident with $B$. Restricting $\widehat g\ge e^{-2\epsilon}g$ to its three-dimensional tangent planes gives <a id="four:ex:cut-volume"></a>$$\label{four:ex:cut-volume}
 |\Gamma|_{\widehat g}\ge e^{-3\epsilon}|\Gamma|_g\ge e^{-3\epsilon}A_*.$$ Apply this to $\Sigma$ to obtain <a href="#four:end:area-comparison" data-reference-type="eqref" data-reference="four:end:area-comparison">[four:end:area-comparison]</a>. ◻

</details>

<a id="pm-h-160"></a>
###### The Riemannian comparison

<a id="four:end:bray-lee"></a>
We use the following dimension-four instance of the boundary Riemannian Penrose inequality (Bray and Lee 2009, Theorem 1.4, p. 84) <a id="pm-cite-73"></a>[[BrayLee2009](#ref-BrayLee2009)]. Let $(N,g_N)$ be a smooth connected four-dimensional Riemannian manifold, complete with its nonempty compact boundary included, having exactly one end, which is asymptotically flat. Suppose in that end $$(g_N)_{ij}-\delta_{ij}=O_2(r^{-p_0}),\quad p_0>1,
 \qquad R_{g_N}=O(r^{-s_0}),\quad s_0>4,$$ and $R_{g_N}\ge0$ everywhere. If its boundary is minimal and outer area-minimizing, then $$\label{four:end:bray-lee}
 E_{g_N}\ge\frac12
          \left(\frac{|\partial N|_{g_N}}{\omega_3}\right)^{2/3}.$$ The boundary may have one or more components, and the ADM normalization is $1/(6\omega_3)$. The numerical inequality does not require a spin assumption; the additional spin hypothesis in the published theorem concerns its equality conclusion. We use only <a href="#four:end:bray-lee" data-reference-type="eqref" data-reference="four:end:bray-lee">[four:end:bray-lee]</a>.

<a id="pm-h-161"></a>
###### The prepared-data energy theorem

<a id="stmt-four-thm-prepared-energy"></a>
<div id="four:thm:prepared-energy" class="theorem">

<a id="four:ex:prepared-inequality"></a>
**Theorem 141** (Energy inequality for prepared data). *Let $(M^4,g,K)$ be smooth, connected, and orientable, complete with a nonempty compact smooth boundary $S$ included, and with exactly one end, which is asymptotically flat. Let $K$ be a smooth compactly supported symmetric covariant tensor. Suppose, with a smooth positive function $r$ equal to the coordinate radius on the end, constants $c_0>0$ and $0<\delta_1<1$, that $$\mu-|J|_g\ge c_0r^{-4-\delta_1}\quad\hbox{on }M,
 \qquad H+\mathop{\mathrm{tr}}_SK<0\quad\hbox{on every component of }S,$$ where the boundary normal points into $M$. Suppose on the end that $$g-\delta=O_k(r^{-2})\quad\hbox{for every integer }k\ge0,
 \qquad \mathop{\mathrm{Scal}}_g=O(r^{-4-\delta_1}),$$ and that the ADM energy $E_g$ is finite in the stated normalization. Let $A_*$ be the infimum of the total $g$-three-volume of the entire intrinsic boundaries of connected closed smooth outer domains containing the distant end, with interiors disjoint from $S$, including disconnected cuts and frontier coincident with $S$. Then $$\label{four:ex:prepared-inequality}
 E_g\ge\frac12\left(\frac{A_*}{\omega_3}\right)^{2/3}.$$*

</div>

<details id="proof-stmt-four-thm-prepared-energy"><summary>Proof of stmt-four-thm-prepared-energy</summary>

*Proof.* Proposition <a href="#four:prop:geometric-preparation" data-reference-type="ref" data-reference="four:prop:geometric-preparation">118</a> supplies the closed exterior $\Omega$ with its nonempty compact smooth boundary $B$ and the data used in this section. It is connected, orientable, and one-ended, and its background energy is still $E_g$. Fix $0<\epsilon<1$. For every sufficiently large $n$, Proposition <a href="#four:prop:existence" data-reference-type="ref" data-reference="four:prop:existence">137</a> constructs a smooth metric $\widehat g$ on this exterior. By <a href="#four:ex:positive-scalar" data-reference-type="eqref" data-reference="four:ex:positive-scalar">[four:ex:positive-scalar]</a> and <a href="#four:ex:final-AF" data-reference-type="eqref" data-reference="four:ex:final-AF">[four:ex:final-AF]</a>, it has nonnegative scalar curvature and the pointwise end bounds $$\widehat g-\delta=O_2(r^{-2}),\qquad
 R_{\widehat g}=O(r^{-4-\delta_1}),\qquad 0<\delta_1<1.$$ It is complete by <a href="#four:ex:metric-comparison" data-reference-type="eqref" data-reference="four:ex:metric-comparison">[four:ex:metric-comparison]</a>, and every component of $B$ has strictly negative mean curvature by <a href="#four:ex:negative-boundary" data-reference-type="eqref" data-reference="four:ex:negative-boundary">[four:ex:negative-boundary]</a>.

Lemma <a href="#four:lem:minimal-enclosure" data-reference-type="ref" data-reference="four:lem:minimal-enclosure">140</a> supplies a nonempty compact smooth minimal boundary $\Sigma$, with connected one-ended exterior and outer area-minimization against disconnected competitors. Restricting the metric to this exterior preserves scalar curvature, asymptotic decay and ADM energy. Thus the metric and scalar exponents in <a href="#four:end:bray-lee" data-reference-type="eqref" data-reference="four:end:bray-lee">[four:end:bray-lee]</a> are $p_0=2>1$ and $s_0=4+\delta_1>4$, and all hypotheses of that theorem hold. Proposition <a href="#four:prop:mass-comparison" data-reference-type="ref" data-reference="four:prop:mass-comparison">139</a> gives its finite energy. The enclosure is an admissible smooth cut, so <a href="#four:end:area-comparison" data-reference-type="eqref" data-reference="four:end:area-comparison">[four:end:area-comparison]</a> compares its three-volume with $A_*$.

Combining the Riemannian inequality with <a href="#four:ex:energy-error" data-reference-type="eqref" data-reference="four:ex:energy-error">[four:ex:energy-error]</a> gives $$E_g+\frac{\Pi_n}{3\omega_3}
                   \left(\ell+\frac{\ell^2}{\eta_n}\right)
 \ge E_{\widehat g}
 \ge\frac12\left(\frac{|\Sigma|_{\widehat g}}{\omega_3}\right)^{2/3}
 \ge\frac12e^{-2\epsilon}
                   \left(\frac{A_*}{\omega_3}\right)^{2/3}.$$ For each fixed $\epsilon$ let $n\to\infty$, after the fixed-$n$ exhaustion already carried out. Then let $\epsilon\downarrow0$. This proves <a href="#four:ex:prepared-inequality" data-reference-type="eqref" data-reference="four:ex:prepared-inequality">[four:ex:prepared-inequality]</a>. ◻

</details>

Theorem <a href="#four:thm:prepared-energy" data-reference-type="ref" data-reference="four:thm:prepared-energy">141</a> supplies the energy estimate used in Proposition <a href="#four:end:transfer" data-reference-type="ref" data-reference="four:end:transfer">112</a>. Removing strictification and then the rest-end replacement, applying the positive-shell argument, and truncating the unwanted ends complete Theorem <a href="#four:thm:main" data-reference-type="ref" data-reference="four:thm:main">98</a>.

<a id="pm-h-162"></a>
###### The general maximal DEC energy inequality

The maximal special case requires no assumption that a momentum limit exists. The following end calculation supplies that limit from the decay and integrability already imposed on the data.

<a id="stmt-four-lem-momentum-exists"></a>
<div id="four:lem:momentum-exists" class="lemma">

**Lemma 142** (Existence of the momentum flux). *On a smooth four-dimensional asymptotically flat end, suppose $g-\delta=O_2(r^{-q})$ and $K=O_1(r^{-1-q})$ for some $q>1$. If $|J|_g$ is integrable, where $J_i=\nabla^j(K_{ij}-(\mathop{\mathrm{tr}}_gK)g_{ij})$, then each ADM momentum limit in <a href="#four:intro:momentum" data-reference-type="eqref" data-reference="four:intro:momentum">[four:intro:momentum]</a> exists and is finite.*

</div>

<details id="proof-stmt-four-lem-momentum-exists"><summary>Proof of stmt-four-lem-momentum-exists</summary>

<a id="four:end:momentum-integrability"></a>
*Proof.* In the given coordinates set $$\pi^g_{ij}=K_{ij}-(\mathop{\mathrm{tr}}_gK)g_{ij},\qquad
 \pi^\delta_{ij}=K_{ij}-(\mathop{\mathrm{tr}}_\delta K)\delta_{ij}.$$ The differentiated decay assumptions give $$\label{four:end:momentum-integrability}
 \pi^g-\pi^\delta=O_1(r^{-1-2q}),\qquad
 \partial_j\pi^\delta_{ij}-J_i=O(r^{-2-2q}).$$ To verify the second bound, expand the covariant divergence as $$J_i=g^{jk}\bigl(\partial_k\pi^g_{ij}
       -\Gamma^a_{ki}\pi^g_{aj}-\Gamma^a_{kj}\pi^g_{ia}\bigr).$$ Replacing $g^{jk}$ by $\delta^{jk}$ costs $O(r^{-q})O(r^{-2-q})$; replacing $\pi^g$ by $\pi^\delta$ costs the derivative of the first bound in <a href="#four:end:momentum-integrability" data-reference-type="eqref" data-reference="four:end:momentum-integrability">[four:end:momentum-integrability]</a>. Each connection term has size $O(r^{-1-q})O(r^{-1-q})$. These are exactly the asserted errors.

Their Euclidean radial volume bound is $Cr^{1-2q}$, integrable because $q>1$. The asymptotic metric and Euclidean volume and covector norms are uniformly comparable, so $\partial_j\pi^\delta_{ij}\in L^1$. The Euclidean divergence theorem between two large spheres makes the flux $\int_{S_R}\pi^\delta_{ij}n_\delta^j\,\,\mathrm dA_\delta$ a Cauchy function of $R$, with finite limit. By the first bound in <a href="#four:end:momentum-integrability" data-reference-type="eqref" data-reference="four:end:momentum-integrability">[four:end:momentum-integrability]</a>, its difference from the flux of $\pi^g$ is $O(R^{2-2q})\to0$. This is the tensor appearing in <a href="#four:intro:momentum" data-reference-type="eqref" data-reference="four:intro:momentum">[four:intro:momentum]</a>, which proves the lemma. ◻

</details>

<a id="stmt-four-ass-energy"></a>
<div id="four:ass:energy" class="corollary">

**Corollary 143** (Maximal DEC energy inequality). *<span id="four:cor:maximal-dec" label="four:cor:maximal-dec"></span>Let $(X^4,g_X,K_X)$ be smooth and connected, with $X$ orientable, $g_X$ complete as a metric space with its nonempty compact smooth boundary $S_X$ included, and with exactly one end, which is asymptotically flat and diffeomorphic to the complement of a closed ball in $\mathbb R^4$. Let $K_X$ be a smooth symmetric covariant two-tensor. Suppose $$\begin{gathered}
 \mathop{\mathrm{tr}}_{g_X}K_X=0,\qquad
 \mu_X=\tfrac12(R_{g_X}-|K_X|_{g_X}^2)
       \ge|\mathop{\mathrm{div}}_{g_X}K_X|_{g_X},\\
 \mu_X,|\mathop{\mathrm{div}}_{g_X}K_X|_{g_X}\in L^1(X,\,\mathrm dV_{g_X}).
\end{gathered}$$ Assume for some $q>1$ that $$g_X-\delta=O_2(r^{-q}),\qquad K_X=O_1(r^{-1-q}),$$ and that the ADM energy $E_X$ in <a href="#four:intro:energy" data-reference-type="eqref" data-reference="four:intro:energy">[four:intro:energy]</a> is finite. On every component of $S_X$, require $H+\mathop{\mathrm{tr}}_{S_X}K_X\le0$ with the normal into $X$. For the one-ended enclosing-cut infimum of Definition <a href="#four:def:cuts" data-reference-type="ref" data-reference="four:def:cuts">97</a>, denoted here by $a_{g_X}(S_X)$, one has $$E_X\ge\frac12\left(\frac{a_{g_X}(S_X)}{2\pi^2}\right)^{2/3}.$$ The boundary may have any topology and finitely many components. No symmetry, vacuum, spin, outermostness, outer area-minimization or momentum-flux assumption is imposed.*

</div>

<details id="proof-stmt-four-ass-energy"><summary>Proof of stmt-four-ass-energy</summary>

*Proof.* Maximality identifies the momentum density with $J_X=\mathop{\mathrm{div}}_{g_X}K_X$. Lemma <a href="#four:lem:momentum-exists" data-reference-type="ref" data-reference="four:lem:momentum-exists">142</a> supplies the finite ADM momentum. All hypotheses of Theorem <a href="#four:thm:main" data-reference-type="ref" data-reference="four:thm:main">98</a> therefore hold for this one-ended exterior. Its invariant-mass inequality in particular gives the displayed energy bound. The theorem has already been proved using the Riemannian inequality <a href="#four:end:bray-lee" data-reference-type="eqref" data-reference="four:end:bray-lee">[four:end:bray-lee]</a>, so this corollary is a consequence of the proof, not an input to it. ◻

</details>

<a id="rig4:var:section"></a>
##### Variation at equality and localization of the area term

<a id="rig4:var:nonnegative-defect"></a>
Throughout this section, $(\Omega,g,K)$ satisfies the hypotheses of Definition <a href="#rig4:def:horizon" data-reference-type="ref" data-reference="rig4:def:horizon">99</a>, and equality holds in Theorem <a href="#four:thm:main" data-reference-type="ref" data-reference="four:thm:main">98</a>. Thus $\Omega$ has one end and its only boundary $S$ is a connected, outermost, outer area-minimizing future MOTS. We use the full enclosing-cut convention of Definition <a href="#four:def:cuts" data-reference-type="ref" data-reference="four:def:cuts">97</a>. Set <a id="rig4:var:constants"></a>$$\begin{gathered}
 A=\mathop{\mathrm{Area}}_g(S),\qquad m=\sqrt{E^2-|P|^2},\qquad
 r_0=(A/\omega)^{1/3}=\sqrt{2m},\\
 b^0=E/m,\qquad b^i=-P_i/m,\qquad
 \mathfrak m(a)=\tfrac12(a/\omega)^{2/3},\qquad
 c=6\omega\mathfrak m'(A)=2/r_0.
\end{gathered}
\label{rig4:var:constants}$$ The strict future timelikeness needed here is already part of Theorem <a href="#four:thm:main" data-reference-type="ref" data-reference="four:thm:main">98</a>. For nearby data with charges $(\widetilde E,\widetilde P)$, define the fixed linear charge functional $$\mathcal E(\widetilde g,\widetilde K)
   =b^0\widetilde E+\sum_{i=1}^4b^i\widetilde P_i.$$ The reverse Cauchy–Schwarz inequality on the future timelike cone gives <a id="rig4:var:supporting-charge"></a>$$\mathcal E(\widetilde g,\widetilde K)
 \ge \sqrt{\widetilde E^2-|\widetilde P|^2}.
\label{rig4:var:supporting-charge}$$ Equality holds at the original data. In particular, whenever the varied data satisfy the numerical theorem, their enclosing infimum $a(\widetilde g)$ satisfies $$\mathcal E(\widetilde g,\widetilde K)
       -\mathfrak m(a(\widetilde g))\ge0.
\label{rig4:var:nonnegative-defect}$$ The varied data need not preserve outermostness or outer area minimization: those assumptions are absent from the numerical theorem.

The right-derivative formula in Proposition <a href="#rig4:enc:area-derivative" data-reference-type="ref" data-reference="rig4:enc:area-derivative">103</a> accounts for all minimizing frontiers without choosing a differentiable family. It gives the positive-measure identity of Proposition <a href="#rig4:var:multiplier" data-reference-type="ref" data-reference="rig4:var:multiplier">149</a>. Compact normal tests and outermostness then localize its area term to $S$ in Proposition <a href="#rig4:var:area-localization" data-reference-type="ref" data-reference="rig4:var:area-localization">151</a>, supplying the identity used to construct the causal adjoint field in Theorem <a href="#rig4:adj:causal-field" data-reference-type="ref" data-reference="rig4:adj:causal-field">152</a>.

<a id="pm-h-164"></a>
###### Constraint derivatives and a strict direction

<a id="rig4:var:active-set"></a>
On the closed unit ball bundle of $g$, introduce $$\begin{gathered}
 C(x,v)=2(\mu(x)+J_x(v))
       =R_g+\tau^2-|K|_g^2+2J_x(v),\qquad |v|_g\le1,\\
 \mathcal A=\{(x,v):C(x,v)=0\}.
\end{gathered}
\label{rig4:var:active-set}$$ DEC is equivalent to $C\ge0$ on this bundle. When the metric varies, we identify its unit ball with the original one by the positive symmetric inverse square root. More precisely, if $g_s(V,W)=g(G_sV,W)$, then $I_s=G_s^{-1/2}$ sends the $g$ unit ball isometrically to the $g_s$ unit ball. For a variation $H=(h,p)=(\dot g_0,\dot K_0)$, all derivatives $C'_H$ below include this identification; in particular, $$\dot I_0v=-\tfrac12h^\sharp v.$$

<a id="stmt-rig4-var-conformal"></a>
<div id="rig4:var:conformal" class="lemma">

<a id="rig4:var:conformal-C"></a>
<a id="rig4:var:conformal-theta"></a>
**Lemma 144** (Conformal constraint identities). *For a positive smooth function $f$, let $g_f=f^2g$ and $K_f=fK$. Using $f^{-1}v$ in the varied unit ball, one has $$\begin{aligned}
 f^2 C_f(x,f^{-1}v)
   &=C(x,v)+6f^{-1}\bigl[-\Delta_g f+K(\nabla f,v)\bigr],
       \label{rig4:var:conformal-C}\\
 f\theta_{+,f}
   &=\theta_++3\partial_\nu\log f.
       \label{rig4:var:conformal-theta}
\end{aligned}$$ Here $\nu$ points into the exterior and $\Delta_g=\operatorname{div}_g\nabla$.*

</div>

<details id="proof-stmt-rig4-var-conformal"><summary>Proof of stmt-rig4-var-conformal</summary>

*Proof.* Apply Lemma <a href="#four:lem:conformal" data-reference-type="ref" data-reference="four:lem:conformal">106</a>. Its density and momentum identities give $$f^2\mu_f=\mu-3f^{-1}\Delta_gf,\qquad
 f^2J_f(f^{-1}v)=J(v)+3f^{-1}K(\nabla f,v).$$ Adding twice these expressions proves <a href="#rig4:var:conformal-C" data-reference-type="eqref" data-reference="rig4:var:conformal-C">[rig4:var:conformal-C]</a>. Equation <a href="#rig4:var:conformal-theta" data-reference-type="eqref" data-reference="rig4:var:conformal-theta">[rig4:var:conformal-theta]</a> is the expansion formula in that same lemma, with the stated orientation. ◻

</details>

<a id="stmt-rig4-var-strict-direction"></a>
<div id="rig4:var:strict-direction" class="lemma">

<a id="rig4:var:phi-properties"></a>
<a id="rig4:var:strict-derivatives"></a>
**Lemma 145** (Strict conformal direction). *Choose $$1<q_0<\min(q,2),\qquad 0<\delta<\min(q_0,1),
 \qquad w=r^{-4-\delta},$$ where the end radius is extended to a positive smooth function on $\Omega$. There is a smooth nonnegative function $\phi$, smooth up to $S$, such that $$\partial_\nu\phi=-1\quad\hbox{on }S,\qquad
 -\Delta_g\phi-|K|_g|\,\mathrm d\phi|_g\ge w,\qquad
 \phi=O_2(r^{-2}),\qquad -\Delta_g\phi/w\longrightarrow1.
\label{rig4:var:phi-properties}$$ Its limiting Euclidean sphere gradient flux exists and is finite. For $$Q=(2\phi g,\phi K)$$ one consequently has $$C'_Q\ge6w\quad\hbox{on }\mathcal A,
 \qquad -\theta'_Q=3\quad\hbox{on }S.
\label{rig4:var:strict-derivatives}$$ Moreover, uniformly for all $|v|_g\le1$ on the end, $C'_Q/w\longrightarrow6$.*

</div>

<details id="proof-stmt-rig4-var-strict-direction"><summary>Proof of stmt-rig4-var-strict-direction</summary>

<a id="rig4:var:phi-equation"></a>
*Proof.* Choose a smooth majorant $d_0\ge |K|_g$ which on the end is a sufficiently large radial multiple of $r^{-1-q_0}$. It can be chosen with all symbol bounds there. We solve $$-\Delta_g\phi
   =d_0\sqrt{|\,\mathrm d\phi|_g^2+r^{-6}}+w,
 \qquad \partial_\nu\phi=-1\text{ on }S,
 \qquad \phi\longrightarrow0\text{ at infinity}.
\label{rig4:var:phi-equation}$$

First truncate at a large coordinate sphere $S_R$, imposing $\phi=0$ on $S_R$, and replace $d_0$ in the equation by $t d_0$, $0\le t\le1$. The inner and outer boundary components are disjoint smooth hypersurfaces; there is no corner where the two boundary conditions meet. The $t=0$ problem is the invertible mixed Laplace problem. Every linearization in $\phi$ adds to $-\Delta_g$ a smooth drift of norm at most $d_0$, with homogeneous Neumann data at $S$ and homogeneous Dirichlet data at $S_R$. The maximum and boundary point principles give uniqueness, and the mixed elliptic Fredholm theory then gives invertibility. These are the usual local elliptic and boundary estimates on a fixed smooth truncated domain; see (Gilbarg and Trudinger 2001) <a id="pm-cite-74"></a>[[GilbargTrudinger2001](#ref-GilbargTrudinger2001)].

Solutions are nonnegative. Indeed a negative minimum cannot occur in the interior because the right side of the equation is positive. At $S$, the outward normal of the truncated domain is $-\nu$, so the prescribed outward derivative is $+1$, also excluding such a minimum by the boundary point principle. The outer Dirichlet value is zero.

For completeness, the continuation bounds do not require a monotonicity assumption in the unknown. Fix $p>4$. The mixed $W^{2,p}$ estimate, the linear growth of the right side in $\,\mathrm d\phi$, and first-derivative interpolation give, on this fixed truncation, $$\|\phi\|_{W^{2,p}}\le C\bigl(1+\|\phi\|_{L^\infty}\bigr),$$ uniformly in $t$. If the supremum were unbounded, division by that supremum and compactness in $C^1$ would produce a nonnegative function $z$ with supremum one satisfying $$-\Delta_g z=t_*d_0|\,\mathrm dz|_g,
 \qquad \partial_\nu z=0\text{ on }S,
 \qquad z=0\text{ on }S_R$$ for some $t_*\in[0,1]$. At points where $\,\mathrm dz\ne0$ the right side is a bounded drift applied to $\,\mathrm dz$, and it is zero otherwise. The strong maximum and boundary point principles for this bounded-drift equation contradict the positive maximum. The resulting $W^{2,p}$ and Schauder bounds close the continuation argument and give a smooth solution at $t=1$ on every sufficiently large truncation.

<a id="rig4:var:tail-barrier"></a>
<a id="rig4:var:tail-bound"></a>
We next make the bounds independent of $R$. For $W=r^{-2}-r^{-2-\delta}$, the Euclidean identity $$-\Delta_\delta W=(2+\delta)\delta r^{-4-\delta}$$ and the AF estimates imply, beyond a fixed radius $R_1$, $$-\Delta_g W-d_0|\,\mathrm dW|_g\ge c_1w>0.
\label{rig4:var:tail-barrier}$$ The metric errors and the drift term are smaller than $w$ because $\delta<q_0<q$. Also $d_0r^{-3}=o(w)$. If $M_R$ is the supremum of the truncated solution on the fixed core bounded by $S_{R_1}$, a sufficiently large fixed multiple of $(1+M_R)W$ is a supersolution on $R_1\le r\le R$. To see this, use $\sqrt{a^2+b^2}\le a+b$ and <a href="#rig4:var:tail-barrier" data-reference-type="eqref" data-reference="rig4:var:tail-barrier">[rig4:var:tail-barrier]</a>; choose the multiple also to dominate $M_R$ on $S_{R_1}$. It dominates the zero outer value. Comparison is valid by writing the difference of the two gradient nonlinearities as a bounded drift. Therefore $$0\le\phi_R\le C(1+M_R)W\qquad (R_1\le r\le R).
\label{rig4:var:tail-bound}$$

If $M_R$ diverged along a sequence, normalize by $M_R$. Local mixed estimates near $S$ and interior estimates elsewhere give a subsequential limit $z$ on every fixed compact set. More precisely, <a href="#rig4:var:tail-bound" data-reference-type="eqref" data-reference="rig4:var:tail-bound">[rig4:var:tail-bound]</a> bounds $\phi_R/M_R$ on a neighborhood of the fixed closed core. Local Neumann $W^{2,p}$ estimates at $S$, and interior $W^{2,p}$ estimates away from it, give uniform bounds there for $p>4$. Compactness in $C^1$ on the closed core retains both $\sup_{\mathrm{core}}z=1$ and $\partial_\nu z=0$. The limit satisfies $-\Delta_gz=d_0|\,\mathrm dz|_g$, homogeneous Neumann data on $S$, and, by <a href="#rig4:var:tail-bound" data-reference-type="eqref" data-reference="rig4:var:tail-bound">[rig4:var:tail-bound]</a>, $z\to0$ at infinity. Its positive global maximum is attained in a compact set. The same strong maximum and boundary point principles again give a contradiction. Thus $M_R$ is bounded, and exhaustion produces a smooth solution of <a href="#rig4:var:phi-equation" data-reference-type="eqref" data-reference="rig4:var:phi-equation">[rig4:var:phi-equation]</a> with $\phi=O(r^{-2})$.

<a id="rig4:var:rescaled-phi"></a>
Here is the derivative control needed later, using only the stated derivatives of the original data. On a fixed annulus in the $y$ variables put $g_\rho(y)=(g_{ij}(\rho y))$, $U_\rho(y)=\rho^2\phi(\rho y)$, and $a_\rho(y)=\rho d_0(\rho y)$. The exact rescaled equation is $$-\Delta_{g_\rho}U_\rho
 =a_\rho\sqrt{|\,\mathrm dU_\rho|_{g_\rho}^2+|y|^{-6}}
       +\rho^{-\delta}|y|^{-4-\delta}.
\label{rig4:var:rescaled-phi}$$ The metric components have uniform $C^{1,1}$ bounds from $g-\delta=O_2$. Consequently both the principal coefficients of this Laplacian and its first-order coefficients have uniform $C^{0,\alpha}$ bounds for every fixed $\alpha<1$. No third derivative of $g$ is needed. The chosen radial $d_0$ gives $a_\rho=O(\rho^{-q_0})$ with uniform symbol bounds, independently of derivatives of $K$. First-derivative interpolation in the local $W^{2,p}$ estimates gives a uniform $W^{2,p}$ bound on a smaller annulus. Taking $p>4$ controls $\,\mathrm dU_\rho$ in $C^{0,\alpha}$ for some $\alpha>0$. The positive $|y|^{-6}$ term is bounded away from zero there, so the entire right side of <a href="#rig4:var:rescaled-phi" data-reference-type="eqref" data-reference="rig4:var:rescaled-phi">[rig4:var:rescaled-phi]</a> is uniformly $C^{0,\alpha}$. The usual Schauder estimate, including the first-order Laplacian coefficients with these $C^{0,\alpha}$ bounds, now gives a uniform $C^{2,\alpha}$ bound on a further smaller annulus. Scaling back proves $\phi=O_2(r^{-2})$ without an additional metric or tensor falloff derivative. The equation now yields $$d_0\sqrt{|\,\mathrm d\phi|_g^2+r^{-6}}=O(r^{-4-q_0})=o(w),$$ which proves both the differential inequality and the last limit in <a href="#rig4:var:phi-properties" data-reference-type="eqref" data-reference="rig4:var:phi-properties">[rig4:var:phi-properties]</a>. The right side of <a href="#rig4:var:phi-equation" data-reference-type="eqref" data-reference="rig4:var:phi-equation">[rig4:var:phi-equation]</a> is integrable. The divergence theorem consequently gives a finite limiting physical sphere flux. Its difference from the Euclidean sphere flux tends to zero, since $g-\delta=O(r^{-q})$ and $\,\mathrm d\phi=O(r^{-3})$.

Finally, differentiating Lemma <a href="#rig4:var:conformal" data-reference-type="ref" data-reference="rig4:var:conformal">144</a> at $f=1+s\phi$ gives $$C'_Q=-2\phi C+6[-\Delta_g\phi+K(\nabla\phi,v)],
 \qquad \theta'_Q=-\phi\theta_++3\partial_\nu\phi.$$ On $\mathcal A$ the first term is zero, and on $S$ we have $\theta_+=0$. This proves <a href="#rig4:var:strict-derivatives" data-reference-type="eqref" data-reference="rig4:var:strict-derivatives">[rig4:var:strict-derivatives]</a>. On the full end ball bundle, $C=O(r^{-2-q})$, $\phi C=O(r^{-4-q})=o(w)$, and $K(\nabla\phi,v)=O(r^{-4-q})=o(w)$. Thus the normalized derivative tends uniformly to six. ◻

</details>

<a id="pm-h-165"></a>
###### Feasible variations and a measure identity

<a id="stmt-rig4-var-variation-space"></a>
<div id="rig4:var:variation-space" class="definition">

<a id="rig4:var:momentum-prototype"></a>
**Definition 146** (Variation space). Let $\mathcal V_0$ be the real vector space generated by all smooth compactly supported pairs $(h,p)$ up to $S$ and the following five pairs, cut off smoothly to the end. The scalar pair is $$h_{ij}=r^{-2}\delta_{ij},\qquad p=0.$$ For each vector $e$ in a fixed basis of $\mathbb R^4$, the momentum pair has $h=0$ and is defined by $$p-(\mathop{\mathrm{tr}}_\delta p)\delta
 =r^{-3}\bigl(e\otimes\widehat x+\widehat x\otimes e
                  -(e\cdot\widehat x)\delta\bigr),
 \qquad \widehat x=x/r.
\label{rig4:var:momentum-prototype}$$ Set $\mathcal V=\mathbb RQ+\mathcal V_0$. We write its elements as $H=aQ+H_0$, where $H_0=(h_0,p_0)\in\mathcal V_0$.

</div>

<a id="stmt-rig4-var-end-variations"></a>
<div id="rig4:var:end-variations" class="lemma">

<a id="rig4:var:prototype-constraint-decay"></a>
<a id="rig4:var:end-value"></a>
**Lemma 147** (End behavior of the variation space). *The five prototypes have independent charge derivatives. For every fixed $H_0\in\mathcal V_0$, $$C'_{H_0}=O(r^{-4-q})=o(w)
\label{rig4:var:prototype-constraint-decay}$$ uniformly on the full end ball bundle. The coefficient $a$ in Definition <a href="#rig4:var:variation-space" data-reference-type="ref" data-reference="rig4:var:variation-space">146</a> is uniquely determined, and $$C'_H/w\longrightarrow6a
\label{rig4:var:end-value}$$ uniformly there. All elements of $\mathcal V$ have well-defined charge derivatives.*

</div>

<details id="proof-stmt-rig4-var-end-variations"><summary>Proof of stmt-rig4-var-end-variations</summary>

*Proof.* Trace reversal on symmetric tensors in dimension four is invertible. The right side of <a href="#rig4:var:momentum-prototype" data-reference-type="eqref" data-reference="rig4:var:momentum-prototype">[rig4:var:momentum-prototype]</a>, written as $$D_{ij}=r^{-4}\bigl(e_i x_j+x_i e_j-(e\cdot x)\delta_{ij}\bigr),$$ satisfies $\partial_jD_{ij}=0$ and $D_{ij}\widehat x^j=r^{-3}e_i$. The scalar prototype satisfies the Euclidean linearized scalar constraint because $\Delta_\delta r^{-2}=0$ off the origin. With the ADM normalizations <a href="#four:intro:energy" data-reference-type="eqref" data-reference="four:intro:energy">[four:intro:energy]</a>–<a href="#four:intro:momentum" data-reference-type="eqref" data-reference="four:intro:momentum">[four:intro:momentum]</a>, the scalar prototype has $E'=1$, $P'=0$, and the momentum prototype for $e$ has $E'=0$, $P'=e/3$. Background corrections to these fluxes vanish by the AF estimates, so the derivatives are independent.

On the end, $h_0=O_2(r^{-2})$ and $p_0=O_1(r^{-3})$. Their Euclidean linearized scalar and momentum constraints vanish. Each remaining linear constraint term has a factor from the decaying background: for example, $(g-\delta)\partial^2h_0$, $\partial g\,\partial h_0$, $\partial^2g\,h_0$, $Kp_0$, or $(g-\delta)\partial p_0$ has order at most $r^{-4-q}$. The variation of the vector identification contributes $-J(h_0^\sharp v)$, of the same order. This proves <a href="#rig4:var:prototype-constraint-decay" data-reference-type="eqref" data-reference="rig4:var:prototype-constraint-decay">[rig4:var:prototype-constraint-decay]</a>. Lemma <a href="#rig4:var:strict-direction" data-reference-type="ref" data-reference="rig4:var:strict-direction">145</a> then proves <a href="#rig4:var:end-value" data-reference-type="eqref" data-reference="rig4:var:end-value">[rig4:var:end-value]</a> and the uniqueness of $a$: an element of $\mathcal V_0$ cannot have the normalized end derivative of $Q$.

Compact variations have zero charge derivatives. The prototypes have the fluxes just computed. For $Q$, the momentum derivative is zero and $$E'_Q=-\frac1\omega\lim_{R\to\infty}
              \int_{|x|=R}\partial_r\phi\,\,\mathrm dA_\delta,$$ which is finite by Lemma <a href="#rig4:var:strict-direction" data-reference-type="ref" data-reference="rig4:var:strict-direction">145</a>. Products with background errors have zero limiting flux. Linearity completes the proof. ◻

</details>

Let $\mathcal T$ be the compact space of minimizing frontiers for $g$, with their filled sets, from Proposition <a href="#rig4:enc:area-derivative" data-reference-type="ref" data-reference="rig4:enc:area-derivative">103</a>. For $T\in\mathcal T$, write <a id="rig4:var:fixed-area-derivative"></a>$$a'_T(h)=\tfrac12\int_T\mathop{\mathrm{tr}}_T h\,\,\mathrm dA_g.
\label{rig4:var:fixed-area-derivative}$$ This is a continuous function of $T$ for each fixed variation $h$.

<a id="stmt-rig4-var-feasible-path"></a>
<div id="rig4:var:feasible-path" class="lemma">

<a id="rig4:var:nonlinear-path"></a>
**Lemma 148** (Strict linear inequalities give feasible nonlinear data). *Suppose $H=aQ+H_0\in\mathcal V$ has $a>0$ and, for some $\varepsilon>0$, $$C'_H\ge\varepsilon w\text{ on }\mathcal A,\qquad
 -\theta'_H>0\text{ on }S.$$ Then, for every sufficiently small $s>0$, $$g_s=e^{2as\phi}(g+sh_0),\qquad
 K_s=e^{as\phi}(K+sp_0)
\label{rig4:var:nonlinear-path}$$ satisfies every hypothesis of Theorem <a href="#four:thm:main" data-reference-type="ref" data-reference="four:thm:main">98</a>. Its boundary has strictly negative future expansion. The path has derivative $H$, is uniformly comparable to $g$, has uniform large-sphere barriers, and its charges are differentiable at $s=0$.*

</div>

<details id="proof-stmt-rig4-var-feasible-path"><summary>Proof of stmt-rig4-var-feasible-path</summary>

*Proof.* Positivity of the metric and uniform comparability hold for small $s$, since $h_0$ and $\phi$ are bounded relative to $g$. They also give completeness with the boundary included. The topology, smoothness, end count and orientability remain those of $\Omega$.

<a id="rig4:var:component-remainders"></a>
We check DEC on the whole ball of test vectors. First use the intermediate metric and tensor $\overline g_s=g+sh_0$, $\overline K_s=K+sp_0$, identifying its vector ball with that of $g$ by $\overline I_s$. For sufficiently large $r$, Taylor expansion and the Euclidean cancellations in Lemma <a href="#rig4:var:end-variations" data-reference-type="ref" data-reference="rig4:var:end-variations">147</a> give, uniformly in $|v|_g\le1$, $$\overline C_s(x,\overline I_sv)
    =C(x,v)+O(sr^{-4-q})+O(s^2r^{-6}).$$ Here the remainder is uniform in $r$, $s$ in a fixed small interval, and the whole vector ball. To check all its components, the coordinate constraint expressions have the schematic forms $$\begin{aligned}
 R_g&=g^{-1}\partial^2g+\operatorname{smooth}(g^{-1})(\partial g)^2,\\
 J&=\operatorname{smooth}(g^{-1})\partial K
       +\operatorname{smooth}(g^{-1})(\partial g)K,
\end{aligned}$$ and $2\mu-R_g$ is quadratic in $K$, with smooth coefficients in $g^{-1}$. Each second $s$ derivative on the intermediate path is $O(r^{-6})$: the largest terms are $h_0\partial^2h_0$, $(\partial h_0)^2$, $p_0^2$, $h_0\partial p_0$, and $(\partial h_0)p_0$. Terms containing an original $K$, $\partial K$, or background metric derivative decay faster. This calculation includes all occurrences of $\tau=g^{ij}K_{ij}$, without a separate trace estimate. The vector identification also has the uniform matrix expansion $$\overline I_s=(\mathop{\mathrm{Id}}+s h_0^\sharp)^{-1/2}
       =\mathop{\mathrm{Id}}-\tfrac{s}{2}h_0^\sharp+O(s^2r^{-4});$$ the eigenvalues lie in a fixed positive interval, so the matrix-function Taylor bound is uniform. Multiplication by the original or varied momentum covector keeps the same remainder order. In fact the preceding calculation gives the componentwise estimates $$\begin{aligned}
 \overline\mu_s&=\mu+O(sr^{-4-q})+O(s^2r^{-6}),\\
 \overline J_s&=J+O(sr^{-4-q})+O(s^2r^{-6}).
\end{aligned}
\label{rig4:var:component-remainders}$$

<a id="rig4:var:end-feasibility-expansion"></a>
Apply Lemma <a href="#rig4:var:conformal" data-reference-type="ref" data-reference="rig4:var:conformal">144</a> to these intermediate data with $f_s=e^{as\phi}$. After multiplication by the positive factor $f_s^2$, the constraint for the final data is $$C(x,v)+s\bigl(6aw+o(w)\bigr)+O(s^2r^{-6}),
\label{rig4:var:end-feasibility-expansion}$$ again uniformly for the full vector ball. Indeed, $-\Delta_g\phi/w\to1$ and $K(\nabla\phi,v)=o(w)$. Changing the metric, tensor, and vector identification in these conformal differential terms adds only the above decay orders, while the extra exponential term uses $|\,\mathrm d\phi|^2=O(r^{-6})$.
