Since $a>0$ and $r^{-6}=O(w)$, one can first choose a fixed large radius so the coefficient of $s$ in <a href="#rig4:var:end-feasibility-expansion" data-reference-type="eqref" data-reference="rig4:var:end-feasibility-expansion">[rig4:var:end-feasibility-expansion]</a> is positive, and then choose $s$ small so its remainder is absorbed. DEC follows on this fixed far end, using $C\ge0$.

The remaining base region and its closed unit ball bundle are compact. The derivative of the constraint is strictly positive on its original zero set. By continuity it is positive on a neighborhood of that zero set; on the complement the original constraint has a positive minimum. A uniform Taylor expansion therefore gives $C_s\ge0$ everywhere in the compact region for small positive $s$. The same compactness argument on $S$, where $\theta_+=0$, gives $\theta_{+,s}<0$.

The new densities are integrable componentwise, not merely after contraction with active vectors. The exact conformal formulas give $$\begin{aligned}
 f_sJ_s&=\overline J_s+
            3as\overline K_s(\nabla_{\overline g_s}\phi,\cdot),\\
 f_s^2\mu_s&=\overline\mu_s-3as\Delta_{\overline g_s}\phi
                          -3a^2s^2|\,\mathrm d\phi|_{\overline g_s}^2.
\end{aligned}$$ The extra covector in the first line is $O(sr^{-4-q})+O(s^2r^{-6})$. Also $\Delta_{\overline g_s}\phi=\Delta_g\phi+O(sr^{-6})$, with $\Delta_g\phi=O(w)$. Together with <a href="#rig4:var:component-remainders" data-reference-type="eqref" data-reference="rig4:var:component-remainders">[rig4:var:component-remainders]</a>, these identities express the new densities as bounded smooth scaling factors times the original integrable densities, plus integrable errors of orders $r^{-4-\delta}$, $r^{-4-q}$, and $r^{-6}$. Uniform metric comparability controls both norms and volume elements. The differentiated falloff has exponent $\min(q,2)>1$, uniformly for $s$ in a small fixed interval, so large coordinate spheres remain mean convex uniformly.

The charge limits can also be checked before differentiation. Write $\pi=K-\tau g$. Since conformal trace reversal gives $\pi_s=f_s(\overline K_s-\overline\tau_s\overline g_s)$, expansion on the end yields $$\pi_s=\pi+s\bigl(p_0-(\mathop{\mathrm{tr}}_\delta p_0)\delta\bigr)
          +O(sr^{-3-q})+O(s^2r^{-5}).$$ The terms with the original trace are of size $h_0K=O(r^{-3-q})$; multiplication by $f_s-1=O(sr^{-2})$ adds only the displayed error orders. All errors have zero limiting sphere flux. Therefore $P_s=P+sP'_{H_0}$ in the prescribed coordinates, without an extra decay assumption on $\tau$. Similarly, $$g_s-g-s(h_0+2a\phi g)=O_1(s^2r^{-4}),$$ whose energy flux vanishes. The finite flux of $\phi$ and the scalar prototype thus give $E_s=E+sE'_H$. In particular both charge functions exist and are differentiable with the derivatives computed in Lemma <a href="#rig4:var:end-variations" data-reference-type="ref" data-reference="rig4:var:end-variations">147</a>. The path and its first two parameter derivatives are uniformly bounded relative to $g$, as required by Proposition <a href="#rig4:enc:area-derivative" data-reference-type="ref" data-reference="rig4:enc:area-derivative">103</a>. This verifies all claims and all hypotheses of the numerical theorem. ◻

</details>

<a id="stmt-rig4-var-multiplier"></a>
<div id="rig4:var:multiplier" class="proposition">

<a id="rig4:var:measure-identity"></a>
**Proposition 149** (Multiplier identity at equality). *There exist a probability measure $\varpi$ on $\mathcal T$, a nonnegative finite measure $\eta$ on $S$, a nonnegative locally finite measure $\Lambda$ on $\mathcal A$, and $z\ge0$, with $\int_{\mathcal A}w\,\,\mathrm d\Lambda<\infty$, such that for every $H=aQ+H_0=(h,p)\in\mathcal V$, $$6\omega\mathcal E'(H)-c\int_{\mathcal T}a'_T(h)\,\,\mathrm d\varpi(T)
   =\langle C'_H,\Lambda\rangle
      -\int_S\theta'_H\,\,\mathrm d\eta+za.
\label{rig4:var:measure-identity}$$ The constraint pairing is absolutely defined, since $C'_H/w$ is bounded on the compactified active set.*

</div>

<details id="proof-stmt-rig4-var-multiplier"><summary>Proof of stmt-rig4-var-multiplier</summary>

<a id="rig4:var:separation-map"></a>
*Proof.* Compactify $\mathcal A$ by one end point. If $\mathcal A$ is already compact, adjoin an isolated point; if it is empty, use just that point. The ball fibers are compact and the base has one end, so this is a compact Hausdorff space, denoted $\overline{\mathcal A}$. By Lemma <a href="#rig4:var:end-variations" data-reference-type="ref" data-reference="rig4:var:end-variations">147</a>, $C'_H/w$ extends continuously to it with value $6a$ at the added point. On the disjoint compact union $$\mathcal K=\overline{\mathcal A}\sqcup S\sqcup\mathcal T$$ consider the linear map to $C(\mathcal K)$ whose three components are $$H\longmapsto
 \left(\frac{C'_H}{w},\ -\theta'_H,\
                   c a'_T(h)-6\omega\mathcal E'(H)\right).
\label{rig4:var:separation-map}$$

Its image does not meet the open cone of functions strictly positive everywhere. Otherwise its value at the added point gives $a>0$, and Lemma <a href="#rig4:var:feasible-path" data-reference-type="ref" data-reference="rig4:var:feasible-path">148</a> supplies actual feasible data <a href="#rig4:var:nonlinear-path" data-reference-type="eqref" data-reference="rig4:var:nonlinear-path">[rig4:var:nonlinear-path]</a>. Let $a(s)$ be their enclosing infimum. The area derivative formula in Proposition <a href="#rig4:enc:area-derivative" data-reference-type="ref" data-reference="rig4:enc:area-derivative">103</a> gives $$a'(0+)=\min_{T\in\mathcal T}a'_T(h).$$ Strict positivity of the third component in <a href="#rig4:var:separation-map" data-reference-type="eqref" data-reference="rig4:var:separation-map">[rig4:var:separation-map]</a>, and compactness of $\mathcal T$, imply $$\left.\frac{\,\mathrm d}{\,\mathrm ds}\right|_{0+}
   6\omega\bigl(\mathcal E(g_s,K_s)-\mathfrak m(a(s))\bigr)
   =6\omega\mathcal E'(H)-c\min_{T\in\mathcal T}a'_T(h)<0.$$ The expression starts at zero and is nonnegative by <a href="#rig4:var:nonnegative-defect" data-reference-type="eqref" data-reference="rig4:var:nonnegative-defect">[rig4:var:nonnegative-defect]</a>, a contradiction.

Hahn–Banach separation of a linear subspace from this open convex cone gives a nonzero positive continuous functional on $C(\mathcal K)$ annihilating the image. The subspace need not be closed: its closure is still disjoint from the open cone. The Riesz representation theorem identifies the functional with a nonzero finite positive measure on $\mathcal K$.

Its mass on $\mathcal T$ is positive. If that mass were zero, testing $Q$ would give a strictly positive value on every remaining component: $C'_Q/w\ge6$ on $\mathcal A$, the added-point value is six, and $-\theta'_Q=3$ on $S$. This would contradict annihilation. Normalize the mass on $\mathcal T$ to one and call the resulting measure there $\varpi$. Call its restriction to $S$ $\eta$. On $\mathcal A$, divide the remaining measure by the positive function $w$ to obtain $\Lambda$; this is locally finite and has finite weighted mass. If the normalized added-point mass is $\lambda_\infty$, put $z=6\lambda_\infty$. Rearranging annihilation of <a href="#rig4:var:separation-map" data-reference-type="eqref" data-reference="rig4:var:separation-map">[rig4:var:separation-map]</a> is exactly <a href="#rig4:var:measure-identity" data-reference-type="eqref" data-reference="rig4:var:measure-identity">[rig4:var:measure-identity]</a>. ◻

</details>

<a id="pm-h-166"></a>
###### Normal graph tests

The measure $\varpi$ may initially be supported on several enclosures of the same area. The next argument uses variations of the original data to show that it is supported on the original horizon. It is local in the open exterior and assumes no complete ambient development.

<a id="stmt-rig4-var-normal-tests"></a>
<div id="rig4:var:normal-tests" class="lemma">

**Lemma 150** (Compact normal tests annihilating active constraints). *For every $\ell\in C^\infty_c(\operatorname{int}\Omega)$, there are smooth variations $H_j=(h_j,p_j)\in\mathcal V_0$, all supported in a fixed compact subset of the open exterior, such that $$h_j=2\ell K,\qquad C'_{H_j}\longrightarrow0$$ uniformly on the active rays over that compact set.*

</div>

<details id="proof-stmt-rig4-var-normal-tests"><summary>Proof of stmt-rig4-var-normal-tests</summary>

<a id="rig4:var:spatial-Einstein"></a>
*Proof.* Use local Lorentzian metrics in Gaussian time, $\mathbf g_j=-\,\mathrm dt^2+g_j(t)$, near a compact neighborhood of $\mathop{\mathrm{supp}}\ell$, and prescribe $g_j(0)=g$, $\partial_tg_j(0)=2K$. At $t=0$, prescribe their spatial Einstein tensors to be $$(\mathbf G_j)_{ik}=(D_j)_{ik},\qquad
 D_j=\frac{J\otimes J}{\mu+1/j}.
\label{rig4:var:spatial-Einstein}$$ This is possible by choosing the second time derivative of $g_j$. Indeed its coefficient in the spatial Einstein equation is a nonzero multiple of trace reversal on symmetric spatial tensors, which is invertible in dimension four. The normal components are fixed by the Gauss–Codazzi constraints: $$\mathbf G_j(n,n)=\mu,\qquad \mathbf G_j(n,e_i)=J_i.$$ A smooth choice of the second time jet realizes the prescribed tensor in a sufficiently small time neighborhood. No equation or energy condition away from the initial slice is required.

<a id="rig4:var:D-bounds"></a>
<a id="rig4:var:D-limit"></a>
We first check the convergence of these tensors along the slice, within the chosen open interior neighborhood. Put $Z=\{\mu=0\}$ there. At every point of $Z$, smoothness and $\mu\ge0$ give $\,\mathrm d\mu=0$. DEC implies $|J|\le\mu$, so $J=0$ and $\nabla J=0$ there as well; for example, along a smooth curve through the point, $\mu=O(t^2)$ and thus $J=O(t^2)$. The bounds $$|D_j|\le\mu,
 \qquad |\nabla D_j|\le2|\nabla J|+|\,\mathrm d\mu|
\label{rig4:var:D-bounds}$$ follow by differentiating the quotient and using $|J|\le\mu$. On every compact subset of this interior neighborhood, these imply convergence in $C^1$ to $$D=\begin{cases}J\otimes J/\mu,&\mu>0,\\0,&\mu=0.\end{cases}
\label{rig4:var:D-limit}$$ To justify the assertion at the zero set, choose a small neighborhood of its intersection with the compact set. The right sides of <a href="#rig4:var:D-bounds" data-reference-type="eqref" data-reference="rig4:var:D-bounds">[rig4:var:D-bounds]</a> are uniformly small there by continuity and their vanishing on $Z$. On the remaining compact part, $\mu$ is bounded away from zero and the usual quotient derivatives converge uniformly. The zero extension in <a href="#rig4:var:D-limit" data-reference-type="eqref" data-reference="rig4:var:D-limit">[rig4:var:D-limit]</a> is differentiable on $Z$, with derivative zero, because $|D|\le\mu$ and $\,\mathrm d\mu=0$ there. The same bounds give continuity of that derivative.

The full tensors $\mathbf G_j$ restricted to the slice, and their covariant derivatives in spatial directions, consequently converge in $C^0$. The spacetime connection in a spatial direction along $t=0$ depends only on the common $g,K$, not on the chosen second time jets.

<a id="rig4:var:tangential-cancellation"></a>
Consider a positive-density active ray. Its activity and DEC imply $|v|=1$, $|J|=\mu$, and $v=-J^\sharp/\mu$. Thus $\zeta=n+v$ is future null. On a neighborhood in the slice where $\mu>0$, define a covector $\alpha$ by $$\alpha(n)=\mu,\qquad \alpha|_{T\Omega}=J.$$ It is causal and nonnegative on the future cone, and the limiting Einstein tensor along that neighborhood is $\mathbf G_0=\alpha\otimes\alpha/\mu$. At the active point, $$\alpha(\zeta)=0,\qquad \alpha=-\mu\zeta^\flat.$$ Parallel transport $\zeta$ along any spatial curve. It remains future null, so its pairing with $\alpha$ is nonnegative and has value zero at the active point. Its derivative there is zero. Consequently $$(\nabla_{e_i}\alpha)(\zeta)=0,
 \qquad (\nabla_{e_i}\mathbf G_0)(e_i,\zeta)=0
\label{rig4:var:tangential-cancellation}$$ at that point, for every spatial orthonormal vector $e_i$.

<a id="rig4:var:Bianchi-cancellation"></a>
Contracted Bianchi, with signature $(-,+,+,+,+)$, gives the exact contraction needed for the graph variation: $$(\nabla_n\mathbf G_j)(n,\zeta)
     =\sum_{i=1}^4(\nabla_{e_i}\mathbf G_j)(e_i,\zeta)
       \longrightarrow0.
\label{rig4:var:Bianchi-cancellation}$$ There is no assertion of convergence for every normal derivative of $\mathbf G_j$; only <a href="#rig4:var:Bianchi-cancellation" data-reference-type="eqref" data-reference="rig4:var:Bianchi-cancellation">[rig4:var:Bianchi-cancellation]</a> is used.

Now vary the hypersurface to the graph $t=s\ell(x)$ in $\mathbf g_j$. Its induced data have metric derivative $h_j=2\ell K$ and some smooth tensor derivative $p_j$. They give compactly supported variations on $\Omega$: outside a fixed neighborhood of $\mathop{\mathrm{supp}}\ell$ the graph is the original slice, so extend the variations by zero. The same first jets of $g_j(t)$ along the initial slice imply uniform compact bounds, independent of $j$, for the derivatives of the unit normal $n_s$ and of the isometrically identified vector $v_s$.

<a id="rig4:var:graph-material-derivative"></a>
These first derivatives can be written explicitly. The graph velocity is $\ell n$. Orthogonality to its tangent vectors and the unit-normal condition give $\nabla_s n_s|_0=\nabla\ell$. The material derivative of a graph-pushed vector $v$ is $\,\mathrm d\ell(v)n+\ell K^\sharp v$. Since $h_j=2\ell K$, its isometric identification has derivative $I'_0v=-\ell K^\sharp v$, canceling the last spatial term. Hence <a id="rig4:var:argument-derivatives"></a>$$\nabla_s n_s|_0=\nabla\ell,\qquad
 \nabla_s v_s|_0=\,\mathrm d\ell(v)n.
\label{rig4:var:argument-derivatives}$$ Differentiating the constraint $2\mathbf G_j(n_s,n_s+v_s)$ and using Bianchi gives the exact formula $$\begin{aligned}
 \tfrac12 C'_{H_j}(x,v)
  ={}&\ell\sum_i(\nabla_{e_i}\mathbf G_j)(e_i,\zeta)
       +\mathbf G_j(\nabla\ell,\zeta)\nonumber\\
    &+\mathbf G_j\bigl(n,\nabla\ell+\,\mathrm d\ell(v)n\bigr).
\label{rig4:var:graph-material-derivative}
\end{aligned}$$ Thus only spatial first derivatives of the Einstein tensor occur in the final expression. At a positive-density active ray the first limiting term is zero by <a href="#rig4:var:tangential-cancellation" data-reference-type="eqref" data-reference="rig4:var:tangential-cancellation">[rig4:var:tangential-cancellation]</a>, the second is zero because $\mathbf G_0(\cdot,\zeta)=0$, and the last is zero because $$\alpha\bigl(\nabla\ell+\,\mathrm d\ell(v)n\bigr)
       =J(\nabla\ell)+\mu\,\,\mathrm d\ell(v)=0.$$ Equivalently, $\zeta_s=n_s+v_s$ remains null at a unit active vector, and its derivative pairs to zero with the proportional null covector $\alpha$.

If $\mu=0$, the full tensor $\mathbf G_j$ and all its spatial covariant derivatives are zero at the point, by <a href="#rig4:var:spatial-Einstein" data-reference-type="eqref" data-reference="rig4:var:spatial-Einstein">[rig4:var:spatial-Einstein]</a>, <a href="#rig4:var:D-bounds" data-reference-type="eqref" data-reference="rig4:var:D-bounds">[rig4:var:D-bounds]</a>, and the vanishing first jets of $\mu,J$. Bianchi therefore proves the same cancellation for every $|v|\le1$, including non-unit active vectors. The argument-derivative terms vanish there as well.

Let $L\Subset\operatorname{int}\Omega$ contain the fixed support. The limiting version of the right side of <a href="#rig4:var:graph-material-derivative" data-reference-type="eqref" data-reference="rig4:var:graph-material-derivative">[rig4:var:graph-material-derivative]</a> is zero at every active ray, by the positive- and zero-density arguments. All its coefficients are bounded on $L$, uniformly for $|v|\le1$. Consequently $$\sup_{\mathcal A|_L}|C'_{H_j}|
       \le C_\ell\|\mathbf G_j-\mathbf G_0\|_{C^1_{\rm sp}(L)}
       \longrightarrow0,$$ where the norm uses the common connection in spatial directions along the initial slice. This estimate contains no division by $\mu$ and includes sequences of active rays approaching $Z$. The support remains strictly inside the open exterior throughout; no vanishing normal derivative of the densities at the original boundary is asserted. This proves the required uniform convergence with the derivative convention <a href="#rig4:var:active-set" data-reference-type="eqref" data-reference="rig4:var:active-set">[rig4:var:active-set]</a>. ◻

</details>

<a id="stmt-rig4-var-area-localization"></a>
<div id="rig4:var:area-localization" class="proposition">

<a id="rig4:var:localized-area"></a>
<a id="rig4:var:localized-identity"></a>
**Proposition 151** (Localization of the area multiplier). *For $\varpi$-almost every element of $\mathcal T$, its frontier equals $S$, where $\varpi$ is the measure in Proposition <a href="#rig4:var:multiplier" data-reference-type="ref" data-reference="rig4:var:multiplier">149</a>. Consequently, for every variation $H=(h,p)$ in $\mathcal V$, $$\int_{\mathcal T}a'_T(h)\,\,\mathrm d\varpi(T)
       =a'_S(h)=\tfrac12\int_S\mathop{\mathrm{tr}}_S h\,\,\mathrm dA_g.
\label{rig4:var:localized-area}$$ In particular the multiplier identity becomes $$6\omega\mathcal E'(H)-c\,a'_S(h)
  =\langle C'_H,\Lambda\rangle
       -\int_S\theta'_H\,\,\mathrm d\eta+za.
\label{rig4:var:localized-identity}$$*

</div>

<details id="proof-stmt-rig4-var-area-localization"><summary>Proof of stmt-rig4-var-area-localization</summary>

<a id="rig4:var:trace-test"></a>
*Proof.* Apply <a href="#rig4:var:measure-identity" data-reference-type="eqref" data-reference="rig4:var:measure-identity">[rig4:var:measure-identity]</a> to the variations in Lemma <a href="#rig4:var:normal-tests" data-reference-type="ref" data-reference="rig4:var:normal-tests">150</a>. Their charge, boundary, and end-coefficient terms vanish, and $\Lambda$ is finite over their fixed compact support. The uniform constraint-derivative convergence therefore gives $$\int_{\mathcal T}\int_T\ell\,\mathop{\mathrm{tr}}_T K\,\,\mathrm dA_g\,\,\mathrm d\varpi(T)=0
 \qquad\text{for every }\ell\in C^\infty_c(\operatorname{int}\Omega).
\label{rig4:var:trace-test}$$

<a id="rig4:var:trace-free-parts"></a>
Define the finite aggregate area measure $\rho$ by $$\int f\,\,\mathrm d\rho
   =\int_{\mathcal T}\int_T f\,\,\mathrm dA_g\,\,\mathrm d\varpi(T).$$ All frontiers lie in one compact set. By Proposition <a href="#rig4:enc:common-plane" data-reference-type="ref" data-reference="rig4:enc:common-plane">104</a>, off $S$ the value $\mathop{\mathrm{tr}}_TK$ is a single continuous function $k(x)$ on their union. Thus <a href="#rig4:var:trace-test" data-reference-type="eqref" data-reference="rig4:var:trace-test">[rig4:var:trace-test]</a> says $k\rho=0$ as a signed measure in the open exterior. It follows that $k=0$ $\rho$-almost everywhere. Fubini, followed by smoothness of each free part of a minimizing frontier, shows that for $\varpi$-almost every $T$, $$\mathop{\mathrm{tr}}_TK=0\quad\hbox{everywhere on }T\setminus S.
\label{rig4:var:trace-free-parts}$$ Indeed a nonzero value on a smooth free part would persist on an open piece of positive area. Such a $T$ is minimal away from $S$ by Proposition <a href="#rig4:enc:minimizing-hull" data-reference-type="ref" data-reference="rig4:enc:minimizing-hull">102</a>, and hence is a MOTS there.

Fix one of these frontiers. At any contact point with $S$, it has the tangent plane and orientation of $S$, because its filled set contains the entire obstacle. In a local graph chart, let $f$ be its graph and $\psi$ the smooth obstacle graph. The regularity in Proposition <a href="#rig4:enc:minimizing-hull" data-reference-type="ref" data-reference="rig4:enc:minimizing-hull">102</a> gives $f\in C^{1,\alpha}\cap W^{2,2}$. On the coincidence set $f=\psi$, one has $Df=D\psi$. Locality of weak Sobolev derivatives, applied to the components of $Df-D\psi$, gives $D^2f=D^2\psi$ almost everywhere there. Since $S$ is a MOTS, the same MOTS equation holds almost everywhere on the contact set. By <a href="#rig4:var:trace-free-parts" data-reference-type="eqref" data-reference="rig4:var:trace-free-parts">[rig4:var:trace-free-parts]</a>, it holds off that set as well.

<a id="rig4:var:graph-equation"></a>
We spell out why no singular contact term remains. In these charts the MOTS equation has the form $$\partial_i\mathcal F^i(x,f,Df)=\mathcal B(x,f,Df),
\label{rig4:var:graph-equation}$$ where the coefficients are smooth after extending the one-sided smooth background across $S$, and the matrix $\mathcal F^i_{p_j}$ is uniformly elliptic on the local bounded gradient range. As $f\in W^{2,2}$, its left side is an $L^2$ function and the almost-everywhere equation is also the weak divergence-form equation. For a local coordinate derivative $f_k$, distributional differentiation of <a href="#rig4:var:graph-equation" data-reference-type="eqref" data-reference="rig4:var:graph-equation">[rig4:var:graph-equation]</a> yields $$\partial_i\bigl(a^{ij}\partial_j f_k\bigr)
   =\partial_i\bigl(\delta_{ik}\mathcal B
             -\mathcal F^i_{x_k}-\mathcal F^i_z f_k\bigr),
 \qquad a^{ij}=\mathcal F^i_{p_j}(x,f,Df).$$ All coefficients and the displayed right-hand vector field are $C^{0,\alpha}$. The interior divergence-form Schauder estimate gives $f_k\in C^{1,\alpha}$ locally, hence $f\in C^{2,\alpha}$. Further differentiation bootstraps to smoothness (Gilbarg and Trudinger 2001) <a id="pm-cite-75"></a>[[GilbargTrudinger2001](#ref-GilbargTrudinger2001)]. Thus $T$ is a smooth MOTS through contact.

If $T$ touches $S$, strong comparison gives local coincidence of the two ordered smooth MOTS with the same orientation. To check the applicable maximum principle, their nonnegative graph difference solves a linear uniformly elliptic equation with bounded lower-order coefficients. Its zeroth-order coefficient can be replaced by a nonpositive one to obtain the inequality for the strong minimum principle; an interior zero then forces local vanishing. Therefore the intersection with $S$ is open and closed in $S$. Connectedness of $S$ implies that $S$ is a component of $T$. Since every minimizing frontier has total area $A=\mathop{\mathrm{Area}}_g(S)$, there can be no additional component, and $T=S$.

If $T$ does not touch $S$, it is a compact smooth embedded two-sided MOTS entirely in $\operatorname{int}\Omega$. Its connected exterior side and full enclosure of the obstacle were proved in Proposition <a href="#rig4:enc:minimizing-hull" data-reference-type="ref" data-reference="rig4:enc:minimizing-hull">102</a>. With all components and the orientation toward the end counted, it is exactly an enclosing hypersurface excluded by the outermostness hypothesis. This alternative is impossible. Thus $T=S$ for $\varpi$-almost every $T$, proving <a href="#rig4:var:localized-area" data-reference-type="eqref" data-reference="rig4:var:localized-area">[rig4:var:localized-area]</a> and <a href="#rig4:var:localized-identity" data-reference-type="eqref" data-reference="rig4:var:localized-identity">[rig4:var:localized-identity]</a>. ◻

</details>

<a id="rig4:adj:section"></a>
##### A causal stationary field on the original exterior

We continue with the original equality data $(\Omega,g,K)$ of Definition <a href="#rig4:def:horizon" data-reference-type="ref" data-reference="rig4:def:horizon">99</a>. In particular, $S=\partial\Omega$ is connected, $\theta_+=0$ on $S$, and $S$ is outer area-minimizing. The constants fixed in Section 9 are $$r_0=\sqrt{2m},\qquad b^0=\frac E m,\qquad b^i=-\frac{P_i}{m},
 \qquad c=\frac2{r_0},\qquad \kappa=\frac c2=\frac1{r_0}.$$ Thus $(b^0)^2-|b|^2=1$ and $b^0>0$. We fix the same exponent $1<q_0<\min\{q,2\}$ as in the strict variation constructed there. The purpose of this section is to extract a smooth field from the multiplier and to retain all information about the original second fundamental form.

<a id="stmt-rig4-adj-causal-field"></a>
<div id="rig4:adj:causal-field" class="theorem">

**Theorem 152** (Causal stationary field). *There are a smooth function $u$ and a smooth vector field $X$ on $\Omega$, smooth up to its one-sided boundary, with the following properties.*

<a id="rig4:adj:complementarity"></a>
<a id="rig4:adj:kid-first"></a>
<a id="rig4:adj:conformal-adjoint"></a>
<a id="rig4:adj:kid-second"></a>
1.  *They satisfy $u\ge |X|_g$, $u>0$ in $\operatorname{int}\Omega$, and $$u\mu+J(X)=0.
     \label{rig4:adj:complementarity}$$ With symmetric indices denoting averaging, their equations are $$\begin{aligned}
     \nabla_{(i}X_{j)}&=-uK_{ij},
     \label{rig4:adj:kid-first}\\
     \Delta u&=-\operatorname{div}_g\bigl(K(X,\cdot)^\sharp\bigr),
     \label{rig4:adj:conformal-adjoint}\\
     \nabla^2u
     &=u(\mathop{\mathrm{Ric}}_g+\tau K-2K^2)-\mathcal L_XK+X_{(i}J_{j)}.
     \label{rig4:adj:kid-second}
    \end{aligned}$$ Here $X_i=g_{ij}X^j$ and $(K^2)_{ij}=K_{ik}K^k{}_j$.*

<a id="rig4:adj:decay"></a>
2.  *On the chosen asymptotically flat end, $$(u,X)=(b^0,b)+O_2(r^{-q_0}).
     \label{rig4:adj:decay}$$*

<a id="rig4:adj:horizon-data"></a>
3.  *At the boundary, for the unit normal $\nu$ pointing into $\Omega$, $$X=u\nu,\qquad
     \partial_\nu u+K(X,\nu)=\kappa.
     \label{rig4:adj:horizon-data}$$ Either $u>0$ everywhere on $S$ or $u=0$ everywhere on $S$.*

<a id="rig4:adj:stationary-metric"></a>
<a id="rig4:adj:ricci"></a>
4.  *On $\mathbb R\times\operatorname{int}\Omega$, set $$\mathbf g=-u^2\,\mathrm dt^2
       +g_{ij}(\mathrm dx^i+X^i\,\mathrm dt)
              (\mathrm dx^j+X^j\,\mathrm dt),
     \qquad \xi=\partial_t,\qquad N=u^2-|X|_g^2.
     \label{rig4:adj:stationary-metric}$$ For the future normal $n=u^{-1}(\xi-X)$, the slice $t=0$ has exactly the original induced metric $g$ and second fundamental form $K$, with the convention of Theorem <a href="#rig4:thm:rigidity" data-reference-type="ref" data-reference="rig4:thm:rigidity">100</a>. Moreover, $$\mathop{\mathrm{Ric}}_{\mathbf g}(\xi,\cdot)=0,
     \qquad \mathop{\mathrm{Ric}}_{\mathbf g}=0\quad\hbox{on }\{N>0\}.
     \label{rig4:adj:ricci}$$*

<a id="rig4:adj:positive-collar"></a>
<a id="rig4:adj:zero-collar"></a>
5.  *We have $N\ge0$, $N\to1$ at infinity, and $N>0$ in a full collar just outside $S$. More precisely, in the positive boundary-lapse case, $$N|_S=0,\qquad
     \mathrm dN|_S=2u\kappa\,\nu^\flat=2\kappa X^\flat.
     \label{rig4:adj:positive-collar}$$ In the zero boundary-lapse case, if $s\ge0$ is the original $g$-normal distance from $S$, there are smooth one-sided fields $d,Y_2$ such that $$u=sd,\qquad X=s^2Y_2,\qquad d|_S=\kappa,\qquad
     N=s^2\bigl(d^2-s^2|Y_2|_g^2\bigr).
     \label{rig4:adj:zero-collar}$$ Consequently all zeros of $N$ in $\operatorname{int}\Omega$ lie in a compact subset of that interior.*

</div>

The proof occupies the remainder of this section. At no point do we assume that the original data are vacuum or that they lie in a prescribed stationary development. The metric in <a href="#rig4:adj:stationary-metric" data-reference-type="eqref" data-reference="rig4:adj:stationary-metric">[rig4:adj:stationary-metric]</a> is constructed from the multiplier.

<a id="rig4:adj:measures"></a>
###### From a positive measure to the interior adjoint equations

<a id="rig4:adj:localized-multiplier"></a>
By Proposition <a href="#rig4:var:multiplier" data-reference-type="ref" data-reference="rig4:var:multiplier">149</a> and the area localization in Proposition <a href="#rig4:var:area-localization" data-reference-type="ref" data-reference="rig4:var:area-localization">151</a>, the multiplier identity is $$6\omega\,\mathcal E'(H)-c\,a'_S(h)
 =\langle C'_H,\Lambda\rangle
   -\int_S\theta'_H\,\mathrm d\eta+za,
 \qquad H=aQ+H_0.
 \label{rig4:adj:localized-multiplier}$$ The coefficient $a$ is the coefficient of the strict direction $Q$ in the variation space. We recall that $$C(x,v)=R_g+\tau^2-|K|^2+2J(v),\qquad |v|_g\le1,$$ that $\Lambda$ is a positive locally finite measure on the active set $C=0$, and that the test-vector identification for a metric variation $h$ has $\dot v=-\tfrac12h^\sharp v$.

Let $u$ be the scalar pushforward of $\Lambda$ to $\Omega$, and let $X$ be its vector first moment. Initially these symbols denote measures: for a compactly supported scalar $f$ and covector $\alpha$, $$\langle u,f\rangle=\int f(x)\,\mathrm d\Lambda(x,v),
 \qquad
 \langle X,\alpha\rangle=\int\alpha_x(v)\,\mathrm d\Lambda(x,v).$$ The unit-ball condition and positivity give $|X|_g\le u$ as measures, while activity gives $\mu u+J(X)=0$ as a measure. We use $\mathrm dV_g$ as the reference density when expressing the resulting distributional equations. After establishing smoothness, we use the same letters for the smooth densities of these measures.

<a id="stmt-rig4-adj-interior-equations"></a>
<div id="rig4:adj:interior-equations" class="lemma">

**Lemma 153** (Interior adjoint equations). *The moment measures have smooth densities on $\operatorname{int}\Omega$. They satisfy <a href="#rig4:adj:complementarity" data-reference-type="eqref" data-reference="rig4:adj:complementarity">[rig4:adj:complementarity]</a>–<a href="#rig4:adj:kid-second" data-reference-type="eqref" data-reference="rig4:adj:kid-second">[rig4:adj:kid-second]</a> there, and $u\ge|X|_g$ there.*

</div>

<details id="proof-stmt-rig4-adj-interior-equations"><summary>Proof of stmt-rig4-adj-interior-equations</summary>

*Proof.* For a variation supported in the open exterior, every term of <a href="#rig4:adj:localized-multiplier" data-reference-type="eqref" data-reference="rig4:adj:localized-multiplier">[rig4:adj:localized-multiplier]</a> except the constraint pairing vanishes. For a pure tensor variation $p=\dot K$, that pairing is $$2\bigl\langle u,\tau\mathop{\mathrm{tr}}_g p-K:p\bigr\rangle
 +2\bigl\langle X,\nabla^j(p_{ij}-(\mathop{\mathrm{tr}}_g p)g_{ij})\bigr\rangle.$$ Its distributional adjoint equation is <a id="rig4:adj:tensor-adjoint"></a>$$u(\tau g-K)-\nabla_{(i}X_{j)}+(\operatorname{div}X)g=0.
 \label{rig4:adj:tensor-adjoint}$$ Taking the trace in four dimensions gives $3u\tau+3\operatorname{div}X=0$. Substitution proves <a href="#rig4:adj:kid-first" data-reference-type="eqref" data-reference="rig4:adj:kid-first">[rig4:adj:kid-first]</a>.

For the conformal variation $(h,p)=(2\psi g,\psi K)$, the constraint transformation already established in Section 9 gives, on active rays, $$C'_H(x,v)=6\{-\Delta\psi+K(\nabla\psi,v)\}.$$ Its adjoint is <a href="#rig4:adj:conformal-adjoint" data-reference-type="eqref" data-reference="rig4:adj:conformal-adjoint">[rig4:adj:conformal-adjoint]</a>. This calculation is valid for measure moments, so both equations hold in distributions before any regularity assertion.

Diverge <a href="#rig4:adj:kid-first" data-reference-type="eqref" data-reference="rig4:adj:kid-first">[rig4:adj:kid-first]</a> and substitute $\operatorname{div}X=-u\tau$. Commuting covariant derivatives gives a Laplace equation for $X$ whose right side consists of smooth coefficients times $u,X,\nabla u$. In <a href="#rig4:adj:conformal-adjoint" data-reference-type="eqref" data-reference="rig4:adj:conformal-adjoint">[rig4:adj:conformal-adjoint]</a>, the right side consists of smooth coefficients times $X,\nabla X$. Thus the coupled system has diagonal Laplace principal part on the scalar and vector bundles; all couplings have order at most one. Distributional interior elliptic regularity, iterated with the smooth coefficients, makes both densities smooth. The measure inequalities and complementarity now give the asserted pointwise statements.

<a id="rig4:adj:metric-functional"></a>
It remains to verify the full metric equation, including its matter term. We may now work with smooth $u,X$. For a pure metric variation $h$, keep covariant $K$, scalar $u$, and contravariant $X$ fixed. The constraint pairing is the variation of $$\int\bigl[u(R+\tau^2-|K|^2)
      +2X^i\nabla^j(K_{ij}-\tau g_{ij})\bigr]\,\mathrm dV_g
 \label{rig4:adj:metric-functional}$$ minus $\int h(X,J^\sharp)\,\mathrm dV_g$. The latter is precisely the contribution of $\dot v=-\tfrac12h^\sharp v$. In using the varying volume form in <a href="#rig4:adj:metric-functional" data-reference-type="eqref" data-reference="rig4:adj:metric-functional">[rig4:adj:metric-functional]</a>, no term has been added: its original integrand is $2u\mu+2J(X)=0$ pointwise.

<a id="rig4:adj:shift-coefficient"></a>
For completeness, put $\pi^{ij}=K^{ij}-\tau g^{ij}$. Integrating the shift term once by parts gives $-\int\pi^{ij}(\mathcal L_Xg)_{ij}\,\mathrm dV_g$, with unchanged boundary terms outside the variation support. At fixed covariant $K$, $$\delta\pi^{ij}
 =-h^i{}_aK^{aj}-h^j{}_aK^{ia}
   +(K:h)g^{ij}+\tau h^{ij}.$$ Variation of the last integral, followed by integration of the term $-\pi^{ij}(\mathcal L_Xh)_{ij}$, has coefficient $$\mathcal L_XK-(\operatorname{div}X)K
  -\{X(\tau)+K^{ab}\nabla_aX_b\}g.
 \label{rig4:adj:shift-coefficient}$$ One can see the cancellations directly: if $B=\mathcal L_Xg$, the variation of $\pi$ contributes $2\mathop{\mathrm{Sym}}(KB)-(\mathop{\mathrm{tr}}B)K-\tau B$; integration of $\mathcal L_Xh$ contributes $(\mathcal L_X\pi)^{ij}+(\operatorname{div}X)\pi^{ij}$ with indices lowered; and the volume variation contributes $-\tfrac12(\pi:B)g$. Together they are <a href="#rig4:adj:shift-coefficient" data-reference-type="eqref" data-reference="rig4:adj:shift-coefficient">[rig4:adj:shift-coefficient]</a>.

<a id="rig4:adj:metric-adjoint-expanded"></a>
<a id="rig4:adj:trace-identity"></a>
The scalar and quadratic terms in <a href="#rig4:adj:metric-functional" data-reference-type="eqref" data-reference="rig4:adj:metric-functional">[rig4:adj:metric-functional]</a> have coefficient $$\nabla^2u-(\Delta u)g-u\mathop{\mathrm{Ric}}_g
       +2u(K^2-\tau K)+u\mu g.$$ Adding <a href="#rig4:adj:shift-coefficient" data-reference-type="eqref" data-reference="rig4:adj:shift-coefficient">[rig4:adj:shift-coefficient]</a> and the test-vector correction therefore gives $$\begin{aligned}
 0={}&\nabla^2u-(\Delta u)g-u\mathop{\mathrm{Ric}}_g+2u(K^2-\tau K)+u\mu g
       \notag\\
    &+\mathcal L_XK-(\operatorname{div}X)K
      -\{X(\tau)+K^{ab}\nabla_aX_b\}g-X_{(i}J_{j)}.
 \label{rig4:adj:metric-adjoint-expanded}
\end{aligned}$$ Equation <a href="#rig4:adj:kid-first" data-reference-type="eqref" data-reference="rig4:adj:kid-first">[rig4:adj:kid-first]</a> gives $K^{ab}\nabla_aX_b=-u|K|^2$. Moreover, using $\nabla^jK_{ij}=J_i+\nabla_i\tau$ in <a href="#rig4:adj:conformal-adjoint" data-reference-type="eqref" data-reference="rig4:adj:conformal-adjoint">[rig4:adj:conformal-adjoint]</a> gives $$\Delta u+X(\tau)
   =u|K|^2-J(X)=u(|K|^2+\mu).
 \label{rig4:adj:trace-identity}$$ Together with $\operatorname{div}X=-u\tau$, these identities cancel the scalar multiples of $g$ in <a href="#rig4:adj:metric-adjoint-expanded" data-reference-type="eqref" data-reference="rig4:adj:metric-adjoint-expanded">[rig4:adj:metric-adjoint-expanded]</a> and give <a href="#rig4:adj:kid-second" data-reference-type="eqref" data-reference="rig4:adj:kid-second">[rig4:adj:kid-second]</a>. ◻

</details>

<a id="pm-h-169"></a>
###### Boundary regularity and the asymptotic constants

<a id="stmt-rig4-adj-boundary-regularity"></a>
<div id="rig4:adj:boundary-regularity" class="lemma">

**Lemma 154** (Prolongation and absence of boundary atoms). *The fields $u,X$ extend smoothly to the one-sided boundary $S$. Their first jet at one interior point determines them on the connected interior. The original moment measures have no boundary-supported part, and hence are exactly $u\,\mathrm dV_g$ and $X\,\mathrm dV_g$ on all of $\Omega$.*

</div>

<details id="proof-stmt-rig4-adj-boundary-regularity"><summary>Proof of stmt-rig4-adj-boundary-regularity</summary>

<a id="rig4:adj:prolongation-x"></a>
<a id="rig4:adj:prolongation-u"></a>
*Proof.* Put $B_{ij}=-uK_{ij}$. Differentiate $\nabla_{(i}X_{j)}=B_{ij}$ in three arrangements, add two of the resulting equations, and subtract the third. Commuting derivatives gives $$\begin{aligned}
 \nabla_i\nabla_jX_k
 &=\nabla_iB_{jk}+\nabla_jB_{ik}-\nabla_kB_{ij}
       +\mathcal R_{ijk}(X),\label{rig4:adj:prolongation-x}\\
 \mathcal R_{ijk}(X)
 &=-\tfrac12\bigl(
       ([\nabla_j,\nabla_i]X)_k
       +([\nabla_i,\nabla_k]X)_j
       +([\nabla_j,\nabla_k]X)_i\bigr).\notag
\end{aligned}$$ Every commutator is a curvature contraction with $X$. Thus this equation uses only $K\nabla u$, $u\nabla K$, and curvature times $X$. Expanding the Lie derivative in <a href="#rig4:adj:kid-second" data-reference-type="eqref" data-reference="rig4:adj:kid-second">[rig4:adj:kid-second]</a> gives $$\begin{aligned}
 \nabla_i\nabla_ju
 ={}&u(\mathop{\mathrm{Ric}}_{g,ij}+\tau K_{ij}-2(K^2)_{ij})-X^a\nabla_aK_{ij}
       \notag\\
 &-K_{aj}\nabla_iX^a-K_{ia}\nabla_jX^a+X_{(i}J_{j)}.
 \label{rig4:adj:prolongation-u}
\end{aligned}$$ Consequently $$\mathcal J=(u,X,\nabla u,\nabla X)$$ obeys a homogeneous linear first-order system, with smooth coefficients built from $g,K$, their required derivatives, and $J$. Along any smooth curve, this is a linear ODE for $\mathcal J$. Uniqueness along curves proves the first-jet assertion.

In a compact collar of $S$, start on an interior collar section and solve this ODE along the normal segments down to $S$. Its coefficients are smooth up to the one-sided boundary. Smooth dependence on the initial point and on the normal parameter provides the smooth extension, agreeing with the original solution for positive collar parameter. The pointwise inequalities and complementarity extend by continuity.

The original moments could still have parts supported on $S$; the interior regularity alone does not exclude them. Let $s$ be geodesic collar distance, let $f\in C^\infty(S)$ be arbitrary and extended constantly along the normal segments, and take a collar cutoff $\chi$ equal to one near $S$. Choose the compact pure metric variation <a id="rig4:adj:boundary-atom-test"></a>$$h=\frac{s^2\chi(s)f}{6}\bigl(g-\mathrm ds\otimes\mathrm ds\bigr),
 \qquad p=0.
 \label{rig4:adj:boundary-atom-test}$$ This is one of the allowed smooth compact variations, with strict-direction coefficient $a=0$. Its value and first jet vanish on $S$. The trace along the three-dimensional collar slices is $s^2\chi f/2$, so its second normal derivative at $S$ is $f$. At $S$, the scalar variation $$R'_g(h)=\nabla^i\nabla^jh_{ij}-\Delta(\mathop{\mathrm{tr}}_gh)-\mathop{\mathrm{Ric}}_g:h$$ therefore equals $-f$: the only nonzero second jets are normal-normal derivatives of tangential components, whereas $h_{ss}=h_{sA}=0$. The variation of $\tau^2-|K|^2$ uses only $h$, that of $J$ at fixed covariant $K$ uses only $h,\nabla h$, and the test-vector correction uses only $h$. Consequently $C'_H|_S=-f$, independently of the active ray $v$.

The area derivative vanishes because $h|_S=0$; the expansion derivative vanishes because $h|_S=\nabla h|_S=p|_S=0$; and the charge derivative vanishes by compact support. Integrating the smooth interior densities by parts gives zero as well: the adjoint vanishes, and its scalar boundary terms involve only $h,\nabla h$, while its momentum boundary terms involve only $h$. This is ordinary integration up to $S$ using the one-sided smooth fields, not distributional differentiation of a zero extension across $S$. Thus <a href="#rig4:adj:localized-multiplier" data-reference-type="eqref" data-reference="rig4:adj:localized-multiplier">[rig4:adj:localized-multiplier]</a> says that the scalar boundary measure annihilates every $f\in C^\infty(S)$, and that measure is zero. The inequality $|X|_g\le u$ as measures eliminates the vector boundary part. Moreover, since $u$ is the pushforward of the positive measure $\Lambda$, the entire measure $\Lambda$ has zero mass over $S$, not merely zero first moment there. ◻

</details>

We first obtain constant limits from a Hessian estimate and causality. Related radial estimates for asymptotic Killing fields appear in (Beig and Chruściel 1996, Proposition 2.1 and Appendix C) <a id="pm-cite-76"></a>[[BeigChrusciel1996](#ref-BeigChrusciel1996)]. The normalization of the limits will then follow from the end variations.

<a id="stmt-rig4-adj-causal-jet-asymptotics"></a>
<div id="rig4:adj:causal-jet-asymptotics" class="lemma">

<a id="rig4:adj:jet-estimate"></a>
**Lemma 155** (Asymptotics of causal fields). *Let $g$ be a smooth metric uniformly comparable to the Euclidean metric on an end $\mathbb R^4\setminus\overline B_R$. Let $u$ be a smooth function and $X$ a smooth vector field there with $u\ge |X|_g$. Write $Y$ for all coordinate components of $(u,X)$. Suppose that, for some $q_0>1$ and a constant $C$, the coordinate derivatives satisfy $$|\partial^2Y|
 \le C r^{-1-q_0}|\partial Y|+C r^{-2-q_0}|Y|.
 \label{rig4:adj:jet-estimate}$$ Then there are constants $u_\infty$ and $X_\infty\in\mathbb R^4$ such that $$(u,X)=(u_\infty,X_\infty)+O_2(r^{-q_0}).$$*

</div>

<details id="proof-stmt-rig4-adj-causal-jet-asymptotics"><summary>Proof of stmt-rig4-adj-causal-jet-asymptotics</summary>

*Proof.* Fix a sufficiently large coordinate sphere of radius $R$ and put $$D(r)=\sup_{\omega\in S^3}|\partial Y(r\omega)|,
 \qquad \mathcal M(r)=\sup_{R\le t\le r}D(t).$$ Along each ray, $|Y(t\omega)|\le C+\int_R^tD(a)\,\mathrm da\le C+t\mathcal M(t)$, uniformly in $\omega$. Integrating $\partial_r(\partial Y)$ using <a href="#rig4:adj:jet-estimate" data-reference-type="eqref" data-reference="rig4:adj:jet-estimate">[rig4:adj:jet-estimate]</a>, and then taking the supremum over directions and radii at most $r$, gives $$\mathcal M(r)\le C+C\int_R^r t^{-1-q_0}\mathcal M(t)\,\mathrm dt.$$ The kernel is integrable. Gronwall therefore bounds $\mathcal M$ uniformly, so $\partial Y=O(1)$ and $Y=O(r)$. Equation <a href="#rig4:adj:jet-estimate" data-reference-type="eqref" data-reference="rig4:adj:jet-estimate">[rig4:adj:jet-estimate]</a> now gives $\partial^2Y=O(r^{-1-q_0})$. Each coordinate derivative has a radial limit $L(\omega)$, with error $O(r^{-q_0})$. Any two points on the sphere of radius $r$ can be joined by a spherical arc of length at most $\pi r$; integrating the Hessian along this arc gives an $O(r^{-q_0})$ difference between their gradients. Letting $r\to\infty$ shows that $L(\omega)$ is one constant matrix $L$. Radial integration of $\partial Y-L$ then gives $$\partial Y=L+O(r^{-q_0}),\qquad Y=Lx+O(1),$$ where boundedness of the second error uses $q_0>1$. Since $u\ge0$ in every direction, the linear part of $u$ vanishes. Uniform comparability of $g$ with the Euclidean metric and $|X|_g\le u$ then force the linear part of $X$ to vanish as well. Thus $Y=O(1)$ and $\partial Y=O(r^{-q_0})$. Substitution in <a href="#rig4:adj:jet-estimate" data-reference-type="eqref" data-reference="rig4:adj:jet-estimate">[rig4:adj:jet-estimate]</a>, using $q_0>1$, improves the Hessian bound to $O(r^{-2-q_0})$. Integrating each gradient component radially toward its zero limit gives $\partial Y=O(r^{-1-q_0})$. A further radial integration gives $Y=B(\omega)+O(r^{-q_0})$; comparison of values along the same spherical arcs now gives an $O(r^{-q_0})$ difference, so $B$ too is independent of direction. This proves the asserted constant limit and both differentiated estimates. ◻

</details>

<a id="stmt-rig4-adj-asymptotics"></a>
<div id="rig4:adj:asymptotics" class="lemma">

**Lemma 156** (Asymptotic normalization and positive lapse). *Equation <a href="#rig4:adj:decay" data-reference-type="eqref" data-reference="rig4:adj:decay">[rig4:adj:decay]</a> holds, and $u>0$ on $\operatorname{int}\Omega$.*

</div>

<details id="proof-stmt-rig4-adj-asymptotics"><summary>Proof of stmt-rig4-adj-asymptotics</summary>

*Proof.* Let $Y$ denote all coordinate components of the pair $(u,X)$. The prolonged system and the original $O_2$ metric and $O_1$ tensor decay imply Equation <a href="#rig4:adj:jet-estimate" data-reference-type="eqref" data-reference="rig4:adj:jet-estimate">[rig4:adj:jet-estimate]</a>. Indeed curvature, $\nabla K$, and $J$ have order $-2-q_0$, while $K$ and the Christoffel symbols have order $-1-q_0$. Equations <a href="#rig4:adj:prolongation-x" data-reference-type="eqref" data-reference="rig4:adj:prolongation-x">[rig4:adj:prolongation-x]</a> and <a href="#rig4:adj:prolongation-u" data-reference-type="eqref" data-reference="rig4:adj:prolongation-u">[rig4:adj:prolongation-u]</a> use no higher background derivatives. Converting their covariant Hessians to coordinate Hessians adds terms with coefficients $\Gamma$, $\partial\Gamma$, and $\Gamma^2$, controlled by the stated $O_2$ metric decay.

<a id="rig4:adj:unnormalized-decay"></a>
Lemma <a href="#rig4:adj:causal-jet-asymptotics" data-reference-type="ref" data-reference="rig4:adj:causal-jet-asymptotics">155</a> now gives constants with $$(u,X)=(u_\infty,X_\infty)+O_2(r^{-q_0}).
 \label{rig4:adj:unnormalized-decay}$$

<a id="rig4:adj:charge-flux"></a>
Use the five end prototypes of Definition <a href="#rig4:var:variation-space" data-reference-type="ref" data-reference="rig4:var:variation-space">146</a>, whose charge derivatives are computed in Lemma <a href="#rig4:var:end-variations" data-reference-type="ref" data-reference="rig4:var:end-variations">147</a>, in <a href="#rig4:adj:localized-multiplier" data-reference-type="eqref" data-reference="rig4:adj:localized-multiplier">[rig4:adj:localized-multiplier]</a>. Their strict-direction coefficient is $a=0$, so the term $za$ is absent; their boundary and area terms vanish because the prototypes are supported away from $S$. Integration by parts using the interior adjoint equations leaves only the outer boundary flux. By <a href="#rig4:adj:unnormalized-decay" data-reference-type="eqref" data-reference="rig4:adj:unnormalized-decay">[rig4:adj:unnormalized-decay]</a>, its limit is $$6\omega\bigl(u_\infty E'+X_\infty^iP'_i\bigr).
 \label{rig4:adj:charge-flux}$$ For clarity, the leading integrand is $$u_\infty(\partial_jh_{ij}-\partial_i h_{jj})
 +2X_\infty^j\bigl(p_{ij}-(\mathop{\mathrm{tr}}_\delta p)\delta_{ij}\bigr).$$ This is exactly <a href="#rig4:adj:charge-flux" data-reference-type="eqref" data-reference="rig4:adj:charge-flux">[rig4:adj:charge-flux]</a> with the energy and momentum normalizations of Equations <a href="#four:intro:energy" data-reference-type="eqref" data-reference="four:intro:energy">[four:intro:energy]</a>–<a href="#four:intro:momentum" data-reference-type="eqref" data-reference="four:intro:momentum">[four:intro:momentum]</a>. Every other boundary term contains a decaying background or adjoint coefficient, or its derivative, paired with $h=O_2(r^{-2})$ or $p=O_1(r^{-3})$ at the corresponding order. Multiplication by the sphere area $O(r^3)$ makes each such flux tend to zero. The volume pairing converges as well: the prototype constraint derivatives are $O(r^{-4-q})$ and the moment densities are bounded.

The scalar prototype $h=r^{-2}\delta$, $p=0$, has $(E',P')=(1,0)$. For the tensor prototype indexed by a constant vector $e$, its Euclidean trace reversal contracts with the sphere normal to $r^{-3}e$, and thus has $(E',P')=(0,e/3)$. These independent charges identify $(u_\infty,X_\infty)=(b^0,b)$ from <a href="#rig4:adj:localized-multiplier" data-reference-type="eqref" data-reference="rig4:adj:localized-multiplier">[rig4:adj:localized-multiplier]</a> and <a href="#rig4:adj:charge-flux" data-reference-type="eqref" data-reference="rig4:adj:charge-flux">[rig4:adj:charge-flux]</a>. This proves <a href="#rig4:adj:decay" data-reference-type="eqref" data-reference="rig4:adj:decay">[rig4:adj:decay]</a>.

If $u$ vanished at an interior point, its nonnegativity would give $\mathrm du=0$ there. Taylor’s theorem and $|X|\le u$ would give $X=0$ and $\nabla X=0$ at the same point. The whole first jet would vanish, contradicting Lemma <a href="#rig4:adj:boundary-regularity" data-reference-type="ref" data-reference="rig4:adj:boundary-regularity">154</a> and $u_\infty=b^0>0$. ◻

</details>

<a id="pm-h-170"></a>
###### Boundary fluxes and the two lapse cases

<a id="stmt-rig4-adj-boundary-data"></a>
<div id="rig4:adj:boundary-data" class="lemma">

**Lemma 157** (Boundary equations). *The multiplier measure at $S$ is $\mathrm d\eta=2u\,\mathrm dA_g$, and <a href="#rig4:adj:horizon-data" data-reference-type="eqref" data-reference="rig4:adj:horizon-data">[rig4:adj:horizon-data]</a> holds.*

</div>

<details id="proof-stmt-rig4-adj-boundary-data"><summary>Proof of stmt-rig4-adj-boundary-data</summary>

*Proof.* Take arbitrary compact pure tensor variations up to $S$. The actual outward normal of the exterior domain at its inner boundary is $-\nu$. Integration by parts in <a href="#rig4:adj:localized-multiplier" data-reference-type="eqref" data-reference="rig4:adj:localized-multiplier">[rig4:adj:localized-multiplier]</a> therefore gives $$-2\int_S\bigl[p(X,\nu)-(\mathop{\mathrm{tr}}_gp)X_\nu\bigr]\,\mathrm dA_g
      -\int_S(\mathop{\mathrm{tr}}_Sp)\,\mathrm d\eta=0.$$ Arbitrary mixed components $p_{\nu A}$ imply $X_{TS}=0$, and arbitrary tangential trace implies $\mathrm d\eta=2X_\nu\,\mathrm dA_g$.

Now take $(h,p)=(2\psi g,\psi K)$ with arbitrary compact support up to $S$. At a MOTS, its expansion derivative is $3\partial_\nu\psi$, while its area derivative is $3\int_S\psi\,\mathrm dA_g$. Integrating its constraint pairing with <a href="#rig4:adj:conformal-adjoint" data-reference-type="eqref" data-reference="rig4:adj:conformal-adjoint">[rig4:adj:conformal-adjoint]</a> gives $$\begin{aligned}
 -3c\int_S\psi\,\mathrm dA_g
 ={}&6\int_S\left[u\partial_\nu\psi
       -\{\partial_\nu u+K(X,\nu)\}\psi\right]\,\mathrm dA_g
       -3\int_S\partial_\nu\psi\,\mathrm d\eta.
\end{aligned}$$ The boundary value and normal derivative of $\psi$ can be prescribed independently. Their coefficients give $\mathrm d\eta=2u\,\mathrm dA_g$ and $\partial_\nu u+K(X,\nu)=c/2$. Together with the tensor-variation conclusions these are exactly <a href="#rig4:adj:horizon-data" data-reference-type="eqref" data-reference="rig4:adj:horizon-data">[rig4:adj:horizon-data]</a>. ◻

</details>

<a id="stmt-rig4-adj-lapse-dichotomy"></a>
<div id="rig4:adj:lapse-dichotomy" class="lemma">

**Lemma 158** (Boundary lapse dichotomy). *Either $u>0$ at every point of $S$ or $u=0$ identically on $S$.*

</div>

<details id="proof-stmt-rig4-adj-lapse-dichotomy"><summary>Proof of stmt-rig4-adj-lapse-dichotomy</summary>

*Proof.* Let $L_S$ be the expansion variation at $S$ under normal motion with speed $s\nu$. Its principal part is $-\Delta_S$. More explicitly, in a geodesic normal extension of $\nu$, if $\mathrm{II}$ is the second fundamental form of $S$ in $(\Omega,g)$, $$L_Ss=-\Delta_Ss+2K(\nu,\nabla_Ss)
  +\left[-|\mathrm{II}|^2-\mathop{\mathrm{Ric}}_g(\nu,\nu)
          +\mathop{\mathrm{tr}}_{TS}(\nabla_\nu K)\right]s.$$ Only the smoothness of the lower coefficients and the displayed principal part will be needed.

Extend $s\nu$ to a smooth compactly supported vector field $Y_1$ up to the boundary, and use $H=(\mathcal L_{Y_1}g,\mathcal L_{Y_1}K)$ in <a href="#rig4:adj:localized-multiplier" data-reference-type="eqref" data-reference="rig4:adj:localized-multiplier">[rig4:adj:localized-multiplier]</a>. These are legitimate one-sided tensor variations; one may compute their jets using any smooth extension across $S$. Their area and expansion derivatives are respectively $\int_SHs\,\mathrm dA_g$ and $L_Ss$.

We check the active-ray derivative with the specified vector identification. At a fixed interior point put $\mathcal A(v)=\nabla_vY_1$, so $h^\sharp=\mathcal A+\mathcal A^*$, where the adjoint uses $g$. Let $\phi_t$ be the local flow of $Y_1$ and let $v_t$ be the isometrically identified test vector for $g_t=\phi_t^*g$. Naturality gives $$C_{\phi_t^*g,\phi_t^*K}(x,v_t)
   =C_{g,K}(\phi_t x,\mathrm d\phi_t(v_t)).$$ At $t=0$, the covariant velocity of the vector on the right, relative to parallel transport along $\phi_t x$, is $$\mathcal A(v)+\dot v
 =\mathcal A(v)-\tfrac12(\mathcal A+\mathcal A^*)v
 =\tfrac12(\mathcal A-\mathcal A^*)v.$$ It is perpendicular to $v$. The base derivative of $C$, with $v$ parallel transported, vanishes at an interior active ray because it differentiates a nonnegative function at a two-sided interior minimum. The remaining vector derivative is $2J(\tfrac12(\mathcal A-\mathcal A^*)v)$, also zero: at an active unit ray $J=-\mu v^\flat$, and at an active ray with $|v|<1$ we have $\mu=J=0$. Therefore $C'_H=0$ at every interior active ray.

The vector field $Y_1$ need not preserve $S$: its compact Lie derivatives are permitted tensor variations, independently of feasibility of a flow on the whole exterior. No normal derivative at a one-sided boundary minimum is being set equal to zero. Such boundary rays contribute no integral because $\Lambda$ has zero mass over $S$ by Lemma <a href="#rig4:adj:boundary-regularity" data-reference-type="ref" data-reference="rig4:adj:boundary-regularity">154</a>. Thus the entire constraint pairing vanishes. The multiplier identity and $\mathrm d\eta=2u\,\mathrm dA_g$ now read $$-c\int_S Hs\,\mathrm dA_g=-2\int_SuL_Ss\,\mathrm dA_g,$$ and hence give <a id="rig4:adj:boundary-stability-adjoint"></a>$$2L_S^*u=cH.
 \label{rig4:adj:boundary-stability-adjoint}$$ Here the adjoint is with respect to $\mathrm dA_g$ on the closed manifold $S$.

Outer area minimization, tested against every nonnegative outward normal speed, gives $H\ge0$ pointwise. Hence $L_S^*u\ge0$ and $u\ge0$ on $S$. Increase the zeroth coefficient of $L_S^*$ by a constant until that coefficient is nonnegative. The inequality remains valid because $u\ge0$. The strong minimum principle for this operator with principal part $-\Delta_S$ shows that a zero of $u$ forces $u$ to vanish on the connected surface $S$. Otherwise it is everywhere positive. ◻

</details>

<a id="pm-h-171"></a>
###### The constructed spacetime and its null stress

<a id="stmt-rig4-adj-killing-development"></a>
<div id="rig4:adj:killing-development" class="lemma">

**Lemma 159** (Killing development and timelike collars). *The metric in <a href="#rig4:adj:stationary-metric" data-reference-type="eqref" data-reference="rig4:adj:stationary-metric">[rig4:adj:stationary-metric]</a> has all the properties in parts <span class="upright">(iv)</span> and <span class="upright">(v)</span> of Theorem <a href="#rig4:adj:causal-field" data-reference-type="ref" data-reference="rig4:adj:causal-field">152</a>.*

</div>

<details id="proof-stmt-rig4-adj-killing-development"><summary>Proof of stmt-rig4-adj-killing-development</summary>

*Proof.* The interior positivity of $u$ makes <a href="#rig4:adj:stationary-metric" data-reference-type="eqref" data-reference="rig4:adj:stationary-metric">[rig4:adj:stationary-metric]</a> a smooth Lorentzian metric, with future normal $n=u^{-1}(\partial_t-X)$ after choosing the indicated time orientation. In the convention of the problem, the second fundamental form of a lapse-shift metric is $$\frac1{2u}\bigl(\partial_tg-\mathcal L_Xg\bigr).$$ Its coefficients here are independent of $t$, and <a href="#rig4:adj:kid-first" data-reference-type="eqref" data-reference="rig4:adj:kid-first">[rig4:adj:kid-first]</a> identifies this tensor with the original $K$. The vector field $\xi=\partial_t$ is Killing by construction.

<a id="rig4:adj:einstein-components"></a>
We record the curvature computation to fix both the matter term and the sign convention. The Gauss and normal-variation identities for a general lapse-shift metric, with positive second fundamental form convention, are $$\begin{aligned}
 \mathop{\mathrm{Ric}}_{\mathbf g,ij}
  &=\mathop{\mathrm{Ric}}_{g,ij}+\tau K_{ij}-2(K^2)_{ij}
    +u^{-1}\bigl(\partial_tK_{ij}
           -(\mathcal L_XK)_{ij}-(\nabla^2u)_{ij}\bigr),\\
 \mathop{\mathrm{Ric}}_{\mathbf g}(n,n)
  &=-u^{-1}(\partial_t\tau-X\tau)-|K|^2+u^{-1}\Delta u.
\end{aligned}$$ Tracing these equations uses $$g^{ij}\bigl(\partial_tK_{ij}-(\mathcal L_XK)_{ij}\bigr)
 =\partial_t\tau-X\tau+2u|K|^2.$$ In the stationary case this yields <a id="rig4:adj:spatial-ricci"></a><a id="rig4:adj:spacetime-scalar"></a>$$\begin{aligned}
 \mathop{\mathrm{Ric}}_{\mathbf g,ij}
 &=\mathop{\mathrm{Ric}}_{g,ij}+\tau K_{ij}-2(K^2)_{ij}
      -u^{-1}\bigl((\mathcal L_XK)_{ij}+(\nabla^2u)_{ij}\bigr),
 \label{rig4:adj:spatial-ricci}\\
 R_{\mathbf g}
 &=R_g+\tau^2+|K|^2-2u^{-1}(\Delta u+X\tau).
 \label{rig4:adj:spacetime-scalar}
\end{aligned}$$ Equation <a href="#rig4:adj:trace-identity" data-reference-type="eqref" data-reference="rig4:adj:trace-identity">[rig4:adj:trace-identity]</a> and complementarity show that $$R_{\mathbf g}=2\mu+\frac{2J(X)}u=0.$$ Writing $\mathbf G$ for the Einstein tensor, the constraints and <a href="#rig4:adj:kid-second" data-reference-type="eqref" data-reference="rig4:adj:kid-second">[rig4:adj:kid-second]</a> consequently give $$\mathbf G(n,n)=\mu,\qquad
 \mathbf G(n,e_i)=J_i,\qquad
 u\mathbf G_{ij}=-X_{(i}J_{j)}.
 \label{rig4:adj:einstein-components}$$ These identities can also be compared with the transversal Killing construction in (Beig and Chruściel 1997) <a id="pm-cite-77"></a>[[BeigChrusciel1997KID](#ref-BeigChrusciel1997KID)]; its momentum symbol has the opposite sign to the one used here. The null-fluid structure of a modified constraint adjoint is discussed in (Huang and Lee 2024, sec. 6.1) <a id="pm-cite-78"></a>[[HuangLee2024Bartnik](#ref-HuangLee2024Bartnik)]. We use the displayed direct calculation, in four spatial dimensions, rather than importing a stationarity or dimensional-transfer theorem.

If $\mu=0$, the dominant energy condition gives $J=0$, so all entries in <a href="#rig4:adj:einstein-components" data-reference-type="eqref" data-reference="rig4:adj:einstein-components">[rig4:adj:einstein-components]</a> vanish. If $\mu>0$, the inequalities $$0=u\mu+J(X)\ge u\mu-|J||X|\ge0$$ force $|J|=\mu$, $|X|=u$, and $J=-\mu X^\flat/u$. Since $\mathbf g(\xi,n)=-u$ and $\mathbf g(\xi,e_i)=X_i$, the tensor with components <a href="#rig4:adj:einstein-components" data-reference-type="eqref" data-reference="rig4:adj:einstein-components">[rig4:adj:einstein-components]</a> is exactly <a id="rig4:adj:null-stress"></a>$$\mathbf G=\frac\mu{u^2}\,\xi^\flat\otimes\xi^\flat
 \quad\hbox{where }\mu>0.
 \label{rig4:adj:null-stress}$$ The Killing one-form in this equation is the spacetime one-form. It is null wherever the displayed tensor is nonzero. Thus $\mathbf G(\xi,\cdot)=0$ everywhere. Since $R_{\mathbf g}=0$, this is the first assertion of <a href="#rig4:adj:ricci" data-reference-type="eqref" data-reference="rig4:adj:ricci">[rig4:adj:ricci]</a>. If $N>0$, then $|X|<u$, so complementarity forces $\mu=J=0$; all the Ricci components vanish. This proves the second assertion. An internal null region has not been excluded or assumed vacuum.

It remains to examine the original boundary and the end. Equation <a href="#rig4:adj:decay" data-reference-type="eqref" data-reference="rig4:adj:decay">[rig4:adj:decay]</a> gives $N\to(b^0)^2-|b|^2=1$. At $S$, Equation <a href="#rig4:adj:horizon-data" data-reference-type="eqref" data-reference="rig4:adj:horizon-data">[rig4:adj:horizon-data]</a> gives $X=u\nu$, so $N=0$ and all tangential derivatives of $N$ vanish. If $u>0$ on $S$, Equation <a href="#rig4:adj:kid-first" data-reference-type="eqref" data-reference="rig4:adj:kid-first">[rig4:adj:kid-first]</a> gives $\langle\nabla_\nu X,\nu\rangle=-uK(\nu,\nu)$. Hence $$\partial_\nu N
 =2u\bigl(\partial_\nu u+uK(\nu,\nu)\bigr)=2u\kappa,$$ which is <a href="#rig4:adj:positive-collar" data-reference-type="eqref" data-reference="rig4:adj:positive-collar">[rig4:adj:positive-collar]</a>. Compactness of $S$ supplies a full collar on which $N>0$.

In the other case, $u|_S=0$ and $X|_S=0$. Tangential derivatives of $X$ vanish. The normal-normal and normal-tangential components of <a href="#rig4:adj:kid-first" data-reference-type="eqref" data-reference="rig4:adj:kid-first">[rig4:adj:kid-first]</a> then give $\nabla_\nu X=0$ on $S$, so every first derivative of $X$ vanishes there. Smooth one-sided division by normal distance gives $u=sd$ and $X=s^2Y_2$. The boundary condition gives $d|_S=\partial_\nu u|_S=\kappa>0$. This is <a href="#rig4:adj:zero-collar" data-reference-type="eqref" data-reference="rig4:adj:zero-collar">[rig4:adj:zero-collar]</a>, and once again compactness gives a full collar with $N>0$. Together with positivity far out on the unique end, these collars place all interior zeros of $N$ in an interior compact set. ◻

</details>

<details id="proof-stmt-rig4-adj-killing-development-2"><summary>Proof of stmt-rig4-adj-killing-development</summary>

*Proof of Theorem <a href="#rig4:adj:causal-field" data-reference-type="ref" data-reference="rig4:adj:causal-field">152</a>.* Combine Lemmas <a href="#rig4:adj:interior-equations" data-reference-type="ref" data-reference="rig4:adj:interior-equations">153</a>, <a href="#rig4:adj:boundary-regularity" data-reference-type="ref" data-reference="rig4:adj:boundary-regularity">154</a>, <a href="#rig4:adj:asymptotics" data-reference-type="ref" data-reference="rig4:adj:asymptotics">156</a>, <a href="#rig4:adj:boundary-data" data-reference-type="ref" data-reference="rig4:adj:boundary-data">157</a>, <a href="#rig4:adj:lapse-dichotomy" data-reference-type="ref" data-reference="rig4:adj:lapse-dichotomy">158</a>, and <a href="#rig4:adj:killing-development" data-reference-type="ref" data-reference="rig4:adj:killing-development">159</a>. ◻

</details>

<a id="rig4:sta:section"></a>
##### Vanishing twist and the complete static base

We continue with the equality data and the fields supplied by Theorem <a href="#rig4:adj:causal-field" data-reference-type="ref" data-reference="rig4:adj:causal-field">152</a>. The stationary metric $$\mathbf g=-u^2dt^2+g_{ij}(dx^i+X^i dt)(dx^j+X^j dt)
 \quad\text{on }\mathbb R\times\operatorname{int}\Omega$$ is smooth because $u>0$ in the interior. Its Killing field is $\xi=\partial_t$. Recall that $$N=u^2-|X|_g^2\ge0,\qquad
 \mathop{\mathrm{Ric}}_{\mathbf g}(\xi,\cdot)=0,
 \qquad \mathop{\mathrm{Ric}}_{\mathbf g}=0\quad\text{where }N>0.$$ Moreover, $N\to1$ at the end, and $N>0$ on a full interior collar of $S$. Thus the interior zero set $$Z=\{x\in\operatorname{int}\Omega:N(x)=0\}$$ is compactly contained in $\operatorname{int}\Omega$. No regularity of $Z$ as a subset is assumed. In particular, it may have interior or infinitely many components.

<a id="pm-h-173"></a>
###### The Killing current near a null set

<a id="rig4:sta:stationary-decomposition"></a>
On the open set $\mathcal P=\{N>0\}\subset\operatorname{int}\Omega$, put <a id="rig4:sta:base-variables"></a>$$\label{rig4:sta:base-variables}
 \begin{aligned}
 h_b&=g+N^{-1}X^\flat\otimes X^\flat,
 & C_b&=g^{-1}-u^{-2}X\otimes X=h_b^{-1},\\
 A_b&=N^{-1}X^\flat,
 & F&=dA_b,\qquad \lambda=\sqrt N .
 \end{aligned}$$ Here $X^\flat$ is formed with $g$. Direct substitution gives $$\label{rig4:sta:stationary-decomposition}
 \mathbf g=-N(dt-A_b)^2+h_b.$$ The tensor $C_b$ extends smoothly and nonnegatively through $Z$, although $h_b$ and $A_b$ need not extend there. For a covector $\alpha$ write $|\alpha|_{C_b}^2=C_b^{ij}\alpha_i\alpha_j$.

<a id="stmt-rig4-sta-current-identities"></a>
<div id="rig4:sta:current-identities" class="lemma">

<a id="rig4:sta:norm-equation"></a>
<a id="rig4:sta:killing-current"></a>
**Lemma 160** (Killing-current identities). *Let $\mathcal G_{\alpha\beta}=\nabla^{\mathbf g}_\alpha\xi_\beta$. On the interior of $\Omega$ one has $$\label{rig4:sta:norm-equation}
 u^{-1}\operatorname{div}_g(uC_b\,dN)
       =-2|\mathcal G|_{\mathbf g}^2.$$ On $\mathcal P$ the antisymmetric tensor $$\label{rig4:sta:killing-current}
 Q^{ij}=uN C_b^{ik}C_b^{j\ell}F_{k\ell}
 \qquad\text{satisfies}\qquad \nabla^g_iQ^{ij}=0.$$ The norm in <a href="#rig4:sta:norm-equation" data-reference-type="eqref" data-reference="rig4:sta:norm-equation">[rig4:sta:norm-equation]</a> is the Lorentzian contraction of both tensor indices; it need not be nonnegative.*

</div>

<details id="proof-stmt-rig4-sta-current-identities"><summary>Proof of stmt-rig4-sta-current-identities</summary>

*Proof.* The Killing identities and $\mathop{\mathrm{Ric}}_{\mathbf g}(\xi,\cdot)=0$ give $$\nabla^{\mathbf g,\alpha}\mathcal G_{\alpha\beta}=0,
 \qquad
 \square_{\mathbf g}\bigl(\mathbf g(\xi,\xi)\bigr)
       =2|\mathcal G|_{\mathbf g}^2.$$ For a stationary scalar function the wave operator is $u^{-1}\operatorname{div}_g(uC_b\,d\,\cdot\,)$: the spacetime volume density is $u\sqrt{\det g}$ and its spatial inverse-metric block is $C_b$. Since $\mathbf g(\xi,\xi)=-N$, this proves <a href="#rig4:sta:norm-equation" data-reference-type="eqref" data-reference="rig4:sta:norm-equation">[rig4:sta:norm-equation]</a>, including at $Z$ where all its entries are smooth.

For the second identity set $\theta=dt-A_b$. On $\mathcal P$, $$\xi^\flat=-N\theta,
 \qquad
 \mathcal G=\tfrac12d\xi^\flat
            =\tfrac12(-dN\wedge\theta+NF).$$ The inverse-metric dual of $\theta$ is proportional to $\partial_t$, so the term containing $\theta$ has zero spatial-spatial component after both indices are raised. Consequently $$\mathcal G^{ij}=\tfrac N2 C_b^{ik}C_b^{j\ell}F_{k\ell}.$$ The stationary divergence identity, with density $u\sqrt{\det g}$, now gives <a href="#rig4:sta:killing-current" data-reference-type="eqref" data-reference="rig4:sta:killing-current">[rig4:sta:killing-current]</a>. In converting coordinate divergence to $g$-covariant divergence, the additional Christoffel term vanishes by antisymmetry. ◻

</details>

<a id="stmt-rig4-sta-log-estimate"></a>
<div id="rig4:sta:log-estimate" class="lemma">

<a id="rig4:sta:null-log-energy"></a>
**Lemma 161** (A transverse logarithmic estimate). *Suppose $Z\ne\varnothing$. On a neighborhood of $Z$ with compact closure in the interior, let $$B=|X|_g,\qquad e=X/B,\qquad D=e^\perp,$$ and denote by $d_DN$ the $g$-orthogonal projection of $dN$ to $D$. This neighborhood can be chosen so that $u$ and $B$ are bounded below by positive constants. For every smooth cutoff $\zeta$ compactly supported there, $$\label{rig4:sta:null-log-energy}
 \sup_{\varepsilon>0}
 \int u\zeta^2\frac{|dN|_{C_b}^2}{(N+\varepsilon)^2}\,dV_g
 <\infty.$$ In particular, $d_D\log N$ is square-integrable on the positive set in every smaller neighborhood of $Z$.*

</div>

<details id="proof-stmt-rig4-sta-log-estimate"><summary>Proof of stmt-rig4-sta-log-estimate</summary>

<a id="rig4:sta:degenerate-norm"></a>
<a id="rig4:sta:nonnegative-gradient"></a>
*Proof.* At a point of $Z$, $B=u>0$. Compactness provides the positive lower bounds after shrinking a neighborhood. On that neighborhood the eigenvalues of $C_b$ relative to $g$ are $1$ on $D$ and $N/u^2$ in the $e$ direction. Thus $$\label{rig4:sta:degenerate-norm}
 |dN|_{C_b}^2=|d_DN|_g^2+\frac N{u^2}(eN)^2.$$ Smoothness and nonnegativity of $N$ also give $$\label{rig4:sta:nonnegative-gradient}
 |dN|_g^2\le C N.$$ For completeness, work in a slightly larger compact interior neighborhood, where the Hessian is bounded. Taylor’s inequality along a short geodesic in the direction $-\nabla N$ gives $0\le N-t|dN|+Ct^2/2$. Increasing $C$ so that $t=|dN|/C$ stays in this neighborhood proves <a href="#rig4:sta:nonnegative-gradient" data-reference-type="eqref" data-reference="rig4:sta:nonnegative-gradient">[rig4:sta:nonnegative-gradient]</a>.

<a id="rig4:sta:killing-norm-bound"></a>
Let $n=u^{-1}(\xi-X)$ be the future unit normal to the original slice. In a local orthonormal frame $n,e,e_a$, with the $e_a$ in $D$, differentiating $\mathbf g(\xi,\xi)=-N$ gives $$\mathcal G_{in}=-\frac{N_i/2+B\mathcal G_{ie}}u
 \quad\text{for each spatial index }i.$$ As $|\mathcal G|_{\mathbf g}^2
 =2\sum_{i<j}\mathcal G_{ij}^2-2\sum_i\mathcal G_{in}^2$, we obtain the exact expansion $$\label{rig4:sta:killing-norm-bound}
 \begin{split}
 -2|\mathcal G|_{\mathbf g}^2
   ={}&\frac{|dN|_g^2}{u^2}
       +\frac{4B}{u^2}\sum_aN_a\mathcal G_{ae}
       -\frac{4N}{u^2}\sum_a\mathcal G_{ae}^2
       -4\sum_{a<b}\mathcal G_{ab}^2\\
   \le{}& C\bigl(N+|d_DN|_g\bigr).
 \end{split}$$ All coefficients of $\mathcal G$ are bounded here. This estimate is pointwise and does not require a global frame for $D$.

Write $f=-2|\mathcal G|_{\mathbf g}^2$ and test $\operatorname{div}_g(uC_b\,dN)=uf$ against $\zeta^2/(N+\varepsilon)$. There is no singular boundary in this test: Equation <a href="#rig4:sta:norm-equation" data-reference-type="eqref" data-reference="rig4:sta:norm-equation">[rig4:sta:norm-equation]</a> is smooth across $Z$, and $\varepsilon>0$. Integration by parts gives <a id="rig4:sta:log-test"></a>$$\label{rig4:sta:log-test}
 \begin{split}
 \int u\zeta^2\frac{|dN|_{C_b}^2}{(N+\varepsilon)^2}\,dV_g
 ={}&\int\frac{u\zeta^2 f}{N+\varepsilon}\,dV_g\\
 &+2\int\frac{u\zeta\langle d\zeta,dN\rangle_{C_b}}
                  {N+\varepsilon}\,dV_g.
 \end{split}$$ In the first term use <a href="#rig4:sta:killing-norm-bound" data-reference-type="eqref" data-reference="rig4:sta:killing-norm-bound">[rig4:sta:killing-norm-bound]</a>, $N/(N+\varepsilon)\le1$, and $|d_DN|\le|dN|_{C_b}$. Young’s inequality absorbs its derivative term into, say, one quarter of the left side. The second integral is handled by Cauchy’s inequality for the nonnegative tensor $C_b$ and another quarter of that side. The remaining terms are bounded by a constant times $\int u(\zeta^2+|d\zeta|_{C_b}^2)\,dV_g$, uniformly in $\varepsilon$. This proves <a href="#rig4:sta:null-log-energy" data-reference-type="eqref" data-reference="rig4:sta:null-log-energy">[rig4:sta:null-log-energy]</a>. Fatou’s lemma and <a href="#rig4:sta:degenerate-norm" data-reference-type="eqref" data-reference="rig4:sta:degenerate-norm">[rig4:sta:degenerate-norm]</a> give the last assertion. ◻

</details>

<a id="pm-h-174"></a>
###### Removal of all twist boundary terms

<a id="stmt-rig4-sta-twist-vanishes"></a>
<div id="rig4:sta:twist-vanishes" class="proposition">

**Proposition 162** (Vanishing of the twist). *On all of $\mathcal P$, including every component, $F=dA_b=0$.*

</div>

<details id="proof-stmt-rig4-sta-twist-vanishes"><summary>Proof of stmt-rig4-sta-twist-vanishes</summary>

<a id="rig4:sta:twist-test"></a>
*Proof.* On the asymptotic end the constant limit of $A_b$ is the covector $a_\infty=b^i\,dx^i$, because $N\to1$ and $g\to\delta$. Choose a smooth function $f$ on $\Omega$ which equals $b^i x^i$ sufficiently far out and is zero off an end neighborhood disjoint from $S$ and $Z$. Then $$\beta=A_b-df,\qquad d\beta=F,
 \qquad \beta=O(r^{-q_0})\quad\text{at infinity}.$$ For any nonnegative smooth function $\chi$ compactly supported in $\mathcal P$, multiply <a href="#rig4:sta:killing-current" data-reference-type="eqref" data-reference="rig4:sta:killing-current">[rig4:sta:killing-current]</a> by $\chi\beta_j$ and integrate. Antisymmetry gives $$\label{rig4:sta:twist-test}
 \frac12\int_{\mathcal P}
   \chi uN C_b^{ik}C_b^{j\ell}F_{ij}F_{k\ell}\,dV_g
  =-\int_{\mathcal P}Q^{ij}(\partial_i\chi)\beta_j\,dV_g.$$ The integrand on the left is nonnegative, and its quadratic form in $F$ is positive definite at each point of $\mathcal P$.

<a id="rig4:sta:current-contraction"></a>
The contraction in the right side has a cancellation that is needed at the null loci. Lowering its remaining index with $g$, one finds $$\label{rig4:sta:current-contraction}
 \begin{split}
 g_{ik}Q^{kj}(A_b)_j
 &=\frac N u F_{ij}X^j\\
 &=\frac1u\left[
 X^j(dX^\flat)_{ij}
 -\frac{|X|^2N_i-X(N)X_i}{N}\right].
 \end{split}$$ Indeed $C_b A_b=X/u^2$, and the projection in the other raised index does not change $F_{ij}X^j$. This covector is orthogonal to $X$. Where $X\ne0$, its last numerator is $B^2(d_DN)_i$. The coordinate-free numerator in <a href="#rig4:sta:current-contraction" data-reference-type="eqref" data-reference="rig4:sta:current-contraction">[rig4:sta:current-contraction]</a> will also be used where $X=0$.

We choose cutoffs near the three possible escape loci with disjoint transition neighborhoods. If $Z=\varnothing$, the first cutoff below is identically one.

<a id="pm-h-175"></a>
###### The interior null set.

Choose nested relatively compact interior neighborhoods of $Z$ on which $u$ and $B$ are bounded below and Lemma <a href="#rig4:sta:log-estimate" data-reference-type="ref" data-reference="rig4:sta:log-estimate">161</a> applies. A smooth cutoff $\eta$ is one on the smaller neighborhood and supported in the larger. Let $\vartheta:[0,\infty)\to[0,1]$ be smooth, zero on $[0,1]$ and one on $[2,\infty)$, with bounded derivative, and set $$\chi_{Z,\varepsilon}=1-\eta+\eta\vartheta(N/\varepsilon).$$ For all sufficiently small $\varepsilon$, $N$ has a positive lower bound on the support of $d\eta$, so differentiation of $\eta$ adds no term. The only transition is $\varepsilon<N<2\varepsilon$, and its derivative is bounded by $C|dN|/\varepsilon$. Here $df=0$. Orthogonality in <a href="#rig4:sta:current-contraction" data-reference-type="eqref" data-reference="rig4:sta:current-contraction">[rig4:sta:current-contraction]</a> replaces $dN$ by $d_DN$ in the contraction. Since $N\asymp\varepsilon$ on the band and the smooth term $X\mathbin{\lrcorner}dX^\flat$ is bounded, the absolute contribution to the right side of <a href="#rig4:sta:twist-test" data-reference-type="eqref" data-reference="rig4:sta:twist-test">[rig4:sta:twist-test]</a> is at most <a id="rig4:sta:null-cutoff-cost"></a>$$\label{rig4:sta:null-cutoff-cost}
 C\int_{\{\varepsilon<N<2\varepsilon\}\cap\mathop{\mathrm{supp}}\eta}
       \bigl(1+|d_D\log N|_g^2\bigr)\,dV_g=o(1).$$ The integrable majorant comes from Lemma <a href="#rig4:sta:log-estimate" data-reference-type="ref" data-reference="rig4:sta:log-estimate">161</a>. The characteristic functions of these bands tend pointwise to zero even at points of $Z$. Thus dominated convergence proves the last assertion without an assumption on the measure or structure of $Z$.

<a id="pm-h-176"></a>
###### The asymptotic end.

Let $\chi_{\infty,R}$ be one for $r\le R$, zero for $r\ge2R$, with derivative bounded by $C/R$, and extend it by one over the compact part. From the adjoint end estimates, $$Q=O(r^{-1-q_0}),\qquad \beta=O(r^{-q_0}).$$ The transition annulus has volume $O(R^4)$, so its contribution is <a id="rig4:sta:end-cutoff-cost"></a>$$\label{rig4:sta:end-cutoff-cost}
 O(R^{2-2q_0})=o(1),$$ since $q_0>1$.

<a id="pm-h-177"></a>
###### The original boundary.

Let $s$ be original $g$-normal distance from $S$, increasing into $\Omega$, and let $\chi_{S,\sigma}$ change from zero to one on $\sigma<s<2\sigma$, with derivative bounded by $C/\sigma$. Again $df=0$ near this collar. If $u|_S>0$, the boundary conclusions of Theorem <a href="#rig4:adj:causal-field" data-reference-type="ref" data-reference="rig4:adj:causal-field">152</a> give $$dN=2\kappa X^\flat\quad\text{on }S,
 \qquad X=u\nu\quad\text{on }S,
 \qquad N\asymp s.$$ In particular $d_DN=O(s)$, so <a href="#rig4:sta:current-contraction" data-reference-type="eqref" data-reference="rig4:sta:current-contraction">[rig4:sta:current-contraction]</a> is bounded. Its contraction with the normal $\nabla s$ is $O(s)$: it annihilates $X$, and $\nabla s-X/u=O(s)$. Multiplication by $1/\sigma$ and integration over a collar of volume $O(\sigma)$ therefore gives $O(\sigma)$.

<a id="rig4:sta:zero-lapse-collar"></a>
If $u|_S=0$, the same theorem supplies smooth one-sided fields $d,Y_2$ with $$\label{rig4:sta:zero-lapse-collar}
 u=sd,\qquad X=s^2Y_2,\qquad d|_S=\kappa,
 \qquad N=s^2(d^2-s^2|Y_2|^2).$$ Thus $u\asymp s$, $N\asymp s^2$, $dX^\flat=O(s)$, and $dN=O(s)$. Both terms inside the brackets of <a href="#rig4:sta:current-contraction" data-reference-type="eqref" data-reference="rig4:sta:current-contraction">[rig4:sta:current-contraction]</a> are $O(s^3)$; its entire value is $O(s^2)$. This gives a boundary cutoff cost $O(\sigma^2)$.

Now take $\chi=\chi_{Z,\varepsilon}\chi_{S,\sigma}\chi_{\infty,R}$. For positive parameters with sufficiently small $\varepsilon,\sigma$ and large $R$, it is a compactly supported smooth test on $\mathcal P$. Multiplication by the other two factors does not increase any of the three estimates. Therefore the absolute value of the right side of <a href="#rig4:sta:twist-test" data-reference-type="eqref" data-reference="rig4:sta:twist-test">[rig4:sta:twist-test]</a> tends to zero as $\varepsilon,\sigma\downarrow0$ and $R\to\infty$. Choose a sequence of such parameters; its cutoffs tend pointwise to one on $\mathcal P$. Fatou’s lemma gives zero for the integral of the nonnegative density on the left. Its continuity and pointwise positive definiteness force $F=0$ everywhere on $\mathcal P$. This integration is on an open manifold with compactly supported tests and remains valid if $\mathcal P$ has infinitely many components. ◻

</details>

<a id="pm-h-178"></a>
###### Static equations and the only finite-distance attachment

<a id="rig4:sta:static-equations"></a>
Let $\mathcal U$ be the component of $\mathcal P$ containing the distant asymptotic end. Since $F=0$ on all of $\mathcal P$, the Poincaré lemma supplies a local primitive of $A_b$ on every sufficiently small ball in any positive component. Replacing $t$ locally by $T=t-a$ with $da=A_b$ turns <a href="#rig4:sta:stationary-decomposition" data-reference-type="eqref" data-reference="rig4:sta:stationary-decomposition">[rig4:sta:stationary-decomposition]</a> into $-\lambda^2dT^2+h_b$. Its Ricci components are $$(\mathop{\mathrm{Ric}}_{\mathbf g})_{TT}=\lambda\Delta_{h_b}\lambda,
 \qquad
 (\mathop{\mathrm{Ric}}_{\mathbf g})_{ij}
      =(\mathop{\mathrm{Ric}}_{h_b})_{ij}-\lambda^{-1}(\mathop{\mathrm{Hess}}_{h_b}\lambda)_{ij}.$$ These follow directly from the nonzero mixed Christoffel symbols $\Gamma^T_{Ti}=\partial_i\log\lambda$ and $\Gamma^i_{TT}=\lambda h_b^{ij}\partial_j\lambda$. Vacuum on $\mathcal P$ therefore gives, on every positive component, $$\label{rig4:sta:static-equations}
 \lambda\mathop{\mathrm{Ric}}_{h_b}=\mathop{\mathrm{Hess}}_{h_b}\lambda,
 \qquad \Delta_{h_b}\lambda=0,
 \qquad \mathop{\mathrm{Scal}}_{h_b}=0.$$ This conclusion uses local primitives only; no global time primitive or topological conclusion has yet been used.

<a id="stmt-rig4-sta-connected-positive-set"></a>
<div id="rig4:sta:connected-positive-set" class="lemma">

**Lemma 163** (Connectedness of the positive set). *The set $\mathcal P$ is connected and equals $\mathcal U$. In particular, the positive collar of $S$ belongs to $\mathcal U$.*

</div>

<details id="proof-stmt-rig4-sta-connected-positive-set"><summary>Proof of stmt-rig4-sta-connected-positive-set</summary>

*Proof.* The unique asymptotic end lies in $\mathcal U$ outside a compact set. Any other component $V$ of $\mathcal P$ therefore has compact closure in the original exterior $\Omega$, with its boundary included. Its frontier lies in $S\cup Z$: an interior frontier point with $N>0$ would have a connected positive neighborhood meeting $V$ and hence belong to $V$. The frontier is nonempty, since otherwise $V$ would be both open and closed in the connected interior of $\Omega$, which also contains $\mathcal U$.

The continuous function $\lambda=\sqrt N$ vanishes on this frontier and is positive in $V$. It therefore attains a positive maximum at an interior point of $V$. The strong maximum principle for $\Delta_{h_b}\lambda=0$ makes $\lambda$ constant on $V$, contradicting its zero frontier values. Thus there is no such component $V$. The collar supplied by Theorem <a href="#rig4:adj:causal-field" data-reference-type="ref" data-reference="rig4:adj:causal-field">152</a> lies in $\mathcal P=\mathcal U$, as claimed. ◻

</details>

<a id="stmt-rig4-sta-complete-base"></a>
<div id="rig4:sta:complete-base" class="proposition">

<a id="rig4:sta:boundary-data"></a>
**Proposition 164** (Completeness and regular horizon attachment). *The component $\mathcal U$ satisfies $0<\lambda<1$. Every approach in $\mathcal U$ to an interior zero of $N$ has infinite $h_b$-length.
