**Proposition 190** (The quadratic deficit). *On the real linear space of all smooth TT seeds with the prescribed decay, the first deficit coefficient is zero and the second coefficient $c_2[q]$ is a continuous, rotation-invariant, nonnegative quadratic form. For a finite-angular-type seed it is given by $$\begin{gathered}
 c_2[q]=\frac1{16\pi}\int_M N\left(
 |q-Q(v)|^2+|U|^2+2FJ_s^0F\right)\,\,\mathrm dV_0,\\
 J_s^0=-\Delta_{r^2\sigma}-\frac2{r^2}+\frac{6m_0}{r^3}.
 \end{gathered}
 \label{ads:eq:quadratic-positive-form}$$ The last term is integrated on the spheres before radial integration. For every actual branch in Theorem <a href="#ads:thm:main" data-reference-type="ref" data-reference="ads:thm:main">176</a>, $$\mathfrak D_q(\epsilon)=c_2[q]\epsilon^2+o(\epsilon^2).
 \label{ads:eq:actual-quadratic-deficit}$$ In particular, $c_2[q]>0$ implies a strictly positive deficit for all sufficiently small positive $\epsilon$.*

</div>

<details id="proof-stmt-ads-prop-quadratic"><summary>Proof of stmt-ads-prop-quadratic</summary>

*Proof.* For a finite-angular-type seed the scalar constraint gives $\mathop{\mathrm{Scal}}_g+6=\epsilon^2|q|^2+O(\epsilon^3)$. Proposition <a href="#ads:prop:leading-energy" data-reference-type="ref" data-reference="ads:prop:leading-energy">188</a>, with $l=1$, shows that the constant and first coefficients of the mass norm minus $b_*(A_{\mathrm{leaf}})$ vanish, and that its second coefficient is $$\frac1{16\pi}\int_M N\bigl(|q|^2+|U|^2+2FJ_s^0F\bigr)\,\,\mathrm dV_0.$$ The areas in <a href="#ads:eq:quadratic-area-gap" data-reference-type="eqref" data-reference="ads:eq:quadratic-area-gap">[ads:eq:quadratic-area-gap]</a> agree through order one, so the first coefficient of the original deficit is also zero. Since $b_*'(4\pi a^2)=\kappa/(8\pi)$, the contribution to its second coefficient from that area difference is $-\kappa(16\pi)^{-1}\int_SvDv\,\,\mathrm dA_0$. Lemma <a href="#ads:lem:tt-square" data-reference-type="ref" data-reference="ads:lem:tt-square">189</a> now proves <a href="#ads:eq:quadratic-positive-form" data-reference-type="eqref" data-reference="ads:eq:quadratic-positive-form">[ads:eq:quadratic-positive-form]</a> with precisely the displayed factor and sign.

On a spherical harmonic with $-\Delta_\sigma$ eigenvalue $\lambda\geq2$, the eigenvalue of $J_s^0$ is $$\frac{\lambda-2}{r^2}+\frac{6m_0}{r^3}>0.$$ Thus its quadratic form is strictly positive on mean-zero functions at every finite $s$, and $N>0$ for $s>0$. This proves nonnegativity for finite-angular-type seeds without any boundary sign restriction.

Proposition <a href="#ads:prop:expansions" data-reference-type="ref" data-reference="ads:prop:expansions">183</a> defines $c_2$ on the full real space $\mathscr T_{\tau,\alpha}$ of smooth TT seeds as a continuous, rotation-invariant quadratic form, independently of branch existence and boundary sign, and proves $c_1=0$. For an arbitrary seed $q$, take the finite-angular-type TT approximants $q_\nu$ from Lemma <a href="#ads:lem:rotation" data-reference-type="ref" data-reference="ads:lem:rotation">182</a>. The formula proved above gives $c_2[q_\nu]\geq0$, and continuity in $\|\cdot\|_\beta$ gives $c_2[q]\geq0$. Proposition <a href="#ads:prop:expansions" data-reference-type="ref" data-reference="ads:prop:expansions">183</a> also supplies <a href="#ads:eq:actual-quadratic-deficit" data-reference-type="eqref" data-reference="ads:eq:actual-quadratic-deficit">[ads:eq:actual-quadratic-deficit]</a> for every prescribed actual branch. ◻

</details>

<a id="pm-h-224"></a>
###### All null directions

Define the fixed vector space <a id="ads:eq:kernel-space"></a>$$\mathcal K=\left\{Q(v):Lv=0,\ v\text{ decays},\quad
 v|_S\in\operatorname{span}_{\mathbb R}\{1,x_1,x_2,x_3\}\right\}.
 \label{ads:eq:kernel-space}$$ The decaying solutions in this definition have finite angular type and $O(r^{-3})$ decay with all the differentiated bounds obtained from their homogeneous radial equations.

<a id="stmt-ads-cor-kernel"></a>
<div id="ads:cor:kernel" class="corollary">

**Corollary 191** (The complete quadratic kernel). *The kernel of $c_2$ is exactly $\mathcal K$, a four-dimensional real vector space. In particular, the nonzero degree-one directions are genuine quadratic null directions.*

</div>

<details id="proof-stmt-ads-cor-kernel"><summary>Proof of stmt-ads-cor-kernel</summary>

*Proof.* First suppose $q$ has finite angular type and $c_2[q]=0$. Equation <a href="#ads:eq:quadratic-positive-form" data-reference-type="eqref" data-reference="ads:eq:quadratic-positive-form">[ads:eq:quadratic-positive-form]</a> and the strict positivity just proved imply <a id="ads:eq:quadratic-equality-conditions"></a>$$q=Q(v),\qquad U=0,\qquad F=0
 \quad\text{on }s>0.
 \label{ads:eq:quadratic-equality-conditions}$$ Smoothness extends these equalities to the boundary. Coordinate spheres are umbilic under conformal changes of $g_0$. At the base minimal sphere, the tracefree second-form variation due to a normal height $h_1$ is $-(\mathop{\mathrm{Hess}}_Sh_1)^{\circ}$: the radial curvature term is pure trace. Since $h_1=-v|_S$, the vanishing of $U|_S$ implies $(\mathop{\mathrm{Hess}}_\sigma(v|_S))^{\circ}=0$. For completeness, the divergence of this equation on the unit sphere gives $\,\mathrm d(\Delta_\sigma v+2v)=0$. Subtracting the mean reduces it to $\mathop{\mathrm{Hess}}_\sigma(v-\bar v)=-(v-\bar v)\sigma$. This equation determines its solution along every geodesic from its value and differential at one point, and its solutions are precisely the linear coordinate functions. Thus $v|_S$ is a constant plus a linear harmonic.

<a id="ads:eq:dipole-radial-ode"></a>
Uniqueness of the decaying Dirichlet problem for $L$ then excludes every other angular mode throughout $M$. Each degree-one radial coefficient is a multiple of the same decaying solution of $$V''+2\frac NrV'-\left(3+\frac2{r^2}\right)V=0.
 \label{ads:eq:dipole-radial-ode}$$ Hence $q\in\mathcal K$. Conversely, every element of $\mathcal K$ is null, as we now check; the conditions $U=F=0$ do not impose a further restriction on its degree-one part.

Take $q=Q(v)\in\mathcal K$. The first conformal coefficient $u$ also has only constant and linear modes, by its Neumann equation and decaying uniqueness. Let $h(s,x)$ be the first height coefficient of the CMC spheres, and put $p=N/r$. Conformal variation of mean curvature and first variation of the lapse give <a id="ads:eq:first-cmc-conformal-variations"></a>$$_1=J_s^0h+4(u_s-pu),
 \qquad [f]_1=h_s+2u.
 \label{ads:eq:first-cmc-conformal-variations}$$ Here the second identity follows by taking the normal component of the velocity of the graph $s+\epsilon h(s,x)$ in $g_0+4\epsilon u g_0$. On the degree-one part, the CMC equation therefore fixes <a id="ads:eq:dipole-cmc-height"></a>$$h=-\frac{2r^3}{3m_0}(u_s-pu).
 \label{ads:eq:dipole-cmc-height}$$ All formulas in the next calculation are componentwise on that part. The background equations and <a href="#ads:eq:dipole-radial-ode" data-reference-type="eqref" data-reference="ads:eq:dipole-radial-ode">[ads:eq:dipole-radial-ode]</a> give $$p'=\frac{3m_0}{r^3}-\frac1{r^2},\qquad
 p^2=1+\frac1{r^2}-\frac{2m_0}{r^3},\qquad
 u''=-2pu'+\left(3+\frac2{r^2}\right)u.$$ Consequently, <a id="ads:eq:dipole-cancellation"></a>$$\begin{aligned}
 \frac1{r^3}\partial_s\bigl[r^3(u'-pu)\bigr]
 &=3p(u'-pu)+u''-p'u-pu'\notag\\
 &=\left(3+\frac2{r^2}-p'-3p^2\right)u
 =\frac{3m_0}{r^3}u.
 \label{ads:eq:dipole-cancellation}
\end{aligned}$$ It follows that $h_s=-2u$ on the degree-one part, so its lapse fluctuation vanishes. The freely chosen radial mean of $h$ changes $[f]_1$ only by a radial function, which disappears upon subtracting the mean. Thus $F=0$ independently of the radial labeling.

At every background sphere, the tracefree second-form variation of these graphs is $-(\mathop{\mathrm{Hess}}_{r^2\sigma}h)^{\circ}$; the conformal variation and radial curvature terms are pure trace. The constant and linear modes of $h$ have vanishing tracefree spherical Hessian, so $U=0$ as well. At $S$ there is also exact agreement with the prescribed first minimal height: on degree one, $$D_1=\frac{6m_0}{a^3},\qquad
 h(0)=-\frac{4u_s(0)}{D_1}=-v(0).$$ We already have $q=Q(v)$, and hence <a href="#ads:eq:quadratic-positive-form" data-reference-type="eqref" data-reference="ads:eq:quadratic-positive-form">[ads:eq:quadratic-positive-form]</a> proves $c_2[q]=0$. Existence and uniqueness for each of the four boundary modes show that $\mathcal K$ has dimension at most four; it has dimension exactly four because <a href="#ads:eq:q-normal-boundary" data-reference-type="eqref" data-reference="ads:eq:q-normal-boundary">[ads:eq:q-normal-boundary]</a> and invertibility of $D$ make the map from these boundary data to $Q(v)$ injective.

It remains to rule out additional null directions of arbitrary angular type. Let $\mathcal Z=\{q:c_2[q]=0\}$ in the full smooth TT space. A nonnegative quadratic form has a linear kernel: if $c_2[q]=0$, nonnegativity of $c_2[q+th]$ for all real $t$ forces its polarized bilinear form to vanish on $(q,h)$ for every $h$. By Proposition <a href="#ads:prop:quadratic" data-reference-type="ref" data-reference="ads:prop:quadratic">190</a>, $\mathcal Z$ is also closed in $\|\cdot\|_\beta$ and invariant under rotations. For $q\in\mathcal Z$, let $q_j$ be its polynomial rotational averages from Lemma <a href="#ads:lem:rotation" data-reference-type="ref" data-reference="ads:lem:rotation">182</a>. Each such average is a norm limit of finite linear combinations of rotations of $q$; therefore $q_j\in\mathcal Z$. Each $q_j$ has finite angular type, so the preceding argument puts it in $\mathcal K$. Since $q_j\to q$ in norm and the fixed finite-dimensional space $\mathcal K$ is closed in that norm, $q\in\mathcal K$. This proves the full assertion without applying a pointwise geometric limit to the CMC fields $U$ and $F$. ◻

</details>

<a id="stmt-ads-rem-kernel-sign"></a>
<div id="ads:rem:kernel-sign" class="remark">

*Remark 192* (The boundary sign and the null space). If $v|_S=c+d\cdot x$, then $$Q(v)_{ss}|_S=D_0c+D_1d\cdot x,
 \qquad D_0=\frac{2\kappa}{a},\quad
 D_1=\frac2{a^2}+\frac{2\kappa}{a}=\frac{6m_0}{a^3}.$$ Thus $Q(v)_{ss}|_S\geq0$ is equivalent to $D_0c\geq D_1|d|$. A nonzero pure dipole fails that condition, but a sufficiently large positive radial component makes a mixed radial–dipole seed satisfy it. This is a compatibility statement about seeds, not an existence claim for branches satisfying outermostness and outer area-minimization. In particular, the boundary sign cannot be used to discard the degree-one null directions from the proof.

</div>

<a id="ads:sec:quartic"></a>
##### Fourth order in the quadratic kernel

We now treat the kernel left by Proposition <a href="#ads:prop:quadratic" data-reference-type="ref" data-reference="ads:prop:quadratic">190</a>. A statement about a fourth-order jet is an identity modulo $\epsilon^5$, in the conventions of Section 2.3; it does not assert the existence of the corresponding geometric object at a nonzero parameter.

<a id="stmt-ads-prop-quartic"></a>
<div id="ads:prop:quartic" class="proposition">

**Proposition 193** (The quartic coefficient). *Suppose that $c_2[q]=0$. Write the representation furnished by Corollary <a href="#ads:cor:kernel" data-reference-type="ref" data-reference="ads:cor:kernel">191</a> as $$q=Q(v):=\mathop{\mathrm{Hess}}_{g_0}v-Bv,\qquad Lv=0,
 \qquad v=v_0(s)+v_1(s,x),$$ where $v_1$ has only degree-one spherical modes and $v$ decays at infinity. Then $$c_0[q]=c_1[q]=c_2[q]=c_3[q]=0,
 \qquad c_4[q]\geq 0.$$ If $v_1\not\equiv0$, then $c_4[q]>0$. In particular, in that case the actual deficit $\mathfrak D_q(\epsilon)$ is strictly positive for all sufficiently small positive $\epsilon$.*

</div>

The proof has three steps. Lemmas <a href="#ads:lem:slice" data-reference-type="ref" data-reference="ads:lem:slice">194</a> and <a href="#ads:lem:null-cut" data-reference-type="ref" data-reference="ads:lem:null-cut">195</a> change the slice and compare its boundary area with a minimal leaf, giving a quartic TT square. If that square vanishes, Sections 6.4–6.5 force the degree-one profile to vanish. The actual expansion from Proposition <a href="#ads:prop:expansions" data-reference-type="ref" data-reference="ads:prop:expansions">183</a> then proves the assertion for the given branch.

Throughout the proof we use the stronger decay supplied by the kernel representation. The homogeneous separated equations for $v$, and Lemma <a href="#ads:lem:inverse" data-reference-type="ref" data-reference="ads:lem:inverse">179</a>, give $O(r^{-3})$ decay with every required derivative for $v$ and $q=Q(v)$. The conformal coefficients through degree four consequently have differentiated $O(r^{-3})$ decay and finite angular type. Put $$u=[\phi_\epsilon]_1,\qquad Lu=0.$$ We use the fourth-order jets of the original data $g_\epsilon=\phi_\epsilon^4g_0$ and $K_\epsilon=\epsilon\phi_\epsilon^{-2}q$. Their initial constraints and their boundary expansion equation hold as Taylor identities.

<a id="pm-h-226"></a>
###### A change of slice at the level of jets

<a id="stmt-ads-lem-slice"></a>
<div id="ads:lem:slice" class="lemma">

<a id="ads:quart:time-graph"></a>
<a id="ads:quart:scalar-four"></a>
<a id="ads:quart:metric-decay"></a>
<a id="ads:quart:metric-two"></a>
**Lemma 194** (The corrected slice). *There is a decaying finite-angular-type function $w$, with $w|_S=0$, for which the following construction is defined through degree four. Formally evolve the initial jets in Gaussian time and take the graph $$T=-\epsilon v+\epsilon^2w.
 \label{ads:quart:time-graph}$$ The induced metric and future second fundamental form, denoted by $\widetilde g$ and $\widetilde K$, satisfy <a id="ads:quart:leading-k"></a>$$\begin{aligned}
 \widetilde K&=\epsilon^2k+O(\epsilon^3),
 &\mathop{\mathrm{tr}}_{g_0}k&=0,&\mathop{\mathrm{div}}_{g_0}k&=0,
 \label{ads:quart:leading-k}\\
 \mathop{\mathrm{Scal}}_{\widetilde g}+6
   &=\epsilon^4|k|_{g_0}^2+O(\epsilon^5).
 \label{ads:quart:scalar-four}
\end{aligned}$$ Here $k=O(r^{-3})$, with all derivatives needed for the fourth-order CMC construction. Coefficientwise through degree four, $$\widetilde g-g_\epsilon=O(r^{-6})
 \label{ads:quart:metric-decay}$$ with the required differentiated bounds. Thus the mass covectors and their Lorentz norms agree through that degree. Moreover, $$_2
   =-2vq-Bv^2-\,\mathrm dv\otimes\,\mathrm dv
   =-\mathop{\mathrm{Hess}}_{g_0}(v^2)+\,\mathrm dv\otimes\,\mathrm dv+Bv^2.
 \label{ads:quart:metric-two}$$*

</div>

<details id="proof-stmt-ads-lem-slice"><summary>Proof of stmt-ads-lem-slice</summary>

<a id="ads:quart:gaussian-evolution"></a>
*Proof.* We give the formal evolution and its constraint justification before performing the graph calculation. Write $$\overline g=-\,\mathrm dt^2+\gamma(t),\qquad
 \gamma(0)=g_\epsilon,\qquad \mathcal K(0)=K_\epsilon,$$ and determine a full formal time series recursively from $$\begin{aligned}
 \partial_t\gamma&=2\mathcal K,\nonumber\\
 \partial_t\mathcal K
   &=-\mathop{\mathrm{Ric}}_\gamma-3\gamma
     -(\mathop{\mathrm{tr}}_\gamma\mathcal K)\mathcal K
     +2\mathcal K\circ_\gamma\mathcal K.
 \label{ads:quart:gaussian-evolution}
\end{aligned}$$ The coefficients take values in the ring of smooth spatial jets modulo $\epsilon^5$. At each time order the right side is a known spatial differential expression in previously determined coefficients, so the recursion is well defined. A substitution $t=T=O(\epsilon)$ uses only finitely many of these coefficients. Keeping a full time series here ensures that taking time derivatives never treats an omitted time coefficient as zero.

<a id="ads:quart:gaussian-ricci"></a>
Let $H=\mathop{\mathrm{tr}}_\gamma\mathcal K$. The time-index Christoffel symbols are $$\overline\Gamma^t_{ij}=\mathcal K_{ij},\qquad
 \overline\Gamma^i_{tj}=\mathcal K^i{}_j,$$ and direct contraction of the curvature gives $$\begin{aligned}
 \overline\mathop{\mathrm{Ric}}_{ij}
  &=\mathop{\mathrm{Ric}}_{\gamma,ij}+\partial_t\mathcal K_{ij}
       +H\mathcal K_{ij}
       -2(\mathcal K\circ_\gamma\mathcal K)_{ij},\nonumber\\
 \overline\mathop{\mathrm{Ric}}_{tt}
  &=-\mathop{\mathrm{tr}}_\gamma(\partial_t\mathcal K)+|\mathcal K|_\gamma^2,
 &\overline\mathop{\mathrm{Ric}}_{ti}
  &=(\mathop{\mathrm{div}}_\gamma\mathcal K)_i-\partial_iH.
 \label{ads:quart:gaussian-ricci}
\end{aligned}$$ Consequently $E:=\overline\mathop{\mathrm{Ric}}+3\overline g$ has $E_{ij}=0$. The initial Hamiltonian and momentum constraints give $E_{tt}=E_{ti}=0$ at $t=0$. For completeness, the Hamiltonian constraint is $\mathop{\mathrm{Scal}}_\gamma+H^2-|\mathcal K|_\gamma^2=-6$; tracing <a href="#ads:quart:gaussian-evolution" data-reference-type="eqref" data-reference="ads:quart:gaussian-evolution">[ads:quart:gaussian-evolution]</a> at $t=0$ therefore gives $\mathop{\mathrm{tr}}_\gamma\partial_t\mathcal K=-3+|\mathcal K|_\gamma^2$, which proves the asserted $tt$ equation with the required sign.

<a id="ads:quart:bianchi-system"></a>
<a id="ads:quart:formal-einstein"></a>
The contracted Bianchi identity propagates these remaining equations formally. Indeed, if $e=E_{tt}$ and $j_i=E_{ti}$, the trace reversal of $E$ has components $$\widehat E_{tt}=e/2,\qquad
 \widehat E_{ti}=j_i,\qquad
 \widehat E_{ij}=e\gamma_{ij}/2.$$ Its vanishing divergence, evaluated with the displayed Christoffel symbols, is $$\partial_t e=2\mathop{\mathrm{div}}_\gamma j-2He,
 \qquad
 \partial_tj_i=\tfrac12\partial_i e-Hj_i.
 \label{ads:quart:bianchi-system}$$ This homogeneous system determines each next time coefficient of $(e,j)$ from the preceding ones. All coefficients vanish by induction. Thus $$\overline\mathop{\mathrm{Ric}}=-3\overline g
 \label{ads:quart:formal-einstein}$$ as a formal time series modulo $\epsilon^5$.

There is no extension hypothesis hidden in this construction. The original coefficient fields are smooth up to $S$, and their constraint residuals and all one-sided spatial derivatives vanish there. The recursion and <a href="#ads:quart:bianchi-system" data-reference-type="eqref" data-reference="ads:quart:bianchi-system">[ads:quart:bianchi-system]</a> therefore also hold in their spatial Taylor jets at $S$. Each finite calculation below involves only finitely many such derivatives. They may, if desired, be realized in a collar across $S$ by their Taylor polynomials in $s$, to an order larger than the differential order of that calculation. Curvature and its residual are formed before substituting a displacement of order $\epsilon$. Their retained boundary jets vanish, so the substitution is valid even when the leading displacement is negative. This neither constructs nor uses an actual Einstein extension on the other side of $S$.

<a id="ads:quart:slice-constraints"></a>
Gauss–Codazzi applied as a differential identity to any spacelike graph now gives $$\mathop{\mathrm{Scal}}_{\rm slice}+6
   =|K_{\rm slice}|^2-(\mathop{\mathrm{tr}}K_{\rm slice})^2,
 \qquad
 \mathop{\mathrm{div}}\bigl(K_{\rm slice}-(\mathop{\mathrm{tr}}K_{\rm slice})g_{\rm slice}\bigr)=0.
 \label{ads:quart:slice-constraints}$$ Equivalently one can form Gaussian coordinates about that graph by the Taylor recursion for its normal geodesics and use <a href="#ads:quart:gaussian-ricci" data-reference-type="eqref" data-reference="ads:quart:gaussian-ricci">[ads:quart:gaussian-ricci]</a>. Either interpretation needs only differential identities of finite jets.

<a id="ads:quart:graph-k"></a>
We next compute the graph second form explicitly. With $T_i=\partial_iT$, its tangent fields are $X_i=\partial_i+T_i\partial_t$, and its future unit normal is $$n_T=\frac{\partial_t+\mathop{\mathrm{grad}}_{\gamma(t)}T}
             {\sqrt{1-|\,\mathrm dT|_{\gamma(t)}^2}}\bigg|_{t=T}.$$ Using $-\overline g(n_T,\overline\nabla_{X_i}X_j)$ gives $$\widetilde K_{ij}
  =\left.
    \frac{\mathcal K_{ij}(t)+(\mathop{\mathrm{Hess}}_{\gamma(t)}T)_{ij}
       -T_k\bigl(T_i\mathcal K^k{}_j(t)
                 +T_j\mathcal K^k{}_i(t)\bigr)}
     {\sqrt{1-|\,\mathrm dT|_{\gamma(t)}^2}}
   \right|_{t=T}.
 \label{ads:quart:graph-k}$$ The Hessian connection in this formula is taken at fixed time before evaluation at $t=T$. The induced metric is $\widetilde g=\gamma(T)-\,\mathrm dT\otimes\,\mathrm dT$.

<a id="ads:quart:k-explicit"></a>
At the background initial slice, $\mathcal K=0$ and $\partial_t\mathcal K=-B$. A first-order time displacement $b$ therefore changes the second form by $\mathop{\mathrm{Hess}}b-Bb=Q(b)$. Equation <a href="#ads:quart:time-graph" data-reference-type="eqref" data-reference="ads:quart:time-graph">[ads:quart:time-graph]</a> gives $$[\widetilde K]_1=q-Q(v)=0.$$ We choose $w$ to remove the trace at the next degree. This can be done with an explicit scalar source. Since $[\gamma(0)]_1=4ug_0$, the conformal Ricci variation and $Lu=0$ give $$[\partial_t\mathcal K(0)]_1
   =2\mathop{\mathrm{Hess}}u-6ug_0,
 \qquad [\mathcal K(0)]_2=-2uq.$$ At the background $\partial_t^2\mathcal K(0)=0$: differentiating <a href="#ads:quart:gaussian-evolution" data-reference-type="eqref" data-reference="ads:quart:gaussian-evolution">[ads:quart:gaussian-evolution]</a> there uses $\partial_t\gamma(0)=0$ and $\mathcal K(0)=0$. Expanding <a href="#ads:quart:graph-k" data-reference-type="eqref" data-reference="ads:quart:graph-k">[ads:quart:graph-k]</a> to degree two thus gives $$\begin{aligned}
 k={}&Q(w)-2uq-2v\mathop{\mathrm{Hess}}u+6uvg_0\nonumber\\
     &\quad+2\,\mathrm du\otimes\,\mathrm dv+2\,\mathrm dv\otimes\,\mathrm du
          -2\langle\,\mathrm du,\,\mathrm dv\rangle_{g_0}g_0.
 \label{ads:quart:k-explicit}
\end{aligned}$$ In particular, $$\mathop{\mathrm{tr}}_{g_0}k=Lw+12uv-2\langle\,\mathrm du,\,\mathrm dv\rangle_{g_0}.$$ Choose the unique decaying solution of <a id="ads:quart:w-equation"></a>$$Lw=2\langle\,\mathrm du,\,\mathrm dv\rangle_{g_0}-12uv,
 \qquad w|_S=0.
 \label{ads:quart:w-equation}$$ Its right side is $O(r^{-6})$, with differentiated bounds, so Lemma <a href="#ads:lem:inverse" data-reference-type="ref" data-reference="ads:lem:inverse">179</a> applies and gives $w=O(r^{-3})$ with the corresponding derivatives. Formula <a href="#ads:quart:k-explicit" data-reference-type="eqref" data-reference="ads:quart:k-explicit">[ads:quart:k-explicit]</a> gives the asserted decay of $k$. The degree-two momentum equation in <a href="#ads:quart:slice-constraints" data-reference-type="eqref" data-reference="ads:quart:slice-constraints">[ads:quart:slice-constraints]</a>, together with $\mathop{\mathrm{tr}}_{g_0}k=0$, gives $\mathop{\mathrm{div}}_{g_0}k=0$.

The full transformed trace is $O(\epsilon^3)$. Its square consequently begins in degree six, whereas $$|\widetilde K|_{\widetilde g}^2
    =\epsilon^4|k|_{g_0}^2+O(\epsilon^5).$$ This proves <a href="#ads:quart:scalar-four" data-reference-type="eqref" data-reference="ads:quart:scalar-four">[ads:quart:scalar-four]</a>; maximality at higher orders on the changed slice is not needed.

Finally, $$\gamma(T)-\gamma(0)
  =2\mathcal K(0)T+\tfrac12\partial_t^2\gamma(0)T^2+\cdots.$$ In every retained coefficient the first term is $O(r^{-6})$, and every subsequent term has at least two decaying time-displacement factors multiplying bounded background time coefficients. The recursion preserves these bounded differentiated estimates: in the scaled coframe $\,\mathrm ds,r\,\,\mathrm dx$, the background connection and curvature, with their required derivatives, are bounded; each coefficient is obtained by finitely many covariant differentiations, contractions, and inverse-metric Taylor operations from the smooth initial coefficients. The same bounds hold for $\,\mathrm dT\otimes\,\mathrm dT$, proving <a href="#ads:quart:metric-decay" data-reference-type="eqref" data-reference="ads:quart:metric-decay">[ads:quart:metric-decay]</a>. An $O(r^{-6})$ metric coefficient with its first covariant derivative contributes $O(r^{-3})$ to the integrated mass flux, since the test potentials and their gradients are $O(r)$ and the sphere area is $O(r^2)$. Thus the leading asymptotic data, every mass component, and the mass norm are unchanged through degree four.

Since $\partial_t^2\gamma(0)=-2B$ at the background, the degree-two difference is $-2vq-Bv^2-\,\mathrm dv\otimes\,\mathrm dv$. Substituting $q=\mathop{\mathrm{Hess}}v-Bv$ and using $\mathop{\mathrm{Hess}}(v^2)=2v\mathop{\mathrm{Hess}}v+2\,\mathrm dv\otimes\,\mathrm dv$ proves <a href="#ads:quart:metric-two" data-reference-type="eqref" data-reference="ads:quart:metric-two">[ads:quart:metric-two]</a>. ◻

</details>

<a id="pm-h-227"></a>
###### Transport of the boundary and its area

<a id="stmt-ads-lem-null-cut"></a>
<div id="ads:lem:null-cut" class="lemma">

<a id="ads:quart:null-area"></a>
<a id="ads:quart:null-h"></a>
<a id="ads:quart:z"></a>
<a id="ads:quart:area-hessian"></a>
**Lemma 195** (The null cut). *For the changed slice of Lemma <a href="#ads:lem:slice" data-reference-type="ref" data-reference="ads:lem:slice">194</a> there is a sphere jet $S^\sharp$, based at $S$, such that $$\begin{aligned}
 |S^\sharp|_{\widetilde g}&=|S|_{g_\epsilon}+O(\epsilon^5),
 \label{ads:quart:null-area}\\
 H_{\widetilde g}(S^\sharp)
      &=\epsilon^2k_{ss}|_S+O(\epsilon^3).
 \label{ads:quart:null-h}
\end{aligned}$$ Let $S_{\min}$ be the minimal Taylor leaf of the CMC construction for $\widetilde g$. Their height jets agree through degree one. If $$z=D^{-1}(k_{ss}|_S),
 \label{ads:quart:z}$$ then the height of $S^\sharp$ minus that of $S_{\min}$ is $\epsilon^2z+O(\epsilon^3)$, and $$|S^\sharp|_{\widetilde g}-|S_{\min}|_{\widetilde g}
     =\tfrac12\epsilon^4\int_S zDz\,\,\mathrm dA_{g_0}+O(\epsilon^5).
 \label{ads:quart:area-hessian}$$ These statements remain valid when some leading boundary displacements are negative.*

</div>

<details id="proof-stmt-ads-lem-null-cut"><summary>Proof of stmt-ads-lem-null-cut</summary>

*Proof.* On the original initial slice take the future outward null normal $\ell=n_{\rm future}+\nu$ to $S$. Its affinely parametrized null geodesics determine a null hypersurface jet, with parameter $\lambda$ zero at $S$. These are Taylor solutions of the geodesic and Jacobi equations for the formal metric $\overline g$ constructed above. At the initial sphere the expansion is identically zero by the original boundary equation.

<a id="ads:quart:initial-chi"></a>
Write $\chi$ for the null second form and $\theta=\mathop{\mathrm{tr}}\chi$ for its expansion. The initial sphere is umbilic in $\phi_\epsilon^4g_0$. Moreover the coefficient of $\epsilon$ in the tracefree tangential part of $K_\epsilon$ equals the tracefree tangential part of $Q(v)$. Since $S$ is totally geodesic in $g_0$, that part is $(\mathop{\mathrm{Hess}}_{a^2\sigma}(v|_S))^{\circ}$. It vanishes for the constant and degree-one modes of $v|_S$. The vanishing initial expansion and this shear calculation together give $$\chi(0,\epsilon)=O(\epsilon^2).
 \label{ads:quart:initial-chi}$$

The screen space is the positive-definite quotient $\ell^\perp/\operatorname{span}\{\ell\}$. In a parallel orthonormal frame of this space the null shape operator obeys the optical Riccati equation $$\partial_\lambda\chi=-\chi^2-\mathcal R_\ell,
 \qquad
 \partial_\lambda\theta
       =-|\chi|^2-\overline\mathop{\mathrm{Ric}}(\ell,\ell).$$ These equations follow directly from the Jacobi equation: angular Jacobi fields remain orthogonal to $\ell$, and their derivative matrix times their inverse is the shape operator. At $(\lambda,\epsilon)=(0,0)$, spherical symmetry makes $\mathcal R_\ell$ a scalar multiple of the screen identity. Its trace is $\overline\mathop{\mathrm{Ric}}(\ell,\ell)=0$ by <a href="#ads:quart:formal-einstein" data-reference-type="eqref" data-reference="ads:quart:formal-einstein">[ads:quart:formal-einstein]</a> and nullness, so this curvature endomorphism is zero. Thus $\partial_\lambda\chi(0,0)=0$.

It follows from <a href="#ads:quart:initial-chi" data-reference-type="eqref" data-reference="ads:quart:initial-chi">[ads:quart:initial-chi]</a> that every retained monomial of $\chi$ has total degree at least two in $(\lambda,\epsilon)$. Raychaudhuri and the identically zero initial expansion then imply <a id="ads:quart:optical-orders"></a>$$\chi=O_{\rm tot}(2),\qquad
 \theta=O_{\rm tot}(5).
 \label{ads:quart:optical-orders}$$ Here $O_{\rm tot}(j)$ means that each monomial $\lambda^a\epsilon^b$ has $a+b\geq j$. The order statements are made in the formal series modulo $\epsilon^5$. Equivalently one can choose any sufficiently high finite Taylor lift: an Einstein residual of order $\epsilon^5$ integrated along a segment $\lambda=O(\epsilon)$ contributes only beyond every degree used here. Since the logarithmic screen area density has derivative $\theta$, its change along such a segment vanishes through degree four.

Intersect this null hypersurface jet with $t=T$. At the background initial point, the derivative of $t-T$ along its generator is one. Successive Taylor substitution therefore solves for the intersection parameter, which is $O(\epsilon)$. The angular projection has identity background differential and likewise has a formal inverse. The resulting cut $S^\sharp$ is a graph over $S$ in the changed slice.

The area conclusion also holds for this variable-parameter cut. If $J_A$ are the transported angular Jacobi fields, its tangent fields are $J_A+(\partial_A\lambda)\ell$. Nullness and $\overline g(J_A,\ell)=0$ show that the additional terms do not change the induced metric. Its area density is just the transported screen density evaluated at the variable parameter. This proves <a href="#ads:quart:null-area" data-reference-type="eqref" data-reference="ads:quart:null-area">[ads:quart:null-area]</a>.

The outward future null normal obtained from the new slice differs from $\ell$ by a scalar with positive, nonzero background value. Expansion is multiplied by that scalar, so it still vanishes through the needed orders. At leading order $$\mathop{\mathrm{tr}}_{S^\sharp,\widetilde g}\widetilde K
       =-\epsilon^2k_{ss}|_S+O(\epsilon^3),$$ because $\mathop{\mathrm{tr}}_{g_0}k=0$. Its zero null expansion gives <a href="#ads:quart:null-h" data-reference-type="eqref" data-reference="ads:quart:null-h">[ads:quart:null-h]</a>.

Both $S^\sharp$ and the minimal Taylor leaf have zero mean-curvature coefficients through degree one. The difference of their first height coefficients is therefore annihilated by the background operator $D$, which is invertible. At degree two, their already equal first coefficients make all common nonlinear terms cancel, leaving $D(h_2^\sharp-h_2^{\min})=k_{ss}|_S$. This proves <a href="#ads:quart:z" data-reference-type="eqref" data-reference="ads:quart:z">[ads:quart:z]</a>. The first variation of area at the minimal Taylor leaf vanishes to the retained order. A height difference beginning with $\epsilon^2z$ consequently has, at degree four, only the base second-variation contribution $\frac12\int_S zDz\,\,\mathrm dA_{g_0}$. This is <a href="#ads:quart:area-hessian" data-reference-type="eqref" data-reference="ads:quart:area-hessian">[ads:quart:area-hessian]</a>.

All of these assertions are identities in the joint spatial, $\lambda$, and $\epsilon$ Taylor jets at the original boundary. The boundary-jet justification in Lemma <a href="#ads:lem:slice" data-reference-type="ref" data-reference="ads:lem:slice">194</a> permits their evaluation at negative leading displacements. Neither the sign of an affine segment nor that of a height coefficient changes the order calculation or the area Hessian. No area inequality for an actually extended manifold is being applied. ◻

</details>

<a id="pm-h-228"></a>
###### The quartic square and its vanishing consequences

Null transport preserves the boundary area through degree four. The subsequent minimal-graph correction contributes the area Hessian in Lemma <a href="#ads:lem:null-cut" data-reference-type="ref" data-reference="ads:lem:null-cut">195</a>; the TT identity absorbs this boundary term.

<figure id="ads:fig:boundary-comparisons">
<p>$$S\text{ in }g_\epsilon
 \ \xrightarrow{\ \text{null transport}\ }\ 
 S^\sharp\text{ in }\widetilde g
 \ \xrightarrow{\ \text{minimal graph}\ }\ 
 S_{\min}\text{ in }\widetilde g .$$</p>
<figcaption>Finite Taylor boundary comparisons. The first arrow preserves area through degree four. The signed height difference for the second is $h^{♯} − h^{min} = ϵ^{2}z + O(ϵ^{3})$, producing the quartic area Hessian <a href="#ads:quart:area-hessian" data-reference-type="eqref" data-reference="ads:quart:area-hessian">[ads:quart:area-hessian]</a>. Negative leading displacements are included.</figcaption>
</figure>

<a id="pm-figsrc-ads-fig-boundary-comparisons"></a>
**Figure source and visual witness** (`ads:fig:boundary-comparisons`)

Visual witness description of PDF page 251 (generated from the PDF page, not source text):

```text
A sequence of three expressions connected horizontally by rightward arrows with labels:
"$S \text{ in } g_\epsilon$" $\xrightarrow{\text{null transport}}$ "$S^\sharp \text{ in } \tilde{g}$" $\xrightarrow{\text{minimal graph}}$ "$S_{\min} \text{ in } \tilde{g}$".
```


<a id="ads:quart:first-geometric-zero"></a>
Apply Proposition <a href="#ads:prop:cmc-jets" data-reference-type="ref" data-reference="ads:prop:cmc-jets">185</a> to $\widetilde g$ through degree four. Its hypotheses follow from Lemma <a href="#ads:lem:slice" data-reference-type="ref" data-reference="ads:lem:slice">194</a>, including the unchanged leading asymptotic data. Denote by $f$ the lapse, by $\bar f$ its area average on each leaf, and set $$\delta f=f-\bar f,\qquad
 U_j=[\mathrm{II}^{\circ}]_j,\qquad \mathcal F_j=[\delta f]_j.$$ At degree two, the scalar contribution is zero by <a href="#ads:quart:scalar-four" data-reference-type="eqref" data-reference="ads:quart:scalar-four">[ads:quart:scalar-four]</a>. Equations <a href="#ads:quart:null-area" data-reference-type="eqref" data-reference="ads:quart:null-area">[ads:quart:null-area]</a> and <a href="#ads:quart:area-hessian" data-reference-type="eqref" data-reference="ads:quart:area-hessian">[ads:quart:area-hessian]</a>, and the preserved mass, identify the quadratic coefficient of mass minus $b_*$ of the minimal-leaf area with the original zero coefficient $c_2[q]$. The leading-energy identity, Proposition <a href="#ads:prop:leading-energy" data-reference-type="ref" data-reference="ads:prop:leading-energy">188</a>, with its scalar tensor equal to zero, gives $$0=\frac1{16\pi}\int_M N
       \bigl(|U_1|^2+2\mathcal F_1J_s^0\mathcal F_1\bigr)\,\,\mathrm dV_{g_0}.$$ The lapse coefficient is mean free on each background sphere, and $J_s^0$ is strictly positive on that space. Since $N>0$ for $s>0$, sphere integration and smoothness imply $$U_1=0,\qquad \mathcal F_1=0.
 \label{ads:quart:first-geometric-zero}$$

We can now use Proposition <a href="#ads:prop:leading-energy" data-reference-type="ref" data-reference="ads:prop:leading-energy">188</a> at order four: the scalar-curvature defect starts with $\epsilon^4|k|^2$, and both geometric square terms start in degree four. It follows first that mass minus $b_*$ of the minimal-leaf area has no coefficients below degree four. The area correction <a href="#ads:quart:area-hessian" data-reference-type="eqref" data-reference="ads:quart:area-hessian">[ads:quart:area-hessian]</a> also starts in that degree. Thus $c_3[q]=0$, as well as the previously known lower vanishings.

<a id="ads:quart:square"></a>
<a id="ads:quart:second-geometric-zero"></a>
Let $v_k$ be the decaying solution <a id="ads:quart:vk"></a>$$Lv_k=0,\qquad v_k|_S=z=D^{-1}(k_{ss}|_S).
 \label{ads:quart:vk}$$ It is supplied by Lemma <a href="#ads:lem:inverse" data-reference-type="ref" data-reference="ads:lem:inverse">179</a>. The TT tensor $k$ has the decay and finite angular type required in Lemma <a href="#ads:lem:tt-square" data-reference-type="ref" data-reference="ads:lem:tt-square">189</a>. Since $b_*'(4\pi a^2)=\kappa/(8\pi)$, subtracting the area correction from the leading-energy identity and applying that lemma gives $$c_4[q]=\frac1{16\pi}\int_M N
   \left(
      |k-Q(v_k)|_{g_0}^2+|U_2|^2+2\mathcal F_2J_s^0\mathcal F_2
   \right)\,\,\mathrm dV_{g_0}.
 \label{ads:quart:square}$$ Indeed the subtracted boundary term is exactly $\kappa(16\pi)^{-1}\int_S zDz\,\,\mathrm dA_{g_0}$. The integrals are understood with sphere integration first, as in Proposition <a href="#ads:prop:leading-energy" data-reference-type="ref" data-reference="ads:prop:leading-energy">188</a>; no pointwise sign is asserted for $\mathcal F_2J_s^0\mathcal F_2$. Its sphere integral is nonnegative. This proves $c_4[q]\geq0$, and equality implies $$\delta f=O(\epsilon^3),\qquad
 \mathrm{II}^{\circ}=O(\epsilon^3)
 \label{ads:quart:second-geometric-zero}$$ on every leaf. Boundary values follow by smoothness. We show next that <a href="#ads:quart:second-geometric-zero" data-reference-type="eqref" data-reference="ads:quart:second-geometric-zero">[ads:quart:second-geometric-zero]</a> excludes a nonzero degree-one part of $v$.

<a id="ads:quart:round-section"></a>
###### Round angular jets and conformal coordinates

We now assume equality in the quartic square. The vanishing in <a href="#ads:quart:second-geometric-zero" data-reference-type="eqref" data-reference="ads:quart:second-geometric-zero">[ads:quart:second-geometric-zero]</a> makes the changed metric a warped product through degree two. The following lemma will round its angular metric before we compare it with the conformal class of $g_0$.

<a id="stmt-ads-lem-round-jet"></a>
<div id="ads:lem:round-jet" class="lemma">

**Lemma 196** (Rounding a two-jet on the sphere). *Let $\gamma_\epsilon=\sigma+\epsilon P_1+\epsilon^2P_2$ be a smooth metric two-jet on $S^2$ of finite angular type. Suppose its scalar curvature is angularly constant through degree two. Then there are a positive scalar two-jet $a_\epsilon$, with $a_0=1$, and a diffeomorphism two-jet $\Phi_\epsilon$, based at the identity, such that $$\gamma_\epsilon=a_\epsilon\Phi_\epsilon^*\sigma+O(\epsilon^3).$$ All coefficients can be chosen of finite angular type.*

</div>

<details id="proof-stmt-ads-lem-round-jet"><summary>Proof of stmt-ads-lem-round-jet</summary>

<a id="ads:quart:sphere-splitting"></a>
*Proof.* We first prove the infinitesimal decomposition used twice below. For a symmetric tensor $P$ on the round sphere, there are a vector field $Y$ and a function $h$ such that $$P=\mathcal L_Y\sigma+h\sigma.
 \label{ads:quart:sphere-splitting}$$ For finite-angular-type $P$, the choices may retain that property.

<a id="ads:quart:conformal-divergence"></a>
Let $P^{\circ}=P-\frac12(\mathop{\mathrm{tr}}_\sigma P)\sigma$, and identify vector fields and one-forms using $\sigma$. Define $$\mathcal C(Y)_{ij}
   =\nabla_iY_j+\nabla_jY_i-(\mathop{\mathrm{div}}Y)\sigma_{ij}.$$ On the curvature-one sphere, commuting covariant derivatives gives $$\mathop{\mathrm{div}}\mathcal C(Y)=(\Delta_\sigma+1)Y,
 \qquad
 (\Delta_\sigma+1)\,\mathrm df=\,\mathrm d(\Delta_\sigma+2)f.
 \label{ads:quart:conformal-divergence}$$ Here the Laplacian on one-forms is the rough Laplacian $\nabla^i\nabla_i$. The second identity also holds after applying the parallel Hodge star $*$ to one-forms.

Put $\alpha=\mathop{\mathrm{div}}P^{\circ}$. To decompose it, solve the scalar equations $$\Delta_\sigma\varphi=\mathop{\mathrm{div}}\alpha,\qquad
 \Delta_\sigma\psi=-\mathop{\mathrm{div}}(*\alpha)$$ with zero means. Both right sides have zero integral. In finite angular spaces these equations are solved by inversion on the nonconstant spherical modes. The residual $\omega=\alpha-\,\mathrm d\varphi-*\,\mathrm d\psi$ is closed and co-closed. Commuting derivatives of a closed one-form of zero divergence gives $\nabla^i\nabla_i\omega=\omega$; integration against $\omega$ forces $\omega=0$. We have therefore obtained $$\alpha=\,\mathrm d\varphi+*\,\mathrm d\psi.$$

The one-forms $\,\mathrm dx_i$ and $*\,\mathrm dx_i$ correspond to conformal Killing vector fields. Integration by parts against the tracefree tensor $P^{\circ}$ consequently shows that $\alpha$ is orthogonal to all of them. It follows that both $\varphi$ and $\psi$ have zero degree-one components. Thus we may solve $$(\Delta_\sigma+2)A=\varphi,\qquad
 (\Delta_\sigma+2)C=\psi$$ on their angular modes, and set $Y^\flat=\,\mathrm dA+*\,\mathrm dC$. Equation <a href="#ads:quart:conformal-divergence" data-reference-type="eqref" data-reference="ads:quart:conformal-divergence">[ads:quart:conformal-divergence]</a> gives $\mathop{\mathrm{div}}\mathcal C(Y)=\mathop{\mathrm{div}}P^{\circ}$.

The tracefree tensor $P_*=P^{\circ}-\mathcal C(Y)$ is consequently divergence free. Such a tensor vanishes on the round sphere; here is a direct verification. In an orthonormal frame write its components as $\left(\begin{smallmatrix}a&b\\b&-a\end{smallmatrix}\right)$. Its two divergence equations are precisely the two independent Codazzi equations $\nabla_i(P_*)_{jk}=\nabla_j(P_*)_{ik}$. Contracting and commuting these equations on the curvature-one sphere gives $$\nabla^i\nabla_i(P_*)_{jk}
      =2(P_*)_{jk}-\sigma_{jk}\mathop{\mathrm{tr}}_\sigma P_*
      =2(P_*)_{jk}.$$ Integration yields $-\int|\nabla P_*|^2=2\int|P_*|^2$, hence $P_*=0$. Taking $h=\frac12\mathop{\mathrm{tr}}_\sigma P-\mathop{\mathrm{div}}Y$ proves <a href="#ads:quart:sphere-splitting" data-reference-type="eqref" data-reference="ads:quart:sphere-splitting">[ads:quart:sphere-splitting]</a>. Every operation used above commutes with rotations or inverts a scalar operator within finitely many spherical eigenspaces, so it preserves finite angular type.

The scalar-curvature derivative in the direction $h\sigma$ is $$(D\mathop{\mathrm{Scal}})_\sigma(h\sigma)=-\Delta_\sigma h-2h.$$ The derivative in a Lie direction is zero because the background scalar curvature is constant. If the scalar-curvature variation of $P$ is constant, <a href="#ads:quart:sphere-splitting" data-reference-type="eqref" data-reference="ads:quart:sphere-splitting">[ads:quart:sphere-splitting]</a> therefore implies that $h$ consists only of a constant and degree-one modes. A degree-one function $h_1$ satisfies $\mathop{\mathrm{Hess}}_\sigma h_1=-h_1\sigma$, so $$h_1\sigma
   =\mathcal L_{-\frac12\mathop{\mathrm{grad}}_\sigma h_1}\sigma.$$ Thus $P$ is a Lie derivative plus a constant multiple of $\sigma$.

Apply this conclusion to $P_1$. A formal inverse flow and a scalar scaling remove its first coefficient. Both operations preserve the property that curvature is angularly constant. The resulting metric two-jet has the form $\sigma+\epsilon^2\widehat P_2$, so its degree-two curvature equation is the same linearized equation, with no quadratic contribution from a first coefficient. The argument just given removes $\widehat P_2$ by a degree-two flow and scaling. Undoing the two operations proves the stated rounding. This proves only an identity of two-jets, which is exactly what is required. ◻

</details>

<a id="pm-h-230"></a>
###### Local conformal tangency forced by equality.

Suppose now that $c_4[q]=0$. Fix a compact interval $I\Subset(0,\infty)$. In coordinates of the CMC sphere jets we can remove tangential shift through degree two by integrating its tangential reparametrization equation on $I$. Its background value is zero, so the coordinate change is based at the identity. In these coordinates <a href="#ads:quart:second-geometric-zero" data-reference-type="eqref" data-reference="ads:quart:second-geometric-zero">[ads:quart:second-geometric-zero]</a> says that the lapse is a function of the leaf parameter only and that $\mathrm{II}=(H/2)g_{\rm leaf}$ through degree two. Since $H$ is constant on each leaf, the normal metric variation is $$\partial_s g_{\rm leaf}=2f\mathrm{II}=fH g_{\rm leaf}.$$ Consequently on $I\times S^2$ the metric has the form <a id="ads:quart:warped-two"></a>$$f_*(s)^2\,\mathrm ds^2+b(s)^2\gamma_\epsilon(x)+O(\epsilon^3),
 \label{ads:quart:warped-two}$$ where all quantities are two-jets, with backgrounds $f_*=1$, $b=r$, and $\gamma_0=\sigma$. Angular finiteness is preserved by these Taylor coordinate changes and integrations.

<a id="ads:quart:warped-scalar"></a>
For this warped metric the scalar curvature through degree two is $$b^{-2}\mathop{\mathrm{Scal}}_{\gamma_\epsilon}
   -\frac4{f_*b}\frac{\,\mathrm d}{\,\mathrm ds}
                      \left(\frac{b'}{f_*}\right)
   -2\left(\frac{b'}{f_*b}\right)^2.
 \label{ads:quart:warped-scalar}$$ Equation <a href="#ads:quart:scalar-four" data-reference-type="eqref" data-reference="ads:quart:scalar-four">[ads:quart:scalar-four]</a> makes it the constant $-6$ through degree two. The last two terms in <a href="#ads:quart:warped-scalar" data-reference-type="eqref" data-reference="ads:quart:warped-scalar">[ads:quart:warped-scalar]</a> are radial, so $\mathop{\mathrm{Scal}}_{\gamma_\epsilon}$ is angularly constant to that order. Lemma <a href="#ads:lem:round-jet" data-reference-type="ref" data-reference="ads:lem:round-jet">196</a> makes $\gamma_\epsilon$ round up to diffeomorphism and scaling. Absorbing the scaling into $b$, we obtain $f_*^2\,\mathrm ds^2+b^2\sigma$.

<a id="ads:quart:conformal-pullback"></a>
This last two-jet is locally conformal to a pullback of $g_0$. Indeed solve, coefficientwise on $I$, <a id="ads:quart:radial-coordinate"></a>$$\frac{y'}{r(y)}=\frac{f_*}{b},
 \label{ads:quart:radial-coordinate}$$ with background $y=s$ and a fixed identity background initial value at an interior point of $I$. This is a nonsingular scalar ODE, and it gives $$f_*^2\,\mathrm ds^2+b^2\sigma
   =\frac{b^2}{r(y)^2}
       \bigl(\,\mathrm dy^2+r(y)^2\sigma\bigr)
       \quad\bmod\epsilon^3.$$ Composing the coordinate changes already made shows, in the original coordinates on the interval, that $$\widetilde g=\omega_\epsilon\Psi_\epsilon^*g_0+O(\epsilon^3),
 \qquad \omega_0=1,\quad\Psi_0=\mathrm{id}.
 \label{ads:quart:conformal-pullback}$$ Only this local statement is used.

<a id="ads:quart:necessary-tangent"></a>
There is a useful consequence of the known first coefficient in <a href="#ads:quart:conformal-pullback" data-reference-type="eqref" data-reference="ads:quart:conformal-pullback">[ads:quart:conformal-pullback]</a>. Write $\omega_\epsilon=1+\epsilon a_1+\epsilon^2a_2$ and express the diffeomorphism two-jet as $$\Psi_\epsilon^*g_0
  =g_0+\epsilon\mathcal L_Xg_0
      +\epsilon^2\bigl(\mathcal L_Zg_0
                      +\tfrac12\mathcal L_X^2g_0\bigr).$$ The graph calculation shows that $\widetilde g-g_\epsilon$ starts in degree two, so $[\widetilde g]_1=4ug_0$. Hence $\mathcal L_Xg_0=\lambda g_0$ for some function $\lambda$. It follows that $$\mathcal L_X^2g_0=(X\lambda+\lambda^2)g_0,$$ and the mixed scalar term $a_1\mathcal L_Xg_0$ is pure trace as well. Therefore <a id="ads:quart:second-tangent"></a>$$_2=\mathcal L_Zg_0+c g_0
 \label{ads:quart:second-tangent}$$ for a function $c$ on $I\times S^2$. The original metric coefficient $[g_\epsilon]_2$ is itself pure trace. Thus the same Lie-derivative-plus-trace conclusion holds for their difference. Since $\mathop{\mathrm{Hess}}(v^2)=\frac12\mathcal L_{\mathop{\mathrm{grad}}(v^2)}g_0$, <a href="#ads:quart:metric-two" data-reference-type="eqref" data-reference="ads:quart:metric-two">[ads:quart:metric-two]</a> gives the necessary condition $$\,\mathrm dv\otimes\,\mathrm dv+Bv^2=\mathcal L_Yg_0+c g_0
 \quad\hbox{on }I\times S^2
 \label{ads:quart:necessary-tangent}$$ for some local $Y,c$. Their choices may depend on $I$.

<a id="ads:quart:obstruction-section"></a>
###### The degree-one obstruction

<a id="stmt-ads-lem-dipole-obstruction"></a>
<div id="ads:lem:dipole-obstruction" class="lemma">

**Lemma 197** (A nonzero degree-one mode is obstructed). *Let $v=v_0(s)+V(s)x$ solve $Lv=0$, where $x$ is one fixed unit-axis linear coordinate on $S^2$ and $V=O(r^{-3})$. If <a href="#ads:quart:necessary-tangent" data-reference-type="eqref" data-reference="ads:quart:necessary-tangent">[ads:quart:necessary-tangent]</a> holds on every compact radial interval in the interior, with possibly different local vector fields and functions, then $V\equiv0$.*

</div>

<details id="proof-stmt-ads-lem-dipole-obstruction"><summary>Proof of stmt-ads-lem-dipole-obstruction</summary>

*Proof.* Set $Y_2=x^2-1/3$, a degree-two spherical eigenfunction. Project <a href="#ads:quart:necessary-tangent" data-reference-type="eqref" data-reference="ads:quart:necessary-tangent">[ads:quart:necessary-tangent]</a> onto its scalar, gradient, and tangential Hessian modes. Write the contributing radial vector-field coefficient as $p(s)Y_2\partial_s$, its tangential coefficient as $d(s)\mathop{\mathrm{grad}}_\sigma Y_2$, and the scalar-multiple coefficient as $c(s)Y_2$. These are the only generator components contributing to the tested modes. This follows either from the one-form decomposition in Lemma <a href="#ads:lem:round-jet" data-reference-type="ref" data-reference="ads:lem:round-jet">196</a> or by integration by parts, using $\Delta_\sigma Y_2=-6Y_2$. In particular, the coexact component is orthogonal to both the gradient test and the electric Hessian test, and the other spherical eigenspaces are orthogonal as well.

<a id="ads:quart:dipole-identity"></a>
For clarity, the angular identity $$\,\mathrm dx\otimes\,\mathrm dx
       =\tfrac12\mathop{\mathrm{Hess}}_\sigma Y_2+x^2\sigma$$ shows all terms of the left side in these modes. With $B=B_s\,\mathrm ds^2+B_t r^2\sigma$, equality of the radial, mixed, Hessian, and tangential scalar coefficients respectively gives <a id="ads:quart:projection-system"></a>$$\begin{aligned}
 V'^2+B_sV^2&=2p'+c,
 &\frac{VV'}2&=p+r^2d',\nonumber\\
 \frac{V^2}2&=2r^2d,
 &V^2+r^2B_tV^2&=2rNp+r^2c.
 \label{ads:quart:projection-system}
\end{aligned}$$ Terms involving $v_0$ have only degrees zero or one and do not enter these equations. Solving the last three equations yields $$d=\frac{V^2}{4r^2},\qquad
 p=\frac{NV^2}{2r},\qquad
 c=\frac{3m_0V^2}{r^3}.$$ Substitute these expressions in the first equation and use $$B_s=1-\frac{2m_0}{r^3},\qquad
 B_t=1+\frac{m_0}{r^3},\qquad
 N'=r+\frac{m_0}{r^2},\qquad
 N^2=1+r^2-\frac{2m_0}{r}.$$ After cancellation one obtains $$\left(V'-\frac NrV\right)^2
       =\frac{6m_0}{r^3}V^2.
 \label{ads:quart:dipole-identity}$$ The local generators have disappeared from this relation. Because the radial interval was arbitrary, it holds throughout the end even though their choices need not agree on overlapping intervals.

For $z=V/r$, <a href="#ads:quart:dipole-identity" data-reference-type="eqref" data-reference="ads:quart:dipole-identity">[ads:quart:dipole-identity]</a> reads $$|z'|=\sqrt{6m_0}\,r^{-3/2}|z|.$$ The coefficient on the right is integrable toward infinity, and $z\to0$. The integral differential inequality, applied backwards between $s$ and $S>s$, gives $$|z(s)|\leq |z(S)|
       \exp\left(\int_s^S\sqrt{6m_0}\,r(t)^{-3/2}\,\,\mathrm dt\right).$$ Letting $S\to\infty$ proves $z=0$ on the end. The homogeneous degree-one ODE obtained from $Lv=0$ then gives $V\equiv0$ by uniqueness. ◻

</details>

<details id="proof-stmt-ads-lem-dipole-obstruction-2"><summary>Proof of stmt-ads-lem-dipole-obstruction</summary>

*Completion of the proof of Proposition <a href="#ads:prop:quartic" data-reference-type="ref" data-reference="ads:prop:quartic">193</a>.* The coefficient vanishings and nonnegativity were proved in <a href="#ads:quart:first-geometric-zero" data-reference-type="eqref" data-reference="ads:quart:first-geometric-zero">[ads:quart:first-geometric-zero]</a>–<a href="#ads:quart:square" data-reference-type="eqref" data-reference="ads:quart:square">[ads:quart:square]</a>. Suppose that the degree-one part of $v$ is nonzero and that $c_4[q]=0$. All three degree-one radial coefficients solve the same decaying homogeneous ODE. Decaying uniqueness makes them proportional, so after a fixed rotation their sum is $V(s)x$ for one axis and a nonzero radial function $V$. The vanishing consequences of <a href="#ads:quart:square" data-reference-type="eqref" data-reference="ads:quart:square">[ads:quart:square]</a> give <a href="#ads:quart:necessary-tangent" data-reference-type="eqref" data-reference="ads:quart:necessary-tangent">[ads:quart:necessary-tangent]</a> on each interior radial interval. Lemma <a href="#ads:lem:dipole-obstruction" data-reference-type="ref" data-reference="ads:lem:dipole-obstruction">197</a> forces $V=0$, a contradiction. Thus $c_4[q]>0$.

Finally this is a statement about the actual deficit, not only a formal inequality. The kernel representation gives precisely the finite angular type and differentiated decay needed for the fourth-order expansion in Proposition <a href="#ads:prop:expansions" data-reference-type="ref" data-reference="ads:prop:expansions">183</a>. Lemma <a href="#ads:lem:green" data-reference-type="ref" data-reference="ads:lem:green">181</a> converts the weighted function and equation remainders to the mass remainder. Consequently $$\mathfrak D_q(\epsilon)=c_4[q]\epsilon^4+O(\epsilon^5)$$ in the case under consideration. Its positive coefficient gives strict positivity for all sufficiently small positive $\epsilon$, with the interval allowed to depend on the fixed data. The radial kernel, including the zero seed, is handled by the exact argument in the next section. ◻

</details>

<a id="ads:sec:conclusion"></a>
##### Radial equality and the nonlinear conclusion

<a id="stmt-ads-prop-radial"></a>
<div id="ads:prop:radial" class="proposition">

**Proposition 198** (Exact radial equality). *Suppose the fixed TT seed $q$ is invariant under rotations of $S^2$. Every branch in Theorem <a href="#ads:thm:main" data-reference-type="ref" data-reference="ads:thm:main">176</a> is radial for all sufficiently small $\epsilon$, and on that parameter interval $$m_{\mathrm{AH}}(\epsilon)=b_*(A_\epsilon).$$ This includes the zero seed, and requires no sign for $q_{ss}|_S$.*

</div>

<details id="proof-stmt-ads-prop-radial"><summary>Proof of stmt-ads-prop-radial</summary>

<a id="ads:eq:radial-uniqueness-equation"></a>
*Proof.* We first prove radiality of the actual solution, rather than merely of its Taylor coefficients. Fix a rotation $\mathcal R$, and set $\widehat\phi=\phi_\epsilon\circ\mathcal R$ and $w=\widehat\phi-\phi_\epsilon$. Because $q$ is radial, $\widehat\phi$ satisfies the same equation and boundary condition as $\phi_\epsilon$. Their difference satisfies $$(\Delta_{g_0}-c_\epsilon)w=0,
 \qquad w_s|_S=c_\epsilon^*w|_S,
 \label{ads:eq:radial-uniqueness-equation}$$ where divided differences of the nonlinearities give, uniformly on $M$ and uniformly in $\mathcal R$, $$c_\epsilon=3+o(1),\qquad c_\epsilon^*=O(\epsilon).$$ Indeed, the derivatives of the interior and boundary nonlinearities with respect to their positive scalar argument $z$ are respectively $$\frac34(5z^4-1)+\frac{7\epsilon^2}{8}|q|^2z^{-8},
 \qquad -\frac{3\epsilon}{4}q_{ss}z^{-4}.$$ The asserted bounds follow from boundedness of $q$ and the given uniform convergence $\phi_\epsilon\to1$.

Choose $3/2<\beta<\min(\tau,\sqrt3)$. Then $w=o(e^{-\beta s})$, and <a href="#ads:eq:radial-uniqueness-equation" data-reference-type="eqref" data-reference="ads:eq:radial-uniqueness-equation">[ads:eq:radial-uniqueness-equation]</a> has the form of Lemma <a href="#ads:lem:inverse" data-reference-type="ref" data-reference="ads:lem:inverse">179</a> with $V=c_\epsilon-3$, Robin coefficient $a_*=c_\epsilon^*$, and zero interior and boundary data. For sufficiently small $\epsilon$, uniformly in the rotation, $\|V\|_\infty\leq c_\beta$ and $\|a_*\|_\infty\leq\beta/2$. The comparison estimate gives $w=0$, so the actual $\phi_\epsilon$ is radial.

<a id="ads:eq:radial-tt-tensor"></a>
<a id="ads:eq:radial-constraints"></a>
Write the invariant seed as $q=A_q(s)\,\,\mathrm ds^2+B_q(s)r^2\sigma$. Its trace and divergence equations give $$B_q=-A_q/2,
 \qquad A_q'+3(N/r)A_q=0.$$ Consequently, for a constant $C_q\in\mathbb R$, $$q=C_qr^{-3}\left(\,\mathrm ds^2-\frac12r^2\sigma\right).
 \label{ads:eq:radial-tt-tensor}$$ Fix a sufficiently small parameter. Define proper radial distance $\ell$ and the actual area radius $R$ by $$\,\mathrm d\ell=\phi_\epsilon^2\,\,\mathrm ds,
 \qquad R=r\phi_\epsilon^2.$$ Then the actual metric and second-form data are $$g_\epsilon=\,\mathrm d\ell^2+R^2\sigma,
 \qquad K_\epsilon=-2k\,\,\mathrm d\ell^2+kR^2\sigma,
 \qquad k=-\frac{\epsilon C_q}{2R^3}.$$ A dot denotes an $\ell$-derivative. The momentum and scalar constraints are therefore $$\dot k=-3\frac{\dot R}{R}k,
 \qquad
 -\frac{4\ddot R}{R}
 +\frac{2(1-\dot R^2)}{R^2}+6=6k^2.
 \label{ads:eq:radial-constraints}$$ The scalar-curvature formula here follows from the sectional curvatures $-\ddot R/R$ and $(1-\dot R^2)/R^2$ of this warped product.

<a id="ads:eq:radial-conserved-mass"></a>
<a id="ads:eq:radial-mass-at-boundary"></a>
Define $$\mathcal M
 =\frac R2\left(1+R^2-\dot R^2+R^2k^2\right).
 \label{ads:eq:radial-conserved-mass}$$ Direct differentiation, using the momentum equation, gives $$\dot{\mathcal M}
 =\frac{\dot R}{2}
 \left(1+3R^2-\dot R^2-2R\ddot R-3R^2k^2\right)=0$$ by the scalar equation in <a href="#ads:eq:radial-constraints" data-reference-type="eqref" data-reference="ads:eq:radial-constraints">[ads:eq:radial-constraints]</a>. No division by $\dot R$ has been used, so conservation is valid at turning points of $R$ as well. At the boundary the MOTS equation reads $$\frac{2\dot R}{R}+2k=0.$$ Substitution in <a href="#ads:eq:radial-conserved-mass" data-reference-type="eqref" data-reference="ads:eq:radial-conserved-mass">[ads:eq:radial-conserved-mass]</a> yields $$\mathcal M|_S
 =\frac{R|_S}{2}\bigl(1+(R|_S)^2\bigr)
 =b_*\bigl(4\pi(R|_S)^2\bigr)=b_*(A_\epsilon).
 \label{ads:eq:radial-mass-at-boundary}$$

<a id="ads:eq:radial-actual-asymptotic"></a>
<a id="ads:eq:radial-mass-at-infinity"></a>
We identify the same constant with the specified mass flux at infinity. Put $\psi=\phi_\epsilon-1$. Its actual radial equation gives $$\psi''+2\frac Nr\psi'-3\psi
 =O(\psi^2)+O(r^{-6}),$$ where <a href="#ads:eq:radial-tt-tensor" data-reference-type="eqref" data-reference="ads:eq:radial-tt-tensor">[ads:eq:radial-tt-tensor]</a> was used in the source estimate. The assumed weighted decay gives $\psi,\psi'=O(e^{-\tau s})$, and $N/r=1+O(e^{-2s})$. It follows that $$\psi''+2\psi'-3\psi=O(e^{-\gamma s}),
 \qquad \gamma=\min(2\tau,\tau+2,6)>3.$$ Variation of constants for the roots $1,-3$ excludes the growing solution by the prescribed decay and yields, as in Lemma <a href="#ads:lem:inverse" data-reference-type="ref" data-reference="ads:lem:inverse">179</a>, a constant $c=c(\epsilon)$ with $$\phi_\epsilon=1+cr^{-3}+o(r^{-3}),
 \qquad
 \partial_s\phi_\epsilon=-3cNr^{-4}+o(r^{-3}).
 \label{ads:eq:radial-actual-asymptotic}$$ In particular, $$R=r+2cr^{-2}+o(r^{-2}),\qquad
 \dot R=N+2r\frac{\partial_s\phi_\epsilon}{\phi_\epsilon}
 =N-6cNr^{-3}+o(r^{-2}).$$ Using $N^2=1+r^2-2m_0/r$, we obtain $$1+R^2-\dot R^2
 =\frac{2m_0+16c}{r}+o(r^{-1}).$$ Also $R^3k^2=O(R^{-3})$, so $$\lim_{\ell\to\infty}\mathcal M=m_0+8c.
 \label{ads:eq:radial-mass-at-infinity}$$

For a direct flux normalization check, rotational invariance implies $p_i=0$ for $i=1,2,3$. Equation <a href="#ads:eq:radial-actual-asymptotic" data-reference-type="eqref" data-reference="ads:eq:radial-actual-asymptotic">[ads:eq:radial-actual-asymptotic]</a> implies $$g_\epsilon-g_0=4cr^{-3}b+o(r^{-3})$$ in scaled components, with its first differentiated asymptotic. For a perturbation $fb$ in dimension three, the mass-flux covector integrand with test function $V$ simplifies to $2(f\,\,\mathrm dV-V\,\,\mathrm df)$. With $f=4cr^{-3}$, $V=V_0=\sqrt{1+r^2}$, and $\nu_b=\sqrt{1+r^2}\,\partial_r$, its normal component is $$2\bigl(f\partial_{\nu_b}V_0
       -V_0\partial_{\nu_b}f\bigr)
 =32cr^{-2}+24cr^{-4}.$$ The error terms give zero limiting flux. Integrating over a coordinate sphere of area $4\pi r^2$ and dividing by $16\pi$ gives $p_0-m_0=8c$. Since $p_0\to m_0>0$ as $\epsilon\to0$, $$m_{\mathrm{AH}}=p_0=m_0+8c=\mathcal M=b_*(A_\epsilon)$$ for sufficiently small $\epsilon$, by <a href="#ads:eq:radial-mass-at-boundary" data-reference-type="eqref" data-reference="ads:eq:radial-mass-at-boundary">[ads:eq:radial-mass-at-boundary]</a>–<a href="#ads:eq:radial-mass-at-infinity" data-reference-type="eqref" data-reference="ads:eq:radial-mass-at-infinity">[ads:eq:radial-mass-at-infinity]</a>. This argument includes $C_q=0$. In that case one can also apply the comparison estimate of Lemma <a href="#ads:lem:inverse" data-reference-type="ref" data-reference="ads:lem:inverse">179</a> to $\phi_\epsilon-1$ and conclude $\phi_\epsilon\equiv1$ directly. ◻

</details>

<details id="proof-stmt-ads-prop-radial-2"><summary>Proof of stmt-ads-prop-radial</summary>

*Completion of the proof of Theorem <a href="#ads:thm:main" data-reference-type="ref" data-reference="ads:thm:main">176</a>.* Fix the seed and the given solution branch. If $q$ is radial, Proposition <a href="#ads:prop:radial" data-reference-type="ref" data-reference="ads:prop:radial">198</a> gives exact equality on a sufficiently small parameter interval. Suppose henceforth that $q$ is not radial. Proposition <a href="#ads:prop:quadratic" data-reference-type="ref" data-reference="ads:prop:quadratic">190</a> gives the actual expansion $$\mathfrak D_q(\epsilon)=c_2[q]\epsilon^2+o(\epsilon^2),
 \qquad c_2[q]\geq0.$$ If $c_2[q]>0$, this proves strict positivity of the deficit for every sufficiently small positive $\epsilon$.

If $c_2[q]=0$, Corollary <a href="#ads:cor:kernel" data-reference-type="ref" data-reference="ads:cor:kernel">191</a> gives $q=Q(v)$ with $Lv=0$ and with only constant and linear angular modes. Its linear part is nonzero, for otherwise $q$ would be radial. These homogeneous modes have the stronger differentiated decay needed for the actual fourth-order expansion in Proposition <a href="#ads:prop:expansions" data-reference-type="ref" data-reference="ads:prop:expansions">183</a>. Proposition <a href="#ads:prop:quartic" data-reference-type="ref" data-reference="ads:prop:quartic">193</a> then gives $$\mathfrak D_q(\epsilon)=c_4[q]\epsilon^4+o(\epsilon^4),
 \qquad c_4[q]>0,$$ with all coefficients below order four equal to zero. Again the actual deficit is strictly positive for every sufficiently small positive $\epsilon$.

At $\epsilon=0$ the background identity $m_0=b_*(4\pi a^2)$ gives equality. The preceding alternatives exhaust all fixed seeds. Choose $\epsilon_0>0$ small enough for the applicable alternative and the given branch, with $\epsilon_0\leq\epsilon_*$. This proves the exact inequality on $0\leq\epsilon<\epsilon_0$, equality for radial seeds, and strict inequality for nonradial seeds at positive parameters in that interval. The size of the interval is allowed to depend on the fixed seed and branch; no uniform positive lower bound for $c_2$ or $c_4$ is asserted or required. ◻

</details>

  "figures": [
    {
      "caption": "The numerical comparison and the equality argument. The bound proved on the left applies to the nearby data used in the variations on the right. Rigidity is obtained from the original data.",
      "figure_id": "intro:proof-routes",
      "pdf_page": 5,
      "source_evidence": [
        {
          "anchor": "intro:proof-routes",
          "exact_quote": "The numerical comparison and the equality argument. The bound\nproved on the left applies to the nearby data used in the variations on\nthe right. Rigidity is obtained from the original data.",
          "source_object": "fig:0001"
        }
      ],
      "source_kind": "tikz_pgf",
      "tikz_pgf_source": "\\begin{tikzpicture}[\n  box/.style={draw=black!45,rounded corners=2pt,align=center,\n    text width=6.2cm,minimum height=14mm,inner sep=5pt,font=\\small},\n  arr/.style={-{Stealth[length=2mm]},thick}]\n\\node[box] (data) at (0,0) {Original data with DEC\\\\and trapped boundary};\n\\node[box] (deform) at (0,-2.2) {End reduction and deformation\\\\to a Riemannian comparison metric};\n\\node[box] (bound) at (0,-4.4) {Riemannian Penrose inequality\\\\and passage to the original bound};\n\\node[box] (equal) at (7.2,0) {Equality on the original data\\\\with the stated horizon hypotheses};\n\\node[box] (field) at (7.2,-2.2) {Area and constraint variations\\\\give a causal stationary field};\n\\node[box] (recover) at (7.2,-4.4) {Static classification and recovery\\\\of the original spacelike hypersurface};\n\\draw[arr] (data)--(deform);\n\\draw[arr] (deform)--(bound);\n\\draw[arr] (equal)--(field);\n\\draw[arr] (field)--(recover);\n\\end{tikzpicture}",
      "witness_description": "Flowchart diagram with two parallel columns of rectangular boxes connected by downward-pointing vertical arrows:\nLeft column (three boxes):\n1. \"Original data with DEC and trapped boundary\"\n   ↓\n2. \"End reduction and deformation to a Riemannian comparison metric\"\n   ↓\n3. \"Riemannian Penrose inequality and passage to the original bound\"\nRight column (three boxes):\n1. \"Equality on the original data with the stated horizon hypotheses\"\n   ↓\n2. \"Area and constraint variations give a causal stationary field\"\n   ↓\n3. \"Static classification and recovery of the original spacelike hypersurface\""
    },
    {
      "caption": "The charged upper-area inequality for $Q > 0$. For $r ≤ Q$, it requires only $m ≥ Q$. For $r ≥ Q$, its boundary is $m = (r+Q^{2}/r)/2$. The mass-lower-bound expression must therefore be restricted to this latter branch.",
      "figure_id": "fig:charged-region",
      "pdf_page": 94,
      "source_evidence": [
        {
          "anchor": "fig:charged-region",
          "exact_quote": "The charged upper-area inequality for $Q>0$.\nFor $r\\le Q$, it requires only $m\\ge Q$.\nFor $r\\ge Q$, its boundary is $m=(r+Q^2/r)/2$.\nThe mass-lower-bound expression must therefore be restricted to this latter branch.",
          "source_object": "fig:0002"
        }
      ],
      "source_kind": "tikz_pgf",
      "tikz_pgf_source": "\\begin{tikzpicture}[x=1.5cm,y=1.5cm]\n \\fill[black!7] (0,1)--(1,1)--\n   plot[domain=1:4,samples=80] (\\x,{(\\x+1/\\x)/2})\n   --(4,2.6)--(0,2.6)--cycle;\n \\draw[->] (0,0)--(4.25,0) node[right] {$r/Q$};\n \\draw[->] (0,0)--(0,2.85) node[above] {$m/Q$};\n \\draw[thick] (0,1)--(1,1);\n \\draw[thick,domain=1:4,samples=80] plot (\\x,{(\\x+1/\\x)/2});\n \\draw[densely dotted] (1,0)--(1,2.6);\n \\draw (1,.04)--(1,-.04) node[below] {$1$};\n \\draw (.04,1)--(-.04,1) node[left] {$1$};\n \\node at (1.95,2.15) {allowed region};\n \\node[below right] at (2.4,1.18) {$m=\\tfrac12(r+Q^2/r)$};\n \\node[above] at (.5,1) {$m=Q$};\n\\end{tikzpicture}",
      "witness_description": "2D plot with horizontal axis labeled $r/Q$ and vertical axis labeled $m/Q$, both ending with arrows. A tick mark 1 is on the vertical axis and 1 on the horizontal axis, with a vertical dashed line connecting $r/Q = 1$ to $(1,1)$. The lower boundary of the allowed region consists of a horizontal line segment from $(0,1)$ to $(1,1)$ labeled \"$m = Q$\" above it, and a curved branch starting at $(1,1)$ bending upward and to the right labeled \"$m = \\frac{1}{2}(r+Q^2/r)$\". The domain above this piecewise boundary is labeled \"allowed region\"."
    },
